docs.title: 1.1. DQ-lang Project Introduction
docs.text:
DQ is a general-purpose and human-friendly programming language.

General-purpose, because it is intended to cover many use cases, including scripts and tools, server applications, embedded applications, GUI applications, and games.

Human-friendly, because DQ syntax and library interfaces are designed to make program source code easy to read and write for people.

The DQ-lang Project is being developed to offer a serious alternative to Python and C++. The DQ language mostly uses established concepts from other programming languages. Its syntax combines elements of Pascal, Python, and C/C++. The name reflects these influences: D is the letter after C, and Q is the letter after P.

DQ source files (.dq files) are translated into directly executable machine code, so DQ applications run very fast, matching the speed of programs written in C++ or Rust. For machine code generation, the DQ compiler uses the well-tested LLVM framework, which also supports different architectures and targets, such as x86, ARM32, ARM64, ARM Cortex-M, RISC-V, and WebAssembly (WASM). The DQ compiler allows you to create applications for Windows, Linux, and bare-metal targets, including through cross-compilation.

docs.title: 1.1.1 DQ Language Self-Introduction
docs.text:
use print

func *Main():
    PrintLn('DQ Short Introduction')

    if 3 / 2 == 1.5  and 3 div 2 == 1  and uint32(3) - uint32(5) < 0:
        PrintLn('DQ is human friendly.')
    endif

    var sarr : [5]int = [2, 3, 5, 7, 11]
    Print('Static array:')
    for i : int = 0 count sarr.length:
        Print(' {}', [sarr[i]])
    endfor
    PrintLn()

    var darr : [*]float = [2, 3.14, 7 / 3]
    darr.Append(13 / 2)
    darr.PopFirst()
    Print('Dynamic array:')
    for f :? in darr:
        Print(' {}', [f])
    endfor
    PrintLn()

    var ds : str = 'This is a'
    ds.Add(' dynamic string.')
    var dpos : int = ds.IndexOf('dynamic')
    ds.Insert(dpos, 'heap allocated ')
    PrintLn(ds)

    PrintLn('String slicing: ds[2:6]="{}", ds[$end-5:]="{}"',
        [ds[2:6], ds[$end-5:]] )

    var x : int = 7
    PrintLn('original x = {}', [x])
    var xptr : ^int = %x   // %x = address of x
    ref xref = x
    xref = 42
    if xptr^ == x  and xref == x:
        PrintLn('Supports pointers and references. x = {}', [x])
    endif

    PrintLn('DQ has many more features. See further examples.');
endfunc

Source: https://github.com/nvitya/dq-lang/blob/main/examples/dq_intro_1.dq

This example covers only a small subset of the capabilities of the DQ language. One very important feature is support for objects with inheritance and virtual functions. For a quick example, see A Short Object Demo in the Objects and Properties chapter.

For a more complete list of features, read Features and Goals.

For a complete description of the DQ language, see the DQ Language Reference.

docs.title: 1.1.2 Getting Started
docs.text: To get the DQ compiler and start experimenting with the language, follow the instructions on the Getting Started page.

docs.title: 1.1.3 Project State
docs.text:
Compiled DQ programs for Windows and Linux use the standard, well-tested C library for low-level system functions. With the reliable LLVM code generator and extensive compiler testing, the DQ compiler and its produced applications are already fairly stable.

During the development of DQ applications, bugs and language defects have been detected and fixed. AI assistance is used - under strict supervision - in compiler development, making it possible to fix bugs or implement changes very quickly.

Using DQ in critical applications is not yet recommended because it has not undergone sufficient field testing. (The DQ-lang project started in January 2026 and became ready for application development only around September 2026.) Every new project must start somewhere, and building a supporting community takes time.

You can already use DQ for less critical applications and tools, and I recommend doing so.

The DQ standard packages offer user-friendly, object-based interfaces for several programming tasks, including database handling, threading, HTTP serving, and JSON handling. Since DQ is a new language (2026), library support is still incomplete. DQ has a very flexible module system and a simple way to import functions from external C-compatible libraries, which opens unlimited possibilities for application development.

docs.title: 1.3. Getting Started
docs.text: This chapter takes you from installing DQ to running your first program. You need the DQ compiler and a text editor. Visual Studio Code is recommended for syntax highlighting, compiler diagnostics, and running programs from the editor.

docs.title: 1.3.1 Install DQ
docs.text:
Download a compiler package for your operating system from the DQ releases page. Choose a compiler archive from the release assets; the GitHub Source code archives contain the project sources rather than ready-to-run compiler tools.

Follow the setup guide for your system, then return here:

  • Linux Development Environment: installing a release, setting up your shell and editor, and adding external libraries.
  • Windows Development Environment: extracting the Windows package, configuring PATH, setting up the editor, and adding external libraries.

The two main tools are:

Tool Purpose dq-comp Compiles DQ source files and links them into an executable. dq-run Compiles a DQ program and immediately runs it.

In a terminal with your DQ environment configured, check that the compiler is available:

dq-comp --version

The command should print the installed compiler version.

docs.title: 1.3.2 Write Your First Program
docs.text:
Create a directory for your experiments. In that directory, use your editor to create a plain text file named hello.dq. The .dq extension identifies DQ source code. On Windows, make sure the file is not accidentally saved as hello.dq.txt.

Put this code in the file and save it:

use print

func *Main():
    PrintLn("Hello from DQ!")
endfunc

The program has three main parts:

  • use print makes the standard package's printing functions available.
  • func *Main(): begins the program's entry function. Execution starts here after the runtime has initialized the program.
  • PrintLn(...) writes text to the terminal and ends the output line. endfunc closes the function.

Text inside double quotes is a string: a sequence of characters representing text. The indentation makes the function body easier to read.

docs.title: 1.3.3 Compile and Run
docs.text:
Open a terminal in the directory containing hello.dq and run:

dq-run hello.dq

The program prints:

Hello from DQ!

dq-run invokes the compiler, creates an executable, and starts it. If compilation reports an error, correct the indicated line in your source file, save it, and run the command again.

You can also compile and run as separate steps. On Linux:

dq-comp -g -O0 hello.dq
./hello

On Windows, in Command Prompt or PowerShell:

dq-comp -g -O0 hello.dq
.\hello.exe

The compiler produces hello on Linux and hello.exe on Windows. The -g option includes debugging information, and -O0 disables optimization so the generated code is easier to debug. When called without compiler options, dq-run uses both options automatically.

docs.title: 1.3.4 Print Values
docs.text:
Formatting lets you insert values into a message. Each {} is replaced by the next value in the list between [ and ]:

use print

func *Main():
    var name : str = "DQ"
    var count : int = 3
    PrintLn("Hello, {}! Count = {}", [name, count])
endfunc

Here, var declares a variable: a named place to store a value. str is a string type, and int is an integer type for whole numbers. This program prints Hello, DQ! Count = 3.

docs.title: 1.3.5 Program Arguments and Exit Status
docs.text:
Programs can receive arguments from the command line. Save this example as args.dq:

use print

func *Main():
    for i : int = 1 count ArgCount() - 1:
        PrintLn("Argument {}: {}", [i, ArgStr(i)])
    endfor
endfunc

Run it with two arguments:

dq-run args.dq -- one two

The output is:

Argument 1: one
Argument 2: two

ArgCount() includes the program name at index 0, so this example starts at index 1. ArgStr(i) reads the argument at that index. These functions are available through the implicit sys runtime interface.

Compiler options go before the source filename. Program arguments go after it; the optional -- separator makes the boundary explicit.

*Main has no return value. The program normally exits with status 0, which means success. Set the global exit_code variable to another value before leaving *Main to report failure, for example exit_code = 1.

docs.title: 1.3.6 Continue Learning
docs.text:
Read the DQ Programming Language overview for the language topics in book order. The Standard Packages provide printing, file access, JSON handling, networking, and other services.

For build options and larger programs, continue with Compiler Usage and Options and Project Files.

docs.title: 2. DQ Programming Language
docs.text:
This chapter is the complete DQ language reference, organized from basic syntax to platform access. Each topic introduces its concepts, then describes syntax, type rules, lifetime constraints, and examples in the same chapter.

If DQ is new to you, begin with Getting Started to install the compiler and run a program. This reference describes DQ 0.93.16. DQ is still under development, so match the documentation to your compiler version.

Most code blocks illustrate declarations or statements in their surrounding context; examples containing func *Main() are complete programs unless they explicitly import companion files. Copy a complete program into a .dq file and run it with dq-run filename.dq. Assembly examples identify their target.

Contents

  • Basic Syntax
  • Basic Types and Conversions
  • Variables, Constants, References, and Scope
  • Expressions and Operators
  • Statements and Control Flow
  • Functions
  • Character and String Types
  • String Functions
  • Text Formatting
  • Arrays and Slices
  • Enumerations
  • Structures and Unions
  • Pointers
  • Objects and Properties
  • Memory Management and Autofree
  • Exceptions and Error Handling
  • anyvalue
  • Modules and Packages
  • Attributes
  • Compiler Directives
  • C Interoperability
  • Assembly Functions

docs.title: 2.1. Basic Syntax
docs.text:
A DQ program is text stored in one or more .dq files. Each file is a module. A function groups statements that perform a task; *Main is the entry function of an ordinary application. For installation and the compile/run commands, see Getting Started.

use print

func *Main():
    // A variable stores a value under a name.
    var count : int = 3
    PrintLn("Count = {}", [count])
endfunc

use print imports printing functions. The colon starts a function body and endfunc closes it. A newline normally finishes a statement.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Source Files and Names
docs.text:
Source text can contain Unicode text in strings and comments. Names are case-sensitive: count, Count, and COUNT are different identifiers. Identifiers start with an ASCII letter or _ and continue with ASCII letters, digits, or _. Unicode identifiers are not supported.

Keywords are lowercase, for example func, var, if, and endfunc. Built-in names such as SizeOf, Ord, Round, and Object keep their documented case. Use descriptive names; the language does not require a particular naming prefix.

A .dq file is a source module. .dqh files conventionally hold public header fragments and .dqi files hold other included fragments. Textual includes are explained in Compiler Directives; module imports are explained in Modules and Packages.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Statements, Whitespace, and Blocks
docs.text:
Spaces and tabs separate tokens. Indentation makes nesting clear, but does not create or close blocks. A semicolon explicitly ends a statement and is needed between multiple statements on the same physical line:

var x : int = 1
var y : int = 2; x += y

Expressions can continue across lines inside balanced parentheses or brackets. Use the matching closer for each colon block: endif, endwhile, endfor, endfunc, endobject, endstruct, endunion, or endtry as appropriate. Supported constructs also allow braces:

func Twice(value : int) -> int {
    return value * 2
}

A block must consistently use its chosen closing style. Assembly function bodies require the colon/endfunc style. This book normally uses named closers.

docs.title: 2.1.3 Comments
docs.text:
// starts a comment through the end of the line. /* and */ enclose a block comment. Comments act as whitespace; comment markers inside a string are text.

// A line comment.
var count : int = 3 /* a comment between tokens */

docs.title: 2.1.4 Literals
docs.text:
A literal writes a value directly in source code:

Kind Examples Whole number 42, 0xFF Floating point 3.14, 2e3 Boolean true, false Empty reference/pointer nil Text "hello", 'hello', "/" Character '/', '€' Array [1, 2, 3] Default aggregate {}

A leading minus is an operator: -42 negates the literal 42. Numeric literals receive the type required by their context; there is no need to add .0 merely to initialize a floating-point variable with a whole number.

Double quotes always denote text. Single quotes containing exactly one Unicode scalar denote a wchar; single quotes containing zero or multiple scalars denote text. Consequently, use "/" when comparing a string with one-character text.

Common escapes are \n, \r, \t, \\, \", and \'. \xNN inserts a byte using exactly two hexadecimal digits. Triple-quoted text spans lines:

var message : str = """
    first line
      indented line
    """

You can use either triple double quotes or triple single quotes. The text has no extra empty line at the start or end. DQ removes the spaces used to line up the text with the closing quotes and keeps any extra indentation. Escape sequences still work. See Multiline Text for examples showing the resulting text. For character and string representations, see Character and String Types. Byte and Unicode operations are described in String Functions.

docs.title: 2.1.5 Declarations and Expressions
docs.text:
The usual declaration forms are var name : Type = value, const NAME : Type = value, and type Name = Type. A colon introduces a type annotation in a declaration. = assigns a value; == compares values. Assignment is a statement without resulting a value. Assignment is not chainable so a = b = 1 is invalid (compiler error).

An expression computes a value, such as 2 + 3 or count > 0. Conditions require bool: write count <> 0, using a number (or anything else than bool) as a condition is not allowed. The inequality operator is <>; != is not accepted.

Read more about operators and expressions in the chapter Expressions and Operators

docs.title: 2.1.6 Attributes and Directives
docs.text: [[...]] attaches attributes to declarations. # starts compiler directives, including conditional compilation and source inclusion. They have different roles from executable statements; see Attributes and Compiler Directives.

docs.title: 2.2. Basic Types and Conversions
docs.text:
A type describes the values a variable can store and the operations allowed on it. DQ checks types during compilation. It distinguishes numbers, Boolean values, characters, text, pointers, and compound types rather than converting freely between unrelated categories.

use print

func *Main():
    var count : int = 3
    var ratio : float = count / 2
    var ready : bool = count > 0
    PrintLn("{} {} {}", [count, ratio, ready])
endfunc

docs.title: 2.2.1 Scalar Types
docs.text:
Type Values and representation bool true or false; not an integer. int, uint (1) Signed/unsigned integers as wide as a pointer. int8, int16, int32, int64 (1) Signed integers of the specified bit width. uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64 (1) Unsigned integers of the specified bit width. byte Alias for uint8. Preferred instead of uint8 float32, float64 Floating-point numbers of the specified width. float (2) Floating-point type chosen by the target. float32 on the single-precision FPU targets arm_m4f-bare, arm_m33f-bare, and arm_m7f-bare. It is float64 on other current targets, including arm_m7fd-bare and WebAssembly. char One unsigned 8-bit byte or UTF-8 code unit. char16 One unsigned 16-bit UTF-16 code unit. wchar One unsigned 32-bit Unicode scalar value. pointer Generic address with no pointee type.

Notes:

(1): For an unsigned integer with N bits, the range is 0 through 2^N - 1. For a signed integer, it is -2^(N-1) through 2^(N-1) - 1.int/uint are 32 bits on 32-bit targets and 64 bits on 64-bit targets.Choose a fixed-width type when a file format, protocol, or external ABI requires it.

(2): Use explicit floating-point widths avoid making a binary interface depend on the target default.

docs.title: 2.2.2 Other Type Categories
docs.text:
Form Purpose Chapter str, rostr, strslice, embstr(N) Text with different storage and borrowing rules. Character and String Types [N]T, [*]T, []T Fixed arrays, dynamic arrays, borrowed array views. Arrays enum A distinct set of named values. Enumerations struct, union Direct field storage or overlapping field storage. Structures and Unions ^T An address pointing to a T. Pointers object, Object Object reference types; Object is the common object base type. Objects func(...) A function reference with a particular signature. Functions anyvalue A boxed scalar/text value for heterogeneous APIs. anyvalue

autofree T qualifies object-reference and pointer types with automatic cleanup; it does not change the underlying pointer representation. See Memory Management and Autofree.

docs.title: 2.2.3 Type Aliases
docs.text:
type introduces another name for an existing type:

type TCount = uint32
type FTransform = func(value : int) -> int

An alias does not create a new, incompatible type. In contrast, two separately declared enumerations, structures, or unions remain distinct even if their contents look identical.

docs.title: 2.2.4 Numeric Conversions
docs.text:
Whole-number literals are contextual. Write var scale : float = 2 or var size : uint8 = 3 directly. Integer expressions can convert to another integer storage width; narrowing keeps the low bits. Integer-to-floating-point conversion is available where the expected numeric type requires it.

var small : uint8 = 250
small = small + 10       // 260 is stored as 4 in eight bits
var real : float64 = small

A destination does not retroactively widen the operands of an expression. The calculation width and signedness rules are explained in Expressions and Operators.

Floating-point values do not implicitly convert to integers. Use Round, Floor, Ceil, or Trunc to choose the rounding operation:

var value : float = 3 / 2
var rounded : int = Round(value)
var downward : int = Floor(value)
var upward : int = Ceil(value)
var truncated : int = Trunc(value)

Type-call syntax such as uint16(value) requests a defined explicit conversion. The expression as Type spelling uses the same conversion rules. A cast is not a substitute for a rounding operation, range check, or valid memory address.

docs.title: 2.2.5 Boolean Isolation
docs.text: Numbers and Boolean values are separate. Conditions and logical operators take bool; if count: and int(true) are not numeric conversion shortcuts. Convert through explicit program logic, for example iif(ready, 1, 0) or n <> 0.

docs.title: 2.2.6 Characters, Enumerations, and Pointers
docs.text:
Character types are distinct from integers. Prefer the read-only ch.ord property to obtain a character code as int; Ord(ch) is equivalent. char(code), char16(code), and wchar(code) request explicit conversions. Checked IntToChar/IntToWchar helpers provide raising and fallback forms. A constant character literal below 256 can initialize a char directly. Perform character arithmetic on its integer code, for example char(ch.ord + 1).

Enums use Ord, .ord, FromOrd, and TryFromOrd; ordinary integer casts do not bypass enum membership checks. See Enumerations.

Integer/address and unrelated pointer conversions require explicit casts. Converting an address does not establish its lifetime, alignment, or ownership.

docs.title: 2.2.7 Size and Layout Queries
docs.text: SizeOf(Type) and SizeOf(value) report storage size in bytes. OffsetOf(Type, field) reports a structure or union member's byte offset. Use these queries rather than assuming pointer widths or padding. Len(value) and .length measure logical array elements or text bytes, not the total storage size.

docs.title: 2.3. Variables, Constants, References, and Scope
docs.text:
A variable names storage whose value can change. A constant names a value known during compilation. A reference gives another name to existing storage. A scope controls where a declaration can be found.

use print

const LIMIT : int = 10

func *Main():
    var count : int = 2
    ref alias = count
    alias += 3
    PrintLn("{} / {}", [count, LIMIT]) // 5 / 10
endfunc

docs.title: 2.3.1 Variables and Initialization
docs.text:
Declare a variable with var name : Type, normally followed by = initializer. An assignment replaces its current value:

var count : int = 0
count = 3
count += 1

Initialize scalar locals before reading them. A declaration such as var count : int reserves storage but does not make its value readable; the compiler tracks definite assignment across branches and reports uninitialized uses. A function result must likewise be assigned on every normal exit path.

Sized embedded strings are initialized automatically: var s : embstr(32) starts empty and can be read or appended to immediately. See Embedded Strings.

Global storage is zero/default-initialized before program startup. Types with managed lifetimes, including dynamic arrays and autofree references, have their own empty/default initialization and cleanup rules. Use an explicit initializer when the intended value matters. {} explicitly zero/default-initializes a supported aggregate such as a structure or fixed array.

Object fixed storage uses <- rather than =; see Objects and Properties.

docs.title: 2.3.2 Restricted Type Inference
docs.text:
Write ? in place of a declared type when an initializer independently supplies an eligible concrete typed pointer, structure, or object-reference type:

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

var point : SPoint = {10, 20}
var copy : ? = point
var address : ? = %point

Inference requires = and preserves the initializer's static type. Numeric, Boolean, text, enum, raw pointer, and other unlisted types are not inferred. In particular, var n : ? = 3 and var p : ? = nil are errors. The separate array notation [?]T infers a fixed array's length, not its element type.

For local variables initialized by new or TryCast(...), the type annotation can be omitted entirely. For example, var child = TryCast(OChild, base) infers OChild from the first argument and creates an ordinary reference without autofree. See Checked Object Casts.

new autofree T provides a shorthand for declaring an autofree variable; ordinary ? inference does not add autofree. See Memory Management and Autofree.

docs.title: 2.3.3 Local References
docs.text:
ref name = existing_value binds an alias to addressable compatible storage. Writes through the alias update the original storage. The binding must remain valid throughout the alias's use. A reference is not a nullable pointer value.

A reference cannot extend the lifetime of a local, a temporary, an array element, or a property result. Function reference parameter modes are described in Functions.

docs.title: 2.3.4 Constants
docs.text:
const requires a compile-time constant initializer:

const BUFFER_SIZE : int = 4096
const HALF_BUFFER : int = BUFFER_SIZE div 2

Related constants can share a declared type:

const(uint32):
    FLASH_BASE = 0x08000000
    FLASH_END  = FLASH_BASE + 0x7FFF
    SRAM_BASE  = 0x20000000
endconst

The group does not create another scope. Later constants can use earlier ones. Restricted ? inference follows the variable rules and does not remove the constant-expression requirement; a grouped const(Type) header cannot use ?.

FirstInt, FirstFloat, and FirstBool provide optional constant fallbacks; see Compiler Directives.

docs.title: 2.3.5 Lexical Scope and Declaration Order
docs.text:
Lookup starts in the innermost active scope and proceeds outward. A declaration must be visible before a use that needs it. Forward declarations explicitly reserve function or object names when their implementations come later. Declarations in an inner block are not visible after that block finishes.

Shadowing a visible name can produce a warning. Choosing distinct names makes it easier to tell which value an expression reads. A local reference and an ordinary variable follow the same scope visibility rules.

docs.title: 2.3.6 Module and Object Visibility
docs.text:
Module declarations before implementation are public. Declarations after it are private unless they implement an earlier public declaration. Imported symbols participate in unqualified lookup according to the use modifiers.

@.Name explicitly selects the current module's global scope. @module.Name selects an imported module namespace. Object methods prioritize members and require qualification for outside value symbols unless an allowed method-local use makes them available. Type names remain available for type annotations and casts.

Object members have public, protected, and private visibility; their rules are in Objects and Properties. See Modules and Packages for import aliases, merged symbols, and reexports.

docs.title: 2.4. Expressions and Operators
docs.text:
An expression computes a typed value, such as count + 1, ready and valid, or a function call. Some expressions also identify storage that can be assigned.

use print

func *Main():
    var ratio : float = 3 / 2
    var quotient : int = 7 div 3
    var remainder : int = -7 rem 3
    var modulo : int = -7 mod 3
    PrintLn("{}, {}, {}, {}", [ratio, quotient, remainder, modulo])
endfunc

This prints 1.5, 2, -1, 2.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Assignments
docs.text:
= stores a value in an assignable destination. The destination must be writable, and the value must be compatible with its type. Use == to compare values for equality.

var count : int = 3
count = 10
count += 2       // count is now 12
count =div= 3    // count is now 4

Modify-assignment reads the destination's current value, performs an operation, and stores the result back. The destination must therefore already be initialized and both readable and writable.

Modify-assignment statements are +=, -=, *=, /=, <<=, >>=, &=, |=, =xor=, =div=, =rem=, and =mod=. A word operator uses the leading = spelling shown here.

Assignment is a statement and does not produce a value. It cannot be used as a Boolean condition or nested to create chained assignments such as a = b = 1. Assignment and modify-assignment are outside the operator precedence table.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Arithmetic and Comparison
docs.text: The tables below use integer for any signed or unsigned integer type, and number for an integer or floating-point value. bool, characters, enums, and pointers are separate categories; they are not implicitly treated as numbers.

docs.title: 2.4.2.1 Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
Operator Operands Result Meaning + Two numbers Common numeric type Addition. - Two numbers Common numeric type; integer subtraction is signed Subtraction. * Two numbers Common numeric type Multiplication. / Two numbers Floating point Floating-point division, including for two integers. div Two integers Common integer type Integer division, truncating toward zero. rem Two integers Common integer type Division remainder; a nonzero result has the dividend's sign. mod Two integers Common integer type Nonnegative modulo, including with a negative divisor.

+ also concatenates compatible text into a str; see String Functions. Typed pointers support separate address arithmetic described in Pointers.

docs.title: 2.4.2.2 Numeric Result Types
docs.text:
For ordinary numeric operations, DQ first converts operands to a common type:

Operand types Common type Two signed integers Signed integer at the wider operand width. Two unsigned integers Unsigned integer at the wider operand width. One signed and one unsigned integer Signed integer at the wider operand width, regardless of operand order. One integer and one floating-point value The floating-point operand's type. Two floating-point values The wider floating-point type.

There are two arithmetic exceptions: integer subtraction always uses a signed result at the wider width, and / always returns floating point. Dividing two integers produces the target's default float type. Shifts have their own rule: the result keeps the left operand's integer type.

var small : uint8 = 10
var signed_value : int16 = -3
var sum : int16 = small + signed_value  // 7; reversing the operands keeps int16
var difference : int8 = small - uint8(12) // -2, although both operands are unsigned
var ratio : float = 3 / 2               // 1.5

A common signed type is not necessarily large enough to represent every value of an unsigned operand of the same width. Conversion retains its bits; it does not add a spare sign bit. Choose a wider type explicitly when the full unsigned range must participate in a signed calculation. Calculation widths and overflow are explained in Integer Calculations.

docs.title: 2.4.2.3 Division, Remainder, and Modulo
docs.text:
/ performs floating-point division. div instead discards the fractional part toward zero, so 7 div 3 is 2 and -7 div 3 is -2.

rem is the remainder associated with that truncating division. For valid integer division, it satisfies a rem b == a - ((a div b) * b). mod starts with that remainder and, when it is negative, adds the magnitude of the divisor to make it nonnegative:

a b a div b a rem b a mod b 7 3 2 1 1 -7 3 -2 -1 2 7 -3 -2 1 1 -7 -3 2 -1 2

For a nonzero divisor, the modulo result is between zero, inclusive, and the divisor's magnitude, exclusive. This is useful for wrapping a possibly negative position into a positive range:

var position : int = -1
var slot : int = position mod 8  // 7

DQ uses rem, not %, for integer remainder. % obtains an address. div, rem, and mod reject floating-point operands; use an explicit rounding operation when an integer calculation is intended. Integer division by zero and signed minimum divided by -1 have no defined result; guard these cases.

docs.title: 2.4.2.4 Comparison Operators
docs.text:
Every comparison returns bool.

Operator Operands Meaning == Compatible values Equality. <> Compatible values Inequality. <, <=, >, >= Numbers, matching character types, values of the same enum type, or compatible text values Less than, less than or equal, greater than, greater than or equal.

Numeric comparisons use the common numeric type rules above. Two integers compare as signed if either is signed, and as unsigned if both are unsigned. If either operand is floating point, comparison is floating point.

Boolean equality requires two Boolean values. Numbers are not converted to Boolean values for comparison: true == 1 is invalid. != is not accepted. Enums compare only with the same enum type; ordering follows their ordinal values. Character comparison follows character codes, without case folding.

var count : int = 3
var limit : float = 3.5
var below_limit : bool = count < limit  // true: numeric conversion is allowed
var ready : bool = true
var unchanged : bool = ready == true   // true

Compatible pointers and object references support identity comparisons with == and <>, including comparison with nil; this does not compare pointed-to contents. Compatible text values support equality and ordering by unsigned byte value, with a shorter prefix coming first. Different string types can be compared; see String Comparison. General array sequence equality is not implicit. Dynamic arrays and slices can be compared with [] to test emptiness.

docs.title: 2.4.2.5 Range Comparisons
docs.text:
DQ supports a chain of two ordering comparisons with three operands. Both comparisons must point in the same direction:

Direction Supported forms Ascending x < y < z, x <= y < z, x < y <= z, x <= y <= z Descending x > y > z, x >= y > z, x > y >= z, x >= y >= z 
var temperature : int = 20
var comfortable : bool = 18 <= temperature < 25  // true
var within_limits : bool = 25 > temperature >= 18 // true

lower <= value < upper tests the same bounds as (lower <= value) and (value < upper), but evaluates the middle expression only once. The final endpoint is evaluated only if the first comparison succeeds:

use print

var calls : int = 0

func MiddleValue() -> int:
    ++calls
    return 2
endfunc

func *Main():
    var inside : bool = 1 < MiddleValue() < 3 // calls becomes 1
    var skipped : bool = 3 < 2 < MiddleValue() // the function is not called
    PrintLn("{} {} {}", [inside, skipped, calls]) // true false 1
endfunc

Longer chains such as w < x < y < z, direction changes such as x < y > z, and equality chains such as a == b == c are invalid. Write separate comparisons joined with and when the condition needs those forms.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Integer Calculations
docs.text:
DQ integer arithmetic uses fixed widths and has no overflow checks. The widest operand determines the calculation width. A whole-number literal has the normal int calculation type and can widen a mixed calculation:

var left : uint8 = 250
var right : uint8 = 10
var narrow_sum : int = left + right // 4: the calculation uses eight bits
var wide_sum : int = left + 10     // 260: the literal makes this an int calculation
left = left + 10                   // 4: storing into uint8 keeps the low bits

The destination does not widen a calculation retroactively. Signed narrowing interprets the retained bits as a two's-complement value. The same rules apply to compile-time and runtime expressions.

Subtraction always produces a signed result at the widest operand width, even when both operands are unsigned. Thus uint(3) - uint(5) is signed -2 at the native width. An assignment to unsigned storage reinterprets the retained bits.

docs.title: 2.4.4.1 Logical Operators
docs.text:
Operator Operands Result Meaning not value One bool bool Reverse the Boolean value. left and right Two bool values bool True when both operands are true. left or right Two bool values bool True when at least one operand is true.

and and or short-circuit. and evaluates its right operand only if the left is true; or evaluates its right operand only if the left is false. This allows a condition to guard a later operation:

func IsPositive(address : ^int) -> bool:
    return address <> nil and address^ > 0
endfunc

For IsPositive(nil), the result is false and address^ is not evaluated. An or condition can supply the opposite guard:

var address : ^int = nil
var missing_or_zero : bool = address == nil or address^ == 0 // true

There is no numeric truthiness: not 0 and 1 and 2 are invalid. Use a comparison such as count <> 0 to produce a Boolean value.

docs.title: 2.4.4.2 Bitwise Operators
docs.text:
Bitwise operators work on integer bits, not Boolean truth values. They require integer operands and do not implicitly round floating-point values.

Operator Operands Result Meaning ~value One integer Operand's integer type Complement every bit. left & right Two integers Common integer type Set bits present in both operands. left \| right Two integers Common integer type Set bits present in either operand. left xor right Two integers Common integer type Set bits present in exactly one operand. value << count Two integers Left operand's type Shift left, filling low bits with zeroes. value >> count Two integers Left operand's type Shift right; signed values extend the sign bit, unsigned values fill with zeroes.

For &, |, and xor, signedness and width follow the common integer rules. For shifts, the count does not change the left operand's type or signedness. The count must be nonnegative and smaller than that type's bit width. Bits shifted out are discarded; shifts do not report overflow.

var a : uint8 = 0x0C       // 00001100
var b : uint8 = 0x0A       // 00001010
var both : uint8 = a & b   // 00001000 = 8
var either : uint8 = a | b // 00001110 = 14
var different : uint8 = a xor b // 00000110 = 6
var inverted : uint8 = ~a  // 11110011 = 243
var shifted : uint8 = a << 1 // 00011000 = 24; result still has type uint8

To test whether any flag bits are set, compare the masked integer with zero:

var flags : uint = 0x12
var mask : uint = 0x02
var enabled : bool = flags & mask <> 0 // true

Bitwise operations bind more tightly than arithmetic and comparison. flags & mask <> 0 therefore means (flags & mask) <> 0. Logical and and or bind more loosely than comparisons. Neither & nor | short-circuits.

docs.title: 2.4.5 Unary and Storage Operations
docs.text:
A unary operator acts on one operand. Most are written before it; pointer dereference is written after it:

Form Operand Result Meaning -value A number Same floating-point type, or signed integer of the operand's width Numerical negation. not value bool bool Logical negation. ~value An integer Same integer type Bitwise complement. %value Addressable storage of type T ^T Obtain its address. address^ A typed pointer ^T The referenced T Access the value at that address.

Negating an unsigned integer produces a signed result at the same width. Like other fixed-width integer calculations, this can overflow when the mathematical result does not fit. Widen the operand before negation when necessary:

var magnitude : uint8 = 7
var negative : int8 = -magnitude // -7
var value : int = 10
var address : ^int = %value
address^ = 42                   // value becomes 42

The prefix ^ in ^int is a type designator, not an expression operator. ^int means pointer to int, and ^^int means pointer to pointer to int. The postfix ^ in address^ instead dereferences a pointer value. % requires an addressable operand; it cannot obtain the address of a literal or a property.

Prefix ++value and --value update an assignable number or typed pointer as statements. They produce no value and do not introduce C-style postfix increment expressions.

Member access and indexing extend an expression:

Form Operand Result value.member A structure, object, or supported pointer The named field, method, or property. array[index] An array and integer index The selected element. pointer[index] A typed pointer ^T and integer offset Another ^T, offset by that many elements.

Pointer indexing does not dereference. Write pointer[index]^ to access the pointed-to element:

var values : [3]int = [10, 20, 30]
var first : ^int = %values[0]
var second : ^int = first[1] // points to values[1]
var value : int = second^   // 20

See Pointers for address arithmetic and lifetime rules, and Arrays and Slices for element access and slicing.

docs.title: 2.4.6 Explicit Conversion and Runtime Type Tests
docs.text:
Type(expression) and expression as Type request the same defined conversion. as binds at comparison precedence and cannot be chained with another comparison-level operator. Parenthesize its result before further operations.

value is OType tests an object's runtime type and returns false for nil. TryCast(TargetType, value) performs a checked object cast; see Objects and Properties. A cast does not validate an arbitrary pointer, encoding, or enum ordinal.

docs.title: 2.4.7 Inline Conditional
docs.text:
iif(condition, when_true, when_false) selects a value within an expression. It evaluates condition first, then evaluates and returns when_true if the condition is true, or when_false otherwise. The condition must have type bool.

var count : int = 0
var label : rostr = iif(count == 0, "empty", "nonempty")

Here label receives "empty". The alternatives can also be numeric or other compatible value types. For example, an integer and a floating-point alternative resolve to a floating-point result:

var use_default : bool = false
var scale : float = iif(use_default, 1, 2.5) // 2.5; true would select 1

The alternatives must resolve to a common result type under DQ's conversion rules. Numeric alternatives use the numeric type rules, and a compatible typed pointer can be paired with nil. The result must also be assignable to its destination: a floating-point result does not implicitly become an integer merely because the destination is int.

Only the selected alternative runs. This makes it possible to guard an operation that would be invalid for the other case:

func ValueOrZero(address : ^int) -> int:
    return iif(address <> nil, address^, 0)
endfunc

ValueOrZero(nil) returns 0 without dereferencing nil. Calls and other side effects in the unselected alternative do not occur. An error in the selected alternative still occurs normally; iif does not catch exceptions.

Both alternatives are parsed and type-checked, even when the condition is a constant. An unselected alternative cannot contain an unknown name or an incompatible type. The following uses are compile errors:

Invalid expression Reason iif(1, 2, 3) The condition is an integer, not bool. iif(true, 1, "text") The alternatives have no compatible common type. iif(true, 1) The false alternative is missing. iif(true, 1, 2, 3) Exactly three arguments are required.

Each alternative must produce a value; a call to a function with no result cannot serve as an alternative. Use an if statement when choosing between actions that do not produce values.

docs.title: 2.4.8 Calls and Evaluation
docs.text:
Calls use parentheses and pass arguments positionally, in declaration order. Arguments may themselves be expressions or calls. Trailing arguments can be omitted when the function declares defaults:

use print

func Subtract(left : int, right : int = 1) -> int:
    return left - right
endfunc

func *Main():
    var difference : int = Subtract(5 + 5, 3)           // 7
    var previous : int = Subtract(10)                 // 9: right defaults to 1
    var nested : int = Subtract(Subtract(10, 3), 2)    // 5
    PrintLn("{} {} {}", [difference, previous, nested])
endfunc

The first argument supplies left, and the second supplies right. Named arguments such as Subtract(right = 3, left = 10) are not supported. In the nested example, the inner call returns 7 before the outer call subtracts 2.

Arguments are evaluated before the called function is entered. Avoid relying on a relative evaluation order between independent expressions with side effects unless a construct explicitly specifies that order. When order matters, use separate statements. With Subtract defined above:

func Next(counter : ref int) -> int:
    ++counter
    return counter
endfunc

func OrderedDifference() -> int:
    var counter : int = 0
    var first : int = Next(counter)   // counter becomes 1
    var second : int = Next(counter)  // counter becomes 2
    return Subtract(first, second)    // -1
endfunc

This explicitly orders the two updates instead of depending on the argument evaluation order in Subtract(Next(counter), Next(counter)). Reference parameters such as ref int are described in Functions.

Built-ins such as Len, SizeOf, OffsetOf, Ord, Round, Defined, and FirstInt use call-like syntax but follow their own type and constant-expression rules:

var values : [3]int = [10, 20, 30]
var count : int = Len(values)       // 3 elements
var bytes : uint = SizeOf(int32)    // 4 bytes
var rounded : int = Round(3 / 2)    // 2

SizeOf accepts a type name as shown here, while an ordinary value parameter expects a value expression. Compiler Directives explains compile-time existence tests and optional constants.

docs.title: 2.4.9 Associativity
docs.text:
Associativity determines grouping when operators have the same precedence. Arithmetic and bitwise binary operators group from left to right:

var left_grouped : int = 10 - 3 - 2   // (10 - 3) - 2 = 5
var right_grouped : int = 10 - (3 - 2) // 10 - 1 = 9
var quotient : int = 20 div 3 div 2    // (20 div 3) div 2 = 3

Comparisons do not form ordinary left-associative chains. The three-operand range comparison is the specific exception described in Range Comparisons. is and as likewise do not form comparison chains; parenthesize a conversion before applying another operator at that precedence level.

Grouping does not establish a general evaluation order for independent calls with side effects. Use separate statements when their order matters, as shown in Calls and Evaluation.

docs.title: 2.4.10 Parentheses
docs.text:
(expression) groups an expression as one operand and overrides the usual precedence. Parentheses can be nested. They do not by themselves convert its type or turn a value into addressable storage.

var ordinary : int = 2 + 3 * 4    // 14
var grouped : int = (2 + 3) * 4   // 20
var divided : int = 8 * 3 div 2   // 8 * (3 div 2) = 8
var multiplied : int = (8 * 3) div 2 // 12

The last two lines illustrate DQ's division precedence: div binds more tightly than *. Bitwise operators also bind more tightly than arithmetic:

var shifted_first : int = 1 << 2 + 1 // (1 << 2) + 1 = 5
var added_first : int = 1 << (2 + 1) // 1 << 3 = 8

Use parentheses to make the intended grouping clear when an expression mixes operator groups. This is especially helpful when translating code from a language with different precedence rules.

docs.title: 2.4.11 Operator Precedence
docs.text:
From tightest to loosest binding:

Level Operators and forms 1 Literals, names, parenthesized expressions, casts, array literals, new, built-ins. 2 Calls, .member, indexing, slicing, postfix ^. 3 Address-of %, unary -, bitwise ~. 4 <<, >> 5 & 6 \|, xor 7 /, div, rem, mod 8 * 9 +, - 10 ==, <>, <, <=, >, >=, is, as 11 not 12 and 13 or

Division binds more tightly than multiplication. Bitwise operations also bind more tightly than arithmetic. Use parentheses whenever mixed operators obscure the intended grouping rather than assuming another language's precedence.

docs.title: 2.5. Statements and Control Flow
docs.text:
Statements declare storage, assign values, call functions, and choose what runs next. Conditions must be Boolean expressions. A block groups statements between : and its matching closer, or between braces where supported.

use print

func *Main():
    var total : int = 0
    for i : int = 1 to 3:
        total += i
    endfor
    if total == 6:
        PrintLn("total = {}", [total])
    endif
endfunc

docs.title: 2.5.1 Declaration and Assignment
docs.text:
var, const, type, and local ref declarations follow the rules in Variables, Constants, References, and Scope. Plain assignment uses =. Modify-assignment reads the existing value, performs an operation, and stores the result. Thus its destination must already be initialized and both readable and writable.

A property can be an assignment destination. Modify-assignment requires both a getter and setter, because the old value must be read before the update. Assignment does not produce a value.

docs.title: 2.5.2 Conditional Statements
docs.text:
var count : int = 3
if count == 0:
    PrintLn("empty")
elif count < 10:
    PrintLn("small")
else:
    PrintLn("large")
endif

Branches are considered in order; at most one body runs. elif and else are optional. Numeric values cannot serve directly as conditions.

docs.title: 2.5.3 While Loops
docs.text:
A loop repeats a group of statements, called its body. Each repetition is called an iteration. A while loop tests its condition before each iteration: if the condition is true, it runs the body and then tests the condition again. When the condition is false, execution continues after the loop. If the condition is false at the first test, the body does not run at all.

The body of a while loop is written between while ... : and endwhile:

var remaining : int = 3
while remaining > 0:
    PrintLn("{}", [remaining])
    remaining -= 1
endwhile

This loop prints 3, 2, and 1, each on a separate line. Each iteration decreases remaining by one. Once remaining reaches zero, the condition remaining > 0 is false and the loop ends.

break exits the nearest enclosing loop. continue starts its next iteration; a while loop then tests its condition again.

var number : int = 0
while number < 10:
    number += 1
    if number == 2:
        continue // Skip the rest of this iteration.
    endif
    if number == 5:
        break // Leave the loop immediately.
    endif
    PrintLn("{}", [number])
endwhile

This loop prints 1, 3, and 4, each on a separate line. continue skips the print when number is 2, and break ends the loop when it reaches 5, even though number < 10 is still true. The increment comes before continue so that number advances even when the rest of the body is skipped.

docs.title: 2.5.4 Numeric For Loops
docs.text:
A numeric for loop requires a control variable of a signed or unsigned integer type, such as int, uint, int32, or uint32. Floating-point types are not supported. A loop can declare its control variable or use an existing compatible variable. The principal forms are:

Form Meaning for i : int = first to last Increase from first through inclusive last. for i : int = first downto last Decrease through inclusive last. for i : int = first count n Run n iterations, increasing the control value. for i : int = first downcount n Run n iterations, decreasing the value. for i : int = first while condition Continue while the Boolean condition is true.

Append step amount before the colon to change the default step of one. to, downto, count, and downcount require a positive step magnitude; the loop form supplies the direction. A while form can use a negative step.

for i : int = 0 to 6 step 2:
    PrintLn("{}", [i]) // 0, 2, 4, 6
endfor

for i : int = 5 downcount 3:
    PrintLn("{}", [i]) // 5, 4, 3
endfor

for i : int = 6 while i > 0 step -2:
    PrintLn("{}", [i]) // 6, 4, 2
endfor

The initial value is evaluated once on entry. count and downcount also evaluate their iteration count once. In contrast, to and downto reevaluate their limit at each test, and the while form reevaluates its condition. The step expression is evaluated for each step. continue still performs the for loop's normal step before the next test. Avoid changing the loop's control values from inside the body; use a while loop for explicit state updates.

docs.title: 2.5.5 For-In Loops
docs.text:
A for ... in loop goes through the elements of a fixed array, slice, or dynamic array in order, from first to last. This is called iterating over the array. On each iteration, the loop variable represents the current element and the loop body runs for that element. If the array is empty, the body does not run.

var values : [3]int = [10, 20, 30]
for value :? in values:
    PrintLn("{}", [value])
endfor

for value : ref in values:
    value += 1
endfor

The first loop prints 10, 20, and 30, each on a separate line. The second loop increases each element by one, leaving values as [11, 21, 31].

:? infers an ordinary element value. : ref binds to each element's storage, so assignment changes the array. An existing variable or an explicit element type can also be used. The source must be an addressable array value.

Do not resize a dynamic array while a reference iteration variable is in use; its element addresses can become invalid. See Arrays and Slices.

docs.title: 2.5.6 Return Values
docs.text:
return exits a function immediately, so statements after it are skipped. In a function with no result, use return on its own:

func PrintIfPositive(value : int):
    if value <= 0:
        return
    endif
    PrintLn("{}", [value])
endfunc

PrintIfPositive(3) prints 3. PrintIfPositive(0) returns before reaching PrintLn, so it prints nothing.

In a value-returning function, return expression sends a value back to the caller. Alternatively, assign the built-in result variable and let execution reach endfunc:

func Add(left : int, right : int) -> int:
    return left + right
endfunc

func Sum(values : []int) -> int:
    result = 0
    for value :? in values:
        result += value
    endfor
endfunc

Add(2, 3) returns 5, and Sum([10, 20, 30]) returns 60. In Sum, result holds the running total, so no separate accumulator variable is needed. It starts at zero, which is also the returned value for an empty slice. Assigning result does not exit the function; the loop keeps adding to it until all elements have been visited, and endfunc returns the total. Every normal exit of a value-returning function must have a valid result; see Functions.

docs.title: 2.5.7 *Main() Exit Status
docs.text:
*Main() has no result, so use the global exit_code to set the application's exit status. Its default value is 0, which means success; a nonzero value indicates failure. Assigning exit_code does not stop execution. Use return to leave *Main() early:

use print

func *Main():
    PrintLn("Operation failed")
    exit_code = 1
    return
endfunc

This application exits with status 1. You can also let execution reach endfunc after setting exit_code.

Alternatively, Exit(n) terminates the application immediately with status n, even when called from a function other than *Main():

use print

func *Main():
    PrintLn("Operation failed")
    Exit(2)
endfunc

This application exits with status 2; Exit does not return to its caller.

docs.title: 2.5.8 Exceptions and Cleanup
docs.text: try, except, finally, and raise transfer control when an operation fails. finally runs on normal exit as well as return, break, continue, and exception propagation. The full rules and examples are in Exceptions and Error Handling.

docs.title: 2.5.9 Method-Local Use
docs.text: Object methods may use use ., use *, or imported module namespaces to opt outside variables, constants, and functions into unqualified lookup. This is a restricted method feature, not a general import statement for arbitrary function bodies. See Objects and Properties.

docs.title: 2.6. Functions
docs.text:
A function gives a name and a parameter list to reusable code. Parameters carry input values; an optional result type describes the value returned to the caller.

use print

func Add(left : int, right : int) -> int:
    return left + right
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [Add(2, 3)])
endfunc

docs.title: 2.6.1 Declaration and Definition
docs.text:
A definition uses func Name(parameters), an optional -> ResultType, and a body closed by endfunc. Omit -> for a function with no result. A declaration reserves the signature without supplying its body:

func Add(left : int, right : int) -> int ..

Implement it later with the matching name, ordered parameter types and modes, result type, and relevant attributes. The public part of a module can declare functions whose definitions follow implementation.

docs.title: 2.6.2 Result Values
docs.text:
A function with a result type has its own built-in result variable. Either return a value directly or assign result before a normal exit:

func Square(value : int) -> int:
    result = value * value
endfunc

Every reachable normal exit must leave the result assigned. A function without a result cannot return value. A returned view, pointer, object reference, or bound method must not refer to storage whose lifetime ends with the function.

docs.title: 2.6.3 Parameter Modes
docs.text:
Plain parameters receive values. Copying an object reference copies its address, and copying str retains its value. Passing by value does not mean deep-copying an object or its data. Dynamic-array parameters require a reference mode; use []T for an ordinary borrowed array parameter.

Form Contract value : T A value parameter; rebinding it does not rebind caller storage. value : ref T A readable and writable alias to caller storage. value : refin T A read-only input alias. value : refout T An output alias whose input value is not part of the contract. value : refnil T A reference that may be omitted by passing nil. 
func SetValue(value : ref int):
    value = 5
endfunc

func MaybeSet(value : refnil int):
    if %value == nil:
        return
    endif
    value = 44
endfunc

A reference argument needs compatible addressable storage with sufficient lifetime. A property is not itself addressable. For refnil, test %value before reading or writing when the caller may have supplied nil.

[]T, rostr, strslice, and unsized embstr borrow storage even when their descriptors are passed by value. A normal object/pointer parameter borrows an autofree variable; ref parameters preserve its autofree qualification exactly. Autofree type restrictions are in Memory Management and Autofree.

docs.title: 2.6.4 Default Arguments
docs.text:
Trailing parameters may have compile-time constant default values. The caller may omit those trailing arguments:

func Scale(value : int, factor : int = 2) -> int:
    return value * factor
endfunc

func Demonstrate() -> int:
    return Scale(4) + Scale(4, 3)
endfunc

This returns 20: the calls use factors 2 and 3. Defaults are converted to their parameter type at the declaration. Reference parameters, array-slice parameters, and unsized embstr parameters cannot have defaults. Calls pass arguments positionally; named arguments are not supported.

docs.title: 2.6.5 Overloading
docs.text:
Functions, methods, or constructors with the same name must be explicitly marked [[overload]]. Parameter signatures must distinguish the alternatives:

func Sum(left : int, right : int) -> int [[overload]]:
    return left + right
endfunc

func Sum(left : int, right : int, third : int) -> int [[overload]]:
    return left + right + third
endfunc

All overloads of one name must have the same result type. Parameter names and reference modes alone do not distinguish signatures. Resolution considers argument count, available defaults, permitted conversions, and whether reference arguments meet the parameter's access requirements. An ambiguous best match is an error.

docs.title: 2.6.6 Variable Argument Lists
docs.text:
C-style variable argument lists use ... after the fixed parameters. They let the caller pass additional arguments of different types. DQ supports this form for external functions such as C's printf:

func printf(format : ^char, ...) -> int32 [[external]] ..

func *Main():
    var answer : int32 = 42
    printf("%s: %d\n", "answer", answer)
endfunc

This prints answer: 42. The extra arguments follow the target's C calling convention, including its argument promotions. DQ cannot check that their types match the format string; see C Interoperability.

A major limitation of C-style variable arguments is forwarding: a function cannot simply pass its unnamed arguments on to another variadic function. In C, this requires a separate va_list interface, such as vprintf instead of printf.

To make forwarding straightforward, DQ borrows Delphi's array of const pattern as []anyvalue: a slice whose elements can hold values of different types. Each anyvalue stores both the value and its type information. The entire argument list is an ordinary parameter that can be forwarded to other functions:

use print

func Log(format : strslice, values : []anyvalue):
    PrintLn(format, values)
endfunc

func *Main():
    Log("{}: {}", ["answer", 42])
endfunc

This also prints answer: 42. The caller groups the arguments in brackets; ["answer", 42] creates a temporary array of anyvalue elements. Log passes the slice directly to PrintLn, without unpacking or rebuilding the arguments. The temporary array remains valid throughout the call, including calls made by Log; do not retain its slice after the call returns. See anyvalue for supported values and lifetime rules.

docs.title: 2.6.7 Function References
docs.text:
A function reference lets you store a function in a variable and call it through that variable. Its type specifies the parameters and return value the function must have:

use print

type FTransform = func(value : int) -> int

func Double(value : int) -> int:
    return value * 2
endfunc

func Square(value : int) -> int:
    return value * value
endfunc

func *Main():
    var transform : FTransform = Double
    PrintLn("{}", [transform(4)])

    transform = Square
    PrintLn("{}", [transform(4)])
endfunc

This prints 8 and then 16. The same variable first refers to Double, then to Square. Both functions take an int and return an int, so either can be assigned to transform.

The parameter types and modes, result, calling convention, and binding form must be compatible. A function reference can be nil; calling it requires a valid callable.

Explicit pointer-to-function-reference casts support low-level interfaces, but the programmer must match the real signature and ABI. They are not implicit.

docs.title: 2.6.8 Object Method References
docs.text:
A method is a function that belongs to an object. An object method reference remembers both the method and the object to call it on. Add of object to the function reference type:

use print

type FAction = func() of object

object OCounter:
    value : int = 0

    func Increment():
        value += 1
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var counter <- OCounter()
    var action : FAction = counter.Increment
    action()
    action()
    PrintLn("{}", [counter.value])
endfunc

This prints 2. Assigning counter.Increment stores the method reference without calling it. Each later action() call runs Increment on counter, so it changes that object's value.

Keep the object alive for every call through the reference; storing its method does not extend the object's lifetime. A virtual method's implementation is resolved for that object when the reference is assigned. Pointer casts to of object references are not supported. See Objects and Properties.

docs.title: 2.6.9 Local Subfunctions
docs.text:
A subfn declares a helper inside a function or object method:

func Count() -> int:
    var count : int = 0
    subfn Inc(amount : int):
        count += amount
    endsubfn
    Inc(2)
    Inc(3)
    result = count
endfunc

Count() returns 5: both calls to Inc add their amount to the same count variable in the enclosing function. Using a variable from the enclosing function is called capturing that variable. Inc works with the original count, so its changes are still visible in Count after each call.

Subfunctions follow declaration-before-use and lexical block visibility. They can access enclosing parameters, locals, constants, and the enclosing method's self and implicit members. Method namespace restrictions still apply: use @. for module-root values unless a method use makes them available. Parameters and locals can shadow enclosing names, with the usual warning. Each value-returning subfunction has its own result; an enclosing result is never implicitly accessible, including from a void subfunction.

The same rule applies to dynamic arrays and parameters of the enclosing function: the subfunction uses those existing variables rather than separate copies. It can also use constants from the enclosing function. Inside an object method, self still refers to the same object. A subfunction can call itself or another subfunction declared earlier in the same scope.

A subfunction cannot declare another subfunction, including inside control-flow blocks. Subfunctions support direct calls only: their addresses cannot be taken, and they cannot be stored, returned, or passed as function references, even when they use no variables from the enclosing function. Variables used by a subfunction keep their usual lifetime and cleanup rules. Exceptions and local cleanup follow normal function rules.

docs.title: 2.6.10 Special Functions
docs.text:
The * marks a function that has a special role, such as starting the application or initializing a module. It tells the compiler to check that the name is a recognized special function name.

This helps catch typos. For example, func *ModulInit() is rejected because ModulInit is not a recognized special name. Without the *, that misspelling could silently declare an ordinary function, which would never be called automatically to initialize the module.

Special functions must always be declared with * before their name. Their names are reserved: declaring them without * is a compiler error. Explicitly calling a special function is rarely needed, but when you do, write its name without *.

The special functions are:

Name Role *Main() Application entry after runtime/module initialization; no result. *ModuleInit() Module initialization; no result. *Create(...) Object constructor. *Destroy() Object destructor.

A common use of *ModuleInit() is to allocate a global object on the heap so that *Main() can use it without any preparation:

use print

object OSettings:
    message : str = "Ready"
endobject

var settings : OSettings = nil

func *ModuleInit():
    settings = new OSettings()
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [settings.message])
    delete settings
endfunc

This prints Ready. Module initialization always finishes before *Main() runs, so settings already refers to the allocated object when *Main() starts.

The runtime function dq_module_init() calls the modules' *ModuleInit() functions once, in use dependency order: a used module is initialized before the module that uses it. There is no module finalization; this example releases the object explicitly with delete settings. See Modules and Packages.

For how to define *Create and *Destroy, including how they work with inheritance, see Constructors and Destructors.

docs.title: 2.7. Character and String Types
docs.text:
A string stores text as a sequence of bytes. A character represents one byte, one UTF-16 code unit, or one Unicode character, depending on its type. DQ provides owned strings, borrowed views, and fixed-capacity buffers so code can choose how storage is allocated and who keeps it alive. For methods, standalone helpers, and text operations, see String Functions.

Example code using strings:

use print

func AppendField(buffer : embstr, key : rostr, value : strslice):
    buffer.AddFmt('"{}":"{}"', [key, value])
endfunc

func *Main():
    var name : rostr = "Ada Lovelace"
    var first_name : strslice = name[0:3]
    var field : embstr(32)
    AppendField(field, "name", first_name)
    field.AddFmt(', "year":{}', [1979])

    var json : str = ""
    json.Reserve(field.length + 2)
    json.Add('{')
    json.Add(field)
    var closing : ^char = "}"
    json.Add(closing)
    PrintLn(json)
endfunc

The output is {"name":"Ada", "year":1979}. name borrows zero-terminated text as rostr, and first_name borrows a byte range as strslice. field owns a fixed buffer as embstr(32); the unsized embstr parameter lets AppendField write into that buffer with a single AddFmt() call. The Add() accepts all string types, including ^char.

Reserve() is optional: a dynamic string grows automatically as text is added. Here it reserves enough capacity for the field and both braces before assembly, improving performance by avoiding heap reallocations and copying as the string grows. It does not change the string's length or contents.

docs.title: 2.7.1 Character Types
docs.text:
Type Meaning char unsigned 8-bit byte: one ASCII character, one character from a single-byte code page, or one UTF-8 code unit (one Unicode character uses 1...4 UTF-8 code units) char16 unsigned 16-bit UTF-16 code unit (one Unicode character uses 1...2 UTF-16 code units)Recommended to use only for Windows API compatibility wchar unsigned 32-bit Unicode character value, excluding UTF-16 surrogate values

UTF-16 uses pairs of surrogate values to encode some characters. A single surrogate value does not represent a complete character on its own.

char, char16, and wchar are distinct types, not integer aliases. The read-only .ord property returns a character's integer code as int. Prefer c.ord; Ord(c) returns the same value. Explicit or checked conversion creates a character from an integer.

A code unit is one storage element of a text encoding. For example, the 😀 symbol uses four char bytes in UTF-8 or two char16 values in UTF-16, but its character value fits in one wchar.

A character literal can initialize any character type whose range includes its value. Character variables do not implicitly convert to integers or to other character types. To convert between character types, pass through the integer code exposed by .ord:

var c8  : char   = 'A'
var c16 : char16 = '€'
var c32 : wchar  = '😀'

var code : int = c8.ord                 // 65
var same_code : int = Ord(c8)           // 65: equivalent function form
var emoji_code : int = c32.ord          // 128512
var same : char = char(code)           // 'A'
var wide : wchar = wchar(c16.ord)       // '€'
var next : char = char(c8.ord + 1)      // 'B'

var checked  : char  = IntToChar(code)     // 'A'; checks the range at runtime
var fallback : wchar = IntToWchar(0xD800, '?') // '?' for an invalid character value

These conversions preserve the numeric code; they do not encode or decode UTF-8 or UTF-16. Explicit casts reject invalid constant values at compile time, but runtime casts can truncate to the destination width and do not validate Unicode character values. Use IntToChar() or IntToWchar() when runtime validation is needed. Without a fallback argument, an invalid value raises a runtime error.

The following examples intentionally produce compiler errors:

var c8     : char = 'A'
var c32    : wchar = 'A'
var code   : int = 65

c8 = code           // error: no implicit integer-to-character conversion
code = c8           // error: use c8.ord
code = int(c8)      // error: an integer cast cannot replace .ord
c32  = c8           // error: no implicit conversion between character types
c8 = char(c32)      // error: use char(c32.ord) or IntToChar(c32.ord)
c8 = c8 + 1         // error: use char(c8.ord + 1)
c8.ord = 66         // error: .ord is read-only

var too_large : char = '€'             // error: the literal does not fit in one byte
var overflow  : char = char(256)       // error: constant is outside 0 .. 255
var non_bmp   : char16 = '😀'          // error: the literal does not fit in one code unit
var surrogate : wchar = wchar(0xD800)  // error: wchar excludes UTF-16 surrogate values

docs.title: 2.7.2 Text Types
docs.text:
Type Ownership and representation str Dynamic, heap-allocated, reference-counted copy-on-write byte string.May contain internal zero bytes and is not necessarily valid UTF-8.A managed type that cannot be a struct field.The current length is always stored. embstr(N) Embedded string: fixed-capacity, mutable, zero-terminated byte storage.A zero-byte scan may be required to calculate the length. embstr Writable, appendable borrowed reference to a shared embedded string descriptor, which carries the storage capacity. Typically used for function parameters.A zero-byte scan may be required to calculate the length. rostr Read-only borrowed, zero-terminated byte string.A zero-byte scan may be required to calculate the length. strslice Read-only borrowed view of text bytes. Zero-termination is not guaranteed.Length is always known; conversion from raw or embedded storage calculates it before creating the view. ^char Raw pointer to text bytes; C string operations expect a terminating zero byte.

On targets built with dynamic strings disabled, str and operations that produce it are unavailable. Text literals, rostr, strslice, and embstr(N) remain available for text processing with borrowed or fixed storage.

docs.title: 2.7.2.1 The Length Calculation Problem
docs.text:
DQ maintains strong compatibility with C APIs, so its zero-terminated string buffers can be passed directly to C functions. C APIs that work with text usually accept a pointer to the start of a text buffer, written as ^char in DQ. This pointer carries no information about the text's length.

Zero-terminated strings mark the end of their text with a byte whose value is zero. This is different from the printable character '0'. The terminating byte is not counted in the text length: "hello" needs five text bytes plus one zero byte.

To calculate the length from that pointer, the program must read from the start until it finds the zero byte. Longer text takes more work, and repeated length calculations can scan the same bytes again.

Storing the byte count avoids this work. DQ's string types handle this in different ways, using stored or cached lengths where possible, as described below.

docs.title: 2.7.2.2 str: Dynamic Strings
docs.text:
str allocates heap memory for its contents. As the contents grow, the backing memory block may be reallocated. The current length is always known. A trailing zero byte maintains C string compatibility. The contents can also hold arbitrary binary data, including internal zero bytes. It is a managed type: the runtime tracks references and frees the memory when the string data is no longer used. A str cannot be a struct field. Its maximum text length is 2147483647 bytes. Its .length reads the stored byte count without scanning the text.

An empty str may require no heap allocation. Internally, it can be represented by a nil pointer, indicating that no dynamic string handler object has been allocated for it yet.

Assigning a str shares storage. Mutation detaches when necessary so other string values retain their contents.

var a : str = "abc"
var b : str = a
b[0] = 'X'       // a remains "abc"

var c : str = a.Clone() // independent storage immediately
c[0] = 'Y'             // a remains "abc"; b remains "Xbc"

c.Reserve(32)          // space for at least 32 text bytes; c is still "Ybc"
c.Add("def")          // reuses the reserved storage; c is now "Ybcdef"

docs.title: 2.7.2.3 embstr(N) and embstr: Embedded Strings
docs.text:
embstr(N) provides fixed storage of N bytes. It holds up to N - 1 text bytes plus a terminating zero byte, making it compatible with C strings. The position of the terminating zero determines the text length, so calculating the length may require a scan at runtime. DQ can cache the length to avoid repeated scans. Embedded strings can be stored in the program's data segment, on the stack, or inside structures and objects. Their maximum text length is 16777215 bytes.

A declaration without an initializer creates an empty string. .Add() and .AddFmt() can be called immediately after the declaration:

var s : embstr(16)
s.Add("value=")           // = "value=": contents of s
s.AddFmt("{}", [42])      // = "value=42": contents of s

For a declaration without an initializer, only the leading zero terminator is guaranteed; bytes beyond it are unspecified.

For embstr(N), .storage_size is N and .maxlength is N - 1. Assignment and append operations truncate to fit the fixed capacity:

var fixbuf : embstr(8) = "abc"
fixbuf.Append("defghi") // stores "abcdefg"

Use an unsized embstr parameter to modify an existing fixed buffer through its shared descriptor. It remains writable and appendable: character writes, assignment, Add(), and AddFmt() modify the original buffer within its fixed capacity.

docs.title: 2.7.2.4 rostr: Read-Only Zero-Terminated Strings
docs.text:
Use rostr for read-only string parameters when zero-termination is required. It borrows text literals, str, embstr(N), unsized embstr, or ^char without copying the text bytes or retaining their storage. Its descriptor can be reassigned, but character writes and writable character references through it are rejected.

A rostr carries a pointer and either a known length or an indication that the length is unknown. Borrowing a literal or a str preserves its known length. Borrowing a raw ^char does not scan immediately; the first operation needing the length, such as .length, scans and caches it in that rostr descriptor.

docs.title: 2.7.2.5 strslice: String Slices
docs.text:
Use strslice for read-only byte ranges with explicit bounds. It borrows text without copying its bytes or retaining its storage. A slice can describe an unterminated range or a range containing zero bytes.

Its length is always known, so .length reads the stored byte count directly. Conversion from raw or embedded storage resolves an unknown length before creating the slice; embedded-string scans stop at the buffer's capacity. Converting a rostr with an unknown length also resolves that length first.

Use StrSlice(data, length) to supply the length explicitly and avoid scanning:

var data : [3]char = ['A', char(0), 'B']
var view : strslice = StrSlice(%data[0], data.length)

docs.title: 2.7.2.6 ^char: Raw C String Pointers
docs.text:
Use ^char for raw C interfaces. It carries only a pointer, with no length or ownership information. Converting it to a borrowed string cannot recover a known length from the pointer alone. If the length is already known, use StrSlice(data, length) to pass it explicitly.

.pchar exposes a borrowed ^char for compatible zero-terminated text storage.

func puts(text : ^char) -> int32 [[external]] ..

func *Main():
    var owned : str = "dynamic text"
    var readonly : rostr = "read-only text"
    var buffer : embstr(16) = "fixed text"

    var owned_ptr : ^char = owned.pchar
    var readonly_ptr : ^char = readonly.pchar
    var buffer_ptr : ^char = buffer.pchar
    puts(owned_ptr)
    puts(readonly_ptr)
    puts(buffer_ptr)
endfunc

This prints dynamic text, read-only text, and fixed text on separate lines. Each pointer refers to the source's existing text bytes; no text is copied. The .pchar property is also available on unsized embstr references.

If the string's text moves to a different memory location, for example when a dynamic string grows, the old pointer must no longer be used. Get a new pointer with .pchar after making the change. A nil ^char is not valid where a C string is required unless the called API explicitly defines nil handling. See C Interoperability for passing text to C functions.

docs.title: 2.7.2.7 Text Descriptors
docs.text:
The compiler carries text pointers together with metadata in small structures called descriptors. For calls with embstr, rostr, or strslice arguments, it creates temporary descriptors as needed during argument conversion. The compiler may pass either a pointer to the descriptor or its members directly as function arguments.

These descriptors are invisible to the user, the compiler creates, updates, and passes them automatically.

For embstr, the runtime uses the following descriptor structure:

struct SDqTextInfo:
    dataptr : ^char   // points to the first text byte
    charlen : int32   // known byte length, or a negative value when unknown
    info    : uint32  // bits 0..23: maximum length; bits 24..31: flags
endstruct

For rostr and strslice, the runtime uses a more compact descriptor:

struct SDqRoStrInfo:
    dataptr : ^char
    charlen : int32   // rostr: negative means unknown; strslice: always non-negative
endstruct

charlen counts text bytes, excluding any terminating zero byte. A non-negative value indicates a known length; 0 represents a known empty string. For embstr and rostr, a negative value means that the length must be calculated when needed. For strslice, the length is always known and non-negative.

docs.title: 2.7.2.8 Conversions and Borrowed Lifetimes
docs.text:
Destination Relevant rule str Owns/retains its text value; accepts compatible text views. rostr Requires existing terminated storage (like a string literal), borrows it. strslice Requires existing storage, borrows a byte range with an always-known length; conversion resolves an unknown source length first. No terminator is promised. embstr(N) Creates an embedded fixed-storage of N bytes. Written texts are truncated to fit. Unsized embstr Shares a fixed-storage, writeable embedded string. ^char A raw C pointer to an existing storage with no automatic lifetime extension.
