Slicing a rostr by byte offsets returns strslice, including full-range and suffix slices. A rostr converts to strslice, resolving any unknown length first. There is no direct conversion from strslice to rostr, even by a cast. When terminated storage is needed for a slice, first copy it into an owning str or a fixed-capacity embstr(N).

Both rostr and strslice convert to owned str or fixed-capacity embstr(N). These conversions copy the byte range, truncating only when the fixed buffer reached its capacity.

var owned    : str = "hello"
var borrowed : rostr = owned
var part     : strslice = borrowed[1:4]  // borrows "ell"
var copied   : str = part             // owns a copy of "ell"

Borrowed text must not outlive its source. The owner must stay alive, and its storage and contents must remain stable while a read-only view is used. An unsized embstr requires live, writable source storage. Neither a cast nor storing a view in anyvalue extends the owner's lifetime. Returning a view into a local buffer is invalid.

See Memory Management and Autofree for managed values and borrowed lifetimes.

docs.title: 2.7.3 Literals
docs.text:
Double quotes always represent text. A single-quoted literal containing exactly one Unicode character is wchar; empty or longer single-quoted literals are text.

var path       : str = "/"
var slash      : wchar = '/'
var byte_slash : char = '/'
var greeting   : rostr = "Hello, world!"
var field      : rostr = '"name":"Amy"'

The byte_slash initialization is accepted because the literal's character code is known at compile time and is below 256. In general, conversion from wchar to char is explicit. Single quotes around longer text let it contain double quotes without escaping them, as in field.

docs.title: 2.7.3.1 Multiline Text
docs.text:
For text that spans several lines, put three double quotes (""") or three single quotes (''') around it:

var message : rostr = """
    First line.
    Second line.
    """
PrintLn(message)

This prints:

First line.
Second line.

The text starts with "F" and ends with the final ".". Putting the quotes on separate lines does not add an empty line before or after the text. The line break between First line. and Second line. is part of the string, just as if you had written "First line.\nSecond line.".

You can indent the text to keep the source code readable. DQ uses the spaces before the closing quotes to decide how much indentation to remove. Extra spaces are kept:

var indented : rostr = '''
    First line.
      Indented second line.
    '''
PrintLn(indented)

There are four spaces before the closing quotes, so DQ removes four spaces from the start of each text line. The second line has six spaces, so two remain:

First line.
  Indented second line.

This also makes longer text, such as JSON, easier to write. Ordinary double quotes inside triple double quotes do not need a backslash:

var document : rostr = """
    {
      "name": "Amy",
      "year": 1999
    }
    """
PrintLn(document)

This prints:

{
  "name": "Amy",
  "year": 1999
}

Escape sequences still work inside multiline text: \n adds a line break, \t adds a tab, and \\ adds one backslash. Three matching quotes end the text; the indentation and line-break rules are the same for both quote styles.

docs.title: 2.8. String Functions
docs.text: Use the reference tables to find string properties, methods, helpers, and operators, then follow their links to detailed explanations and examples. For storage, conversions, and lifetime rules, see Character and String Types.

docs.title: 2.8.1 Properties and Methods Listing
docs.text:
In the Types column, * means all string types: str, rostr, strslice and embstr.

Properties are read-only. A result of — means that the method modifies the string and returns no value. Lengths, positions, and counts are in bytes, except for the explicitly Unicode-oriented members .wclen and .wchar[...].

Property or method Types Result Purpose .Add(value) str, embstr — Append text or one char byte .AddFmt(fmt, args) str, embstr — Append formatted values .Append(value) str, embstr — Alias for .Add(value) .AppendChar(ch) str, embstr — Append one char byte .capacity str int Allocated capacity for text bytes .Clear() str, embstr — Remove all contents; retain storage .Clear(free_storage) str — Optionally release the string's storage .Clone() str str Create an independent copy immediately .Compact() str — Reduce capacity to the current length .Contains(needle) * bool Test whether text contains a value .Delete(index, count = 1) str, embstr — Remove bytes .EndsWith(suffix) * bool Test the end of the text .IndexOf(needle, start = 0) * int First matching byte offset, or -1 .Insert(index, value) str, embstr — Insert text or a byte at a byte position .LastIndexOf(needle) * int Last matching byte offset, or -1 .length * int Current byte length, excluding the terminator .Lower() * str Copy with ASCII letters in lowercase .LPad(length, fill) * str Copy with padding on the left .LTrim().LTrim(set) * str Copy without matching bytes at the left end .maxlength embstr int Maximum number of text bytes that fit .pchar * ^char Borrow a pointer to the text bytes .Pop() str char Remove and return the last byte .Pop(count) str str Remove and return bytes from the end .PopFirst() str char Remove and return the first byte .PopFirst(count) str str Remove and return bytes from the beginning .Prepend(value) str, embstr — Insert text or a byte at the beginning .refcount str int Number of references sharing the string handler .Reserve(capacity) str — Ensure room for at least this many text bytes .RPad(length, fill) * str Copy with padding on the right .RTrim().RTrim(set) * str Copy without matching bytes at the right end .Set(value) str, embstr — Replace the contents .SetCapacity(capacity) str — Set capacity, shortening the text if necessary .SetLength(length, fill) str — Resize, filling new bytes with a char .StartsWith(prefix) * bool Test the beginning of the text .storage_size embstr int Buffer size including space for the terminator .ToFloat().ToFloat(defvalue) * float Parse a number; raise on invalid input or return a fallback .ToInt().ToInt(defvalue) * int Parse an integer; raise on invalid input or return a fallback .ToWchars() * [*]wchar Decode the whole UTF-8 string into Unicode characters .Trim().Trim(set) * str Copy without matching bytes at either end .Truncate(length) str — Shorten without growing .Upper() * str Copy with ASCII letters in uppercase .wchar[index] * wchar Read one Unicode character .wchar[start:end] * [*]wchar Decode a range of Unicode characters .wclen * int Count Unicode characters in UTF-8 text

Methods returning str require dynamic-string support even when called on an embedded string or borrowed view. Numeric conversion, search methods, embedded-string mutations, and Unicode decoding remain available with dynamic strings disabled. Using str always requires dynamic-string support.

For equivalents of substring(), substr(), slice(), Left(), Right(), or Mid() from other languages, see Byte Indexing and Slicing. Use text[start:end] to extract a substring, or text[start:start + count] when you have a starting position and a byte count. Positions are zero-based byte offsets, and end is excluded. For Unicode character positions, see Unicode Indexing and Slicing.

docs.title: 2.8.2 Standalone String Helpers Listing
docs.text:
These functions are available through the implicit sys runtime interface; ordinary modules need no use declaration. Text parameters accept the string types through their normal conversions. Functions returning str require dynamic-string support.

Function Result Purpose Format(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue) str Create formatted text StrFromUtf16(chars : []char16) str Convert a UTF-16 array to UTF-8 StrFromUtf16Fallback(chars : []char16, fallback_wchar : wchar) str Convert UTF-16, replacing malformed sequences StrFromUtf16Ptr(chars : ^char16, count : int) str Convert an explicit number of UTF-16 code units StrFromUtf16PtrFallback(chars : ^char16, count : int, fallback_wchar : wchar) str Convert a UTF-16 pointer range with replacement StrFromWchars(chars : []wchar) str Encode Unicode characters as UTF-8 StrLower(text : strslice) str Copy with ASCII letters in lowercase StrSlice(data : ^char, length : int) strslice Borrow a pointer and an explicit byte count StrSliceCmp(a : strslice, b : strslice) int Compare two byte ranges StrToFloat(text : strslice)StrToFloat(text : strslice, defvalue : float) float Parse a number; raise on invalid input or return a fallback StrToInt(text : strslice)StrToInt(text : strslice, defvalue : int) int Parse an integer; raise on invalid input or return a fallback StrUpper(text : strslice) str Copy with ASCII letters in uppercase

docs.title: 2.8.3 Text Operators
docs.text:
+ concatenates compatible text operands into a new str. += appends to a dynamic string. Both require dynamic-string support.

var greeting : str = "Hello, " + "world"
greeting += "!"           // "Hello, world!"

Using + repeatedly to assemble text creates temporary strings and can cause repeated heap allocations and copies. Prefer .Add() for plain text and .AddFmt() for formatted values, with .Reserve() when the expected size can be estimated.

docs.title: 2.8.4 String Comparison
docs.text:
Text values support ==, <>, <, <=, >, and >= across different string types, including embedded strings with or without an explicit capacity. Strings are compared byte by byte, using unsigned byte values. The first difference determines the order; when one string is a prefix of the other, the shorter string comes first.

var name : str = "alpha"
var limit : rostr = "beta"
var before : bool = name < limit       // true
var prefix : bool = "app" < "apple"    // true
var inside : bool = "a" <= name < "z" // true
var equal : bool = name == "alpha"     // true

Comparison is case-sensitive. It does not validate UTF-8, normalize Unicode, or apply language-specific sorting rules. Known string lengths include internal zero bytes; raw C strings end at their first zero.

docs.title: 2.8.4.1 StrSliceCmp
docs.text:
StrSliceCmp(a : strslice, b : strslice) -> int

StrSliceCmp(a, b) provides the same bytewise comparison as a function. It returns a negative value if a comes before b, zero if equal, and a positive value if a comes after b. It compares the entire known byte range without requiring a terminator.

var order : int = StrSliceCmp("app", "apple") // negative
var same : int = StrSliceCmp("abc", "abc")   // 0
var a : ^char = "alpha"
var b : ^char = "beta"
var before : bool = StrSliceCmp(a, b) < 0     // true: compares text

A raw ^char operand compares text when paired with a string value or, for ordering, a text literal. Two raw pointer variables compare their addresses; use StrSliceCmp to compare their text contents explicitly.

docs.title: 2.8.5.1 Format
docs.text:
Format(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue) -> str

Format(fmt, args) creates a new string using the same placeholders as .AddFmt(). Its strslice format parameter accepts substring views directly, including text without a terminating zero. See Text Formatting for the full syntax.

var label : str = Format("value={:04X}", [255]) // "value=00FF"

docs.title: 2.8.5.2 StrToInt and StrToFloat
docs.text:
StrToInt(text : strslice) -> int
StrToInt(text : strslice, defvalue : int) -> int
StrToFloat(text : strslice) -> float
StrToFloat(text : strslice, defvalue : float) -> float

StrToInt parses decimal digits with an optional leading + or - and rejects values outside the range of int. StrToFloat accepts an optional leading sign, a dot or comma decimal separator, and an optional e/E exponent. An exponent may have a leading sign and must contain digits. The entire input must match; surrounding whitespace and internal zero bytes are rejected. Use .Trim() first when surrounding whitespace should be ignored.

Without defvalue, invalid or empty input raises EStrError. Supplying defvalue returns that fallback on conversion errors. When exceptions are disabled, the no-fallback form reports a runtime error and returns zero if the error handler returns; the fallback form still returns defvalue.

var count : int = StrToInt("+42")              // 42
var fallback : int = StrToInt("invalid", -1)   // -1
var value : float = StrToFloat("1.25e2")       // 125
var comma : float = StrToFloat("1,5")          // 1.5
var invalid : float = StrToFloat("1e+", -1)    // -1: missing exponent digits

docs.title: 2.8.5.3 StrUpper and StrLower
docs.text:
StrUpper(text : strslice) -> str
StrLower(text : strslice) -> str

These functions copy the text, converting only ASCII letters. They leave non-ASCII bytes unchanged and do not modify the source. The methods .Upper() and .Lower() provide the same conversions.

var text : rostr = "Hello, é!"
var upper : str = StrUpper(text) // "HELLO, é!"
var lower : str = StrLower(text) // "hello, é!"

docs.title: 2.8.5.4 StrSlice
docs.text:
StrSlice(data : ^char, length : int) -> strslice

StrSlice(data, length) borrows exactly length bytes without scanning for a terminator or copying the text. The memory must remain alive and stable. A negative length raises a runtime error; a nil pointer is valid only with a zero length.

var data : [3]char = ['A', char(0), 'B']
var view : strslice = StrSlice(%data[0], data.length)
var bytes : int = view.length // 3: the internal zero does not end the view

docs.title: 2.8.5.5 StrFromWchars
docs.text:
StrFromWchars(chars : []wchar) -> str

StrFromWchars(chars) encodes Unicode characters as UTF-8. Invalid Unicode character values, such as surrogate values, raise a runtime encoding error.

var chars : [3]wchar = ['A', 'é', '€']
var text : str = StrFromWchars(chars[:]) // "Aé€"

docs.title: 2.8.5.6 StrFromUtf16 and StrFromUtf16Ptr
docs.text:
StrFromUtf16(chars : []char16) -> str
StrFromUtf16Ptr(chars : ^char16, count : int) -> str

StrFromUtf16(chars) converts a UTF-16 array slice to UTF-8, ignoring one final zero code unit if present. Internal zeros are preserved. StrFromUtf16Ptr(chars, count) converts exactly count code units, including any zeros in that range. Surrogate pairs represent one Unicode character; malformed UTF-16 raises a runtime encoding error. The pointer form returns empty text for nil or a non-positive count.

var units : [4]char16 = [char16(65), char16(0), char16(66), char16(0)]
var text : str = StrFromUtf16(units[:])          // "A\0B": 3 bytes
var prefix : str = StrFromUtf16Ptr(%units[0], 1) // "A"

docs.title: 2.8.5.7 UTF16 Fallback Conversion
docs.text:
StrFromUtf16Fallback(chars : []char16, fallback_wchar : wchar) -> str
StrFromUtf16PtrFallback(chars : ^char16, count : int, fallback_wchar : wchar) -> str

StrFromUtf16Fallback and StrFromUtf16PtrFallback use the same input bounds as their strict counterparts but replace malformed UTF-16 sequences with fallback_wchar. Passing wchar(0) as the fallback skips malformed sequences.

var units : [3]char16 = [char16(0xD800), char16(65), char16(0)]
var replaced : str = StrFromUtf16Fallback(units[:], '?') // "?A"
var skipped : str = StrFromUtf16PtrFallback(%units[0], 2, wchar(0)) // "A"

docs.title: 2.8.6.1 Length
docs.text:
.length counts text bytes, including internal zero bytes when the source has a known length. It excludes the trailing terminator. str and strslice store their lengths; embedded strings and rostr may need to scan for the first zero byte when the length is unknown.

var text : str = "Aé€"
var bytes : int = text.length  // 6 bytes
var empty : str
var zero : int = empty.length // 0, even without an allocated handler

docs.title: 2.8.6.2 Capacity
docs.text:
.capacity is the number of text bytes a str can hold before it needs more storage. It excludes the extra terminating zero byte and can exceed .length. An empty string with no allocated handler has capacity zero.

var text : str = "abc"
text.Reserve(100)
var length : int = text.length     // 3
var has_room : bool = text.capacity >= 100 // true

docs.title: 2.8.6.3 Embedded Storage Size
docs.text:
For embstr(N), .storage_size is N and .maxlength is N - 1. An unsized embstr reports these values for the buffer it references.

var buffer : embstr(8) = "abc"
var size : int = buffer.storage_size // 8
var limit : int = buffer.maxlength   // 7
buffer.Add("defghi")                 // buffer is "abcdefg": truncated to fit

docs.title: 2.8.6.4 Reference Count
docs.text:
.refcount reports how many references share a dynamic string handler. Assigning one str to another shares the handler; modifying one value detaches its storage when necessary. A string with no handler has reference count zero. Temporary values and function arguments can also retain references.

var a : str = "abc"
var b : str = a
var shared : int = a.refcount // 2
b[0] = 'X'                   // a is "abc"; b is "Xbc"
var unique : int = a.refcount // 1

docs.title: 2.8.6.5 Raw Byte Pointer
docs.text:
.pchar borrows a pointer to the first text byte without copying or retaining storage. str, rostr, and embedded strings provide terminated storage; a strslice pointer is not guaranteed to be zero-terminated. Copy a slice to str or embstr(N) before passing it to a C API that expects a C string.

var text : str = "hello"
var pointer : ^char = text.pchar
var first : char = pointer^ // 'h'

var part : strslice = text[:2] // "he", followed by more source bytes
var terminated : str = part
var c_text : ^char = terminated.pchar // points to "he" plus a zero terminator

Keep the source alive and its storage stable while using the pointer. Obtain a new pointer after a mutation that can move the text. For str, .pchar returns terminated empty text even when the internal handler pointer is nil. C string functions see only the prefix before the first zero byte. See C Interoperability.

docs.title: 2.8.7 String Methods
docs.text:
These methods modify str or embedded string storage. Dynamic strings grow as needed and preserve other values that share their storage. Embedded strings keep their fixed capacity and truncate inserted or appended text to fit. An unsized embstr modifies the original buffer through its shared descriptor.

Text-source arguments accept str, rostr, strslice, embstr(N), unsized embstr, or ^char. .Set, .Add, .Append, .Prepend, and .Insert also accept one char byte. A wchar variable must be encoded as UTF-8 to append its text; it is not a single-byte source.

docs.title: 2.8.7.1 .Set
docs.text:
.Set(value : strslice)
.Set(value : char)

.Set(value) replaces the contents. For text values, assignment provides the same replacement syntax. Embedded destinations truncate the source to fit.

var text : str = "old"
text.Set("new")           // "new"
text.Set('!')             // "!"
var buffer : embstr(8)
buffer.Set("abcdefghij")  // "abcdefg"

docs.title: 2.8.7.2 .Add, .Append, and .AppendChar
docs.text:
.Add(value : strslice)
.Add(value : char)
.Append(value : strslice)
.Append(value : char)
.AppendChar(ch : char)

.Add(value) and .Append(value) append text or a char byte. .AppendChar(ch) accepts only a char. These methods modify the string and return no value. An embstr(N) declaration starts empty, so it can be appended to immediately.

var text : str = "abc"
text.Add("def")           // "abcdef"
text.Append('!')          // "abcdef!"
text.AppendChar('?')      // "abcdef!?"

docs.title: 2.8.7.3 .AddFmt
docs.text:
.AddFmt(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue)

.AddFmt(fmt, args) appends text containing formatted values. The format parameter is strslice, so substring views can be passed directly. An embstr(N) declaration starts empty and can be used directly with .AddFmt(). Embedded destinations truncate the output to fit. Placeholder syntax and supported value types are explained in Text Formatting.

var text : str = "value="
text.AddFmt("{:04X}", [255]) // "value=00FF"
var buffer : embstr(16)
buffer.AddFmt("{} items", [3]) // "3 items"

docs.title: 2.8.7.4 .Prepend and .Insert
docs.text:
.Prepend(value : strslice)
.Prepend(value : char)
.Insert(index : int, value : strslice)
.Insert(index : int, value : char)

.Prepend(value) inserts at the beginning. .Insert(index, value) inserts before the specified byte position. The insertion position is clamped to 0 .. text.length; $end inserts at the end.

var text : str = "bc"
text.Prepend('a')         // "abc"
text.Insert(1, "--")      // "a--bc"
text.Insert($end, '!')    // "a--bc!"
text.Insert(100, '?')     // "a--bc!?": position clamped to the end

Performance: .Insert() shifts the bytes after the insertion position to make room. Inserting near the beginning of a large string can take significant time. .Prepend() moves all existing text bytes.

docs.title: 2.8.7.5 .Delete
docs.text:
.Delete(index : int, count : int = 1)

.Delete(index, count = 1) removes up to count bytes starting at index. The position is clamped to 0 .. text.length, and the count is limited to the remaining bytes. A non-positive count or a position at the end removes nothing.

var text : str = "abcdef"
text.Delete(1)            // "acdef"
text.Delete(2, 100)       // "ac": removes the entire remaining suffix
text.Delete(100)          // "ac": unchanged

Performance: .Delete() shifts the bytes after the removed range to close the gap. Deleting near the beginning of a large string can take significant time because most of the remaining text must move.

docs.title: 2.8.7.6 .Clear
docs.text:
.Clear(free_storage : bool = false)  // str
.Clear()                           // embstr

.Clear() makes the string empty and retains its storage for reuse. For str, this is equivalent to .Clear(false). .Clear(true) releases that value's reference to the dynamic storage and leaves its length and capacity at zero. Other strings sharing the old storage retain their text. Embedded strings support only the no-argument form.

var text : str = "abc"
text.Reserve(100)
text.Clear()              // empty; capacity is retained
text.Add("reused")
text.Clear(true)          // empty; capacity is 0
var buffer : embstr(16) = "abc"
buffer.Clear()            // empty; the 16-byte buffer remains

docs.title: 2.8.7.7 .SetLength and .Truncate
docs.text:
.SetLength(length : uint, fill : char)
.Truncate(length : uint)

.SetLength(length, fill) sets the byte length, using the supplied char for new bytes when growing. Shortening discards the suffix. .Truncate(length) only shortens: a length greater than the current length leaves the text unchanged. Lengths must be non-negative.

var text : str = "abc"
text.SetLength(5, '.')    // "abc.."
text.SetLength(4, ' ')    // "abc."
text.Truncate(2)          // "ab"
text.Truncate(100)        // "ab": does not grow

docs.title: 2.8.7.8 .Pop and .PopFirst
docs.text:
.Pop() -> char
.Pop(count : int) -> str
.PopFirst() -> char
.PopFirst(count : int) -> str

.Pop() removes and returns the last char; .PopFirst() removes and returns the first. These no-argument forms raise a runtime error on an empty string.

With a count argument, both methods return a str containing the removed bytes. Counts greater than the length remove everything. A non-positive count or an empty string returns empty text.

var text : str = "abcdef"
var tail : str = text.Pop(2)        // "ef"; text is "abcd"
var head : str = text.PopFirst(2)   // "ab"; text is "cd"
var last : char = text.Pop()        // 'd'; text is "c"
var first : char = text.PopFirst()  // 'c'; text is empty
var empty : str = text.Pop(10)      // "": count form accepts an empty string

Performance: Both forms of .PopFirst() shift all remaining text bytes to the beginning of the string. This can take significant time for large strings, especially when repeatedly removing one byte at a time.

docs.title: 2.8.7.9 Overlapping Source and Destination
docs.text:
Dynamic string mutation preserves the logical source when it aliases the destination, including a view into the same string across a reallocation.

var text : str = "abcd"
text.Insert(2, text[1:3]) // "abbccd": inserts the original "bc"
text.Add(text)           // "abbccdabbccd"

docs.title: 2.8.8.1 .Reserve
docs.text:
.Reserve(capacity : uint)

.Reserve(capacity) ensures space for at least the specified number of text bytes without changing the length or contents. It does not reduce existing capacity. Reserving an estimated final size avoids repeated reallocations and copying while assembling text. The runtime doubles capacity as needed when a growing string exceeds its current allocation.

var text : str
text.Reserve(32)
text.Add("Hello, ")
text.AddFmt("{}!", ["world"]) // "Hello, world!"

docs.title: 2.8.8.2 .SetCapacity and .Compact
docs.text:
.SetCapacity(capacity : uint)
.Compact()

.SetCapacity(capacity) sets the capacity to the requested number of text bytes. Reducing it below .length also truncates the contents. .SetCapacity(0) releases the storage. .Compact() sets capacity to the current length. Call these after building text when reducing retained storage is useful.

var text : str = "abcdef"
text.SetCapacity(4)       // "abcd"; capacity is 4
text.Reserve(100)
text.Compact()            // "abcd"; capacity is 4 again

docs.title: 2.8.8.3 .Clone
docs.text:
.Clone() -> str

.Clone() returns an independent copy immediately. Ordinary str assignment shares storage and detaches on mutation; use .Clone() when the copy should already have its own storage before either value changes.

var original : str = "abc"
var copy : str = original.Clone()
copy[0] = 'X'             // copy is "Xbc"; original is "abc"

docs.title: 2.8.9 String Utility Methods
docs.text: These methods work on every string type. They do not modify the original string. Needles, prefixes, suffixes, trim sets, and padding accept text or a char byte. Searches compare bytes exactly, with case sensitivity and no Unicode normalization. Case conversion, trimming, and padding return a new str; assign the result to keep it.

docs.title: 2.8.9.1 .Upper and .Lower
docs.text:
.Upper() -> str
.Lower() -> str

.Upper() and .Lower() return a copy with ASCII letters converted to uppercase or lowercase. They preserve non-ASCII bytes, including UTF-8 characters, and do not modify the original string. They are equivalent to StrUpper(text) and StrLower(text) and require dynamic-string support.

var text : embstr(32) = "Hello, é!"
var upper : str = text.Upper() // "HELLO, é!"
var lower : str = text.Lower() // "hello, é!"; text is still "Hello, é!"

docs.title: 2.8.9.2 .ToInt and .ToFloat
docs.text:
.ToInt() -> int
.ToInt(defvalue : int) -> int
.ToFloat() -> float
.ToFloat(defvalue : float) -> float

These methods parse a number using the same rules as StrToInt and StrToFloat. Without a fallback, invalid or empty text raises EStrError; with defvalue, conversion errors return that value. Integer conversion also checks the range of int. Neither method skips surrounding whitespace. Both work without dynamic-string support.

var integer : embstr(16) = "-42"
var count : int = integer.ToInt()        // -42
var decimal : rostr = "1,25e2"
var value : float = decimal.ToFloat()    // 125
var invalid : strslice = "invalid"
var fallback : int = invalid.ToInt(-1)   // -1
var default_value : float = invalid.ToFloat(0) // 0
var padded : rostr = " 42 "
var trimmed : int = padded.Trim().ToInt() // 42

docs.title: 2.8.9.3 .IndexOf and .LastIndexOf
docs.text:
.IndexOf(needle : strslice, start : int = 0) -> int
.IndexOf(needle : char, start : int = 0) -> int
.LastIndexOf(needle : strslice) -> int
.LastIndexOf(needle : char) -> int

.IndexOf(needle, start = 0) returns the first matching byte offset at or after start. .LastIndexOf(needle) searches for the final occurrence in the entire text. Both return -1 when no match exists.

.IndexOf clamps start to 0 .. text.length. An empty needle matches at the normalized start position; .LastIndexOf("") returns text.length.

var text : rostr = "abcdefabc"
var first : int = text.IndexOf("abc")      // 0
var next : int = text.IndexOf("abc", 1)    // 6
var last : int = text.LastIndexOf("abc")   // 6
var byte : int = text.IndexOf('d')         // 3
var missing : int = text.IndexOf("xyz")    // -1
var end : int = text.IndexOf("", 100)      // 9

docs.title: 2.8.9.4 .Contains, .StartsWith, and .EndsWith
docs.text:
.Contains(needle : strslice) -> bool
.Contains(needle : char) -> bool
.StartsWith(prefix : strslice) -> bool
.StartsWith(prefix : char) -> bool
.EndsWith(suffix : strslice) -> bool
.EndsWith(suffix : char) -> bool

.Contains(needle) tests for a match anywhere. .StartsWith(prefix) and .EndsWith(suffix) test only the corresponding end. An empty needle, prefix, or suffix matches every text value, including empty text.

var path : embstr(32) = "docs/reference.md"
var found : bool = path.Contains("reference") // true
var prefix : bool = path.StartsWith("docs/")  // true
var suffix : bool = path.EndsWith(".md")      // true
var case_match : bool = path.EndsWith(".MD")  // false

docs.title: 2.8.9.5 .Trim, .LTrim, and .RTrim
docs.text:
.Trim() -> str
.Trim(set : strslice) -> str
.Trim(set : char) -> str
.LTrim() -> str
.LTrim(set : strslice) -> str
.LTrim(set : char) -> str
.RTrim() -> str
.RTrim(set : strslice) -> str
.RTrim(set : char) -> str

.Trim() removes ASCII whitespace from both ends; .LTrim() removes it only from the left, and .RTrim() only from the right. Default whitespace is space, tab, line feed, carriage return, vertical tab, and form feed.

An explicit argument is a set of bytes, not a substring pattern. Bytes in that set are removed repeatedly from the selected ends. Interior bytes remain.

var text : strslice = "  abc  "
var both : str = text.Trim()       // "abc"
var left : str = text.LTrim()      // "abc  "
var right : str = text.RTrim()     // "  abc"
var marked : rostr = "-=-abc-=-"
var name : str = marked.Trim("-=") // "abc"
var dashes : str = "---abc---"
dashes = dashes.Trim('-')          // "abc": assign to replace the original

docs.title: 2.8.9.6 .LPad and .RPad
docs.text:
.LPad(length : int, fill : strslice) -> str
.LPad(length : int, fill : char) -> str
.RPad(length : int, fill : strslice) -> str
.RPad(length : int, fill : char) -> str

.LPad(length, fill) and .RPad(length, fill) return text padded to the requested byte length. They repeat the fill value and truncate the last repetition as needed. If the requested length is no greater than the source length, the result has the original contents. An empty fill value raises a runtime error. Padding operates on bytes and can split a multibyte UTF-8 fill value.

var code : rostr = "abc"
var left : str = code.LPad(8, "01") // "01010abc"
var right : str = code.RPad(5, '.') // "abc.."
var same : str = code.LPad(2, ' ')  // "abc": no truncation

docs.title: 2.8.10 Byte Indexing and Slicing
docs.text:
text[index] reads one char byte from any string type. str and embedded strings also permit replacing a byte; rostr and strslice are read-only. Indices are zero-based. An index outside the existing bytes raises a runtime range error. Negative indices do not count backward from the end; use text[$last] or text[$end - 1] for the last byte. These operations do not decode or validate UTF-8.

text[start:end] borrows a half-open byte range as strslice, while text[start::end] includes the end byte. Slicing is supported on every string type: str, rostr, strslice, embstr(N), and unsized embstr. Slice bounds are clamped to [0, length]; reversed normalized bounds produce an empty slice.

$last is the last existing byte index and $end is the one-past-end position for the string being indexed or sliced. Omitting a slice bound selects the beginning or end. Negative slice bounds are clamped, rather than counted from the end; use $end - count to select a suffix.

var text : str = "abcdef"
var first : char = text[0]             // 'a'
text[0] = 'A'                          // text is "Abcdef"
var last : char = text[$last]          // 'f'
var part : strslice = text[1:3]        // "bc": end byte excluded
var inclusive : strslice = text[1::3]  // "bcd": end byte included
var head : strslice = text[:2]         // "Ab"
var tail : strslice = text[$end - 2:]  // "ef"
var all : strslice = text[-5:100]      // "Abcdef": bounds clamped
var empty : strslice = text[4:2]       // ""
var buffer : embstr(16) = "abcdef"
var from_buffer : strslice = buffer[1:4] // "bcd": borrows embedded storage

Slices borrow the source bytes. Keep the owner alive and its storage and contents stable while using them. Assign a slice to str to make an owned copy.

docs.title: 2.8.11 Unicode Operations
docs.text: The following members decode UTF-8 and report a runtime encoding error for malformed input. A displayed symbol can combine multiple Unicode characters, for example a letter and a combining accent. .wclen and .wchar[...] are available on every string type, including embstr(N) and unsized embstr.

docs.title: 2.8.11.1 Unicode Character Count
docs.text:
.wclen counts decoded Unicode characters. Unlike .length, it requires UTF-8 decoding rather than reading a stored byte count.

var text : embstr(16) = "Aé€"
var bytes : int = text.length // 6
var characters : int = text.wclen // 3

docs.title: 2.8.11.2 Unicode Indexing and Slicing
docs.text:
.wchar[index] reads one Unicode character as wchar. .wchar[start:end] returns a decoded range as [*]wchar; the start::end form includes the final character. In this context, $last and $end refer to Unicode character positions. Slice bounds are clamped; an invalid character index raises a runtime range error.

var text : embstr(16) = "Aé€"
var second : wchar = text.wchar[1]          // 'é'
var chars : [*]wchar = text.wchar[1:$end]   // ['é', '€']
var part : str = StrFromWchars(chars[:])   // "é€": encode the selected characters

docs.title: 2.8.11.3 .ToWchars
docs.text:
.ToWchars() -> [*]wchar

.ToWchars() decodes the whole string into [*]wchar. It works on every string type, including strslice, embstr(N), and unsized embstr. For repeated indexed Unicode processing, convert once and index the resulting array to avoid decoding the UTF-8 prefix for every lookup.

var text : embstr(16) = "Aé€"
var chars : [*]wchar = text.ToWchars()
var second : wchar = chars[1] // 'é'
var view : strslice = text
var from_view : [*]wchar = view.ToWchars() // ['A', 'é', '€']

docs.title: 2.9. Text Formatting
docs.text:
Text formatting inserts values into a string at placeholders such as {}. The format string supplies the surrounding text; a separate argument list supplies the values. DQ uses this text formatting syntax in multiple places, such as printing or creating exception messages.

DQ aims to be compatible with the brace-based formatting syntax of C++ std::format and Python str.format(). This chapter describes the currently supported placeholders and options.

docs.title: 2.9.1 A Simple Print Example
docs.text:
The examples use PrintLn from use print. Unless stated otherwise, they use these single-letter variables. The type-specific subsections repeat the relevant declarations so their examples can be read independently.

var i : int = 42
var n : uint = 255
var f : float = 3.5
var s : rostr = "Amy"
var b : bool = true
var c : char = 'A'
var w : wchar = '€'
var p : ^int = %i
var v : anyvalue
v.SetNull()

PrintLn("Hello, {}!", [s]) // = "Hello, Amy!"

{} is replaced by the first value in [s]. The square brackets belong to the DQ argument-list expression; they are not printed. PrintLn adds a newline after the result. Multiple placeholders consume values from left to right:

PrintLn("{} has {} messages.", [s, i]) // = "Amy has 42 messages."

docs.title: 2.9.2 Formatting Arguments: []anyvalue
docs.text:
To print formatted text to the standard output use these functions from the print package:

Print(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue)
PrintLn(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue)

fmt is the format string. args is an array slice of anyvalue. An anyvalue holds one supported value together with its type, so the formatter can tell whether to print text, a number, a Boolean, or a character.

docs.title: 2.9.2.1 Writing the Argument List
docs.text:
The usual syntax is [s, i, b]. Separate the elements with commas. The compiler knows that the formatting call expects []anyvalue, so it converts each element to anyvalue automatically. The elements can have different types; no explicit conversions to anyvalue are needed.

PrintLn("name={}, count={}, active={}", [s, i, b]) // = "name=Amy, count=42, active=true"

Each element can also be an expression:

PrintLn("next={}, doubled={}", [i + 1, i * 2]) // = "next=43, doubled=84"

Even a single value needs brackets, because the second parameter must be an array, not one value:

PrintLn("count={}", [i]) // = "count=42"

These calls have the wrong argument syntax and do not compile:

PrintLn("count={}", i) // ERROR: second parameter must be []anyvalue
PrintLn("{} {}", s, i) // ERROR: values belong together in [s, i]

docs.title: 2.9.2.2 Which Values Can Be Passed?
docs.text:
Value type Example argument Default output with {} Signed integers 42, -7, an int32 variable Decimal number Unsigned integers A uint or uint32 variable Decimal number; use {:u} for unsigned decimal formatting Floating-point numbers 3.5, a float32, float64, or float variable Decimal number Boolean values true, false, a comparison true or false char A char variable One byte written as a character wchar '€', a wchar variable One Unicode character encoded as UTF-8 char16 A char16 variable One Unicode character; converted to wchar Text A literal, str, rostr, strslice, embstr(N), or unsized embstr The text bytes ^char A pointer to zero-terminated text The pointed-to text Other typed or generic pointers A ^int or pointer variable Address in hexadecimal with a leading ^ Null stored in anyvalue A value initialized with .SetNull() null An existing anyvalue A previously stored supported value The representation of its stored value

The formatter preserves the value's type. A text value containing "42" is still text, and an integer containing 42 is still a number. The placeholder can choose a representation, but it does not perform arbitrary conversions between these categories.

PrintLn("{} / {} / {} / {}", [i, f, b, w]) // = "42 / 3.5 / true / €"

Objects, structures, function references, and whole arrays cannot be passed as values for automatic formatting. Select their fields or elements instead.

var a : [3]int = [10, 20, 30]

PrintLn("first={}, count={}", [a[0], a.length]) // = "first=10, count=3"

See anyvalue for its accessors and lifetime rules.

docs.title: 2.9.2.3 Reusing an Argument Array
docs.text:
An existing argument slice can be passed on to further functions. Pass the slice directly:

var m : rostr = "{} has {} messages."
var a : []anyvalue = [s, i]

PrintLn(m, a) // = "Amy has 42 messages."

There is no need to rebuild the list. PrintLn(m, [a]) would be a compile error: [a] is [1][]anyvalue, which is not compatible with []anyvalue.

docs.title: 2.9.2.4 Matching Values to Format String Placeholders
docs.text:
Each placeholder uses the next value. To print the same value multiple times, include it in the args multiple times:

PrintLn("{} + {} = {}", [i, i, i + i]) // = "42 + 42 = 84"

One argument is used for each placeholder. There are no named or numbered argument references. The current formatter writes null for a missing argument and ignores arguments left over after the last placeholder:

PrintLn("{} / {}", [s]) // = "Amy / null"
PrintLn("{}", [s, i])   // = "Amy"

These mismatches do not generate compile-time or runtime errors.

docs.title: 2.9.3 Format String Placeholders
docs.text: Ordinary characters in the format string are copied to the output. Each {...} placeholder inserts the next argument. {} uses the default representation; a colon introduces formatting options.

docs.title: 2.9.3.1 Main Placeholder Variants
docs.text: Form Accepted values Meaning {} / {:?} Any supported value Default representation. Use this for bool types {:d} Integers, characters Signed decimal number or character code {:u} Integers, characters Unsigned decimal number or character code {:x} Integers, characters Lowercase hexadecimal {:X} Integers, characters Uppercase hexadecimal {:p} Pointer values Hexadecimal address with a leading ^ {:s} Text, characters Text bytes or a character {:f} Floating-point values Decimal floating-point output {{ No argument Literal { }} No argument Literal }

docs.title: 2.9.3.2 Signed Integers: {:d}
docs.text:
Use {:d} for signed decimal output. {} gives the same result for a signed integer.

var i : int = 42

PrintLn("{:d}", [i])     // = "42"
PrintLn("[{:6d}]", [i])  // = "[    42]": minimum width
PrintLn("{:06d}", [i])   // = "000042": zero padding
PrintLn("{:+d}", [i])    // = "+42": explicit sign
PrintLn("{:+06d}", [i])  // = "+00042": sign followed by zero padding
PrintLn("[{: d}]", [i])  // = "[ 42]": reserve a sign position
PrintLn("{:06d}", [-i])  // = "-00042": negative sign before the zeros
PrintLn("[{:<6d}]", [i]) // = "[42    ]": left alignment

docs.title: 2.9.3.3 Unsigned Integers: {:u}
docs.text:
Use {:u} for unsigned decimal output, including the full range of uint.

var n : uint = 255

PrintLn("{:u}", [n])     // = "255"
PrintLn("[{:6u}]", [n])  // = "[   255]"
PrintLn("{:06u}", [n])   // = "000255"
PrintLn("[{:<6u}]", [n]) // = "[255   ]"

docs.title: 2.9.3.4 Hexadecimal Integers: {:x} and {:X}
docs.text:
Use x for lowercase digits and X for uppercase digits. These formats accept signed and unsigned integers.

var n : uint = 255

PrintLn("{:x}", [n])   // = "ff"
PrintLn("{:X}", [n])   // = "FF"
PrintLn("{:08X}", [n]) // = "000000FF": zero-padded hexadecimal
PrintLn("0x{:x}", [n]) // = "0xff": add the prefix as literal text

docs.title: 2.9.3.5 Floating-Point Numbers: {:f}
docs.text:
Use {:f} for decimal floating-point output.

var f : float = 3.5

PrintLn("{:f}", [f])       // = "3.5"
PrintLn("{:.2f}", [f])     // = "3.50": two fractional digits
PrintLn("{:.0f}", [f])     // = "4": rounded to a whole number
PrintLn("[{:8.2f}]", [f])  // = "[    3.50]": width includes the decimal point
PrintLn("{:+.2f}", [f])    // = "+3.50"
PrintLn("{:+08.2f}", [f])  // = "+0003.50"
PrintLn("[{:<8.2f}]", [f]) // = "[3.50    ]"

An explicit precision fixes the number of digits after the decimal point, rounding as needed and retaining trailing zeros. The decimal separator is a dot. Without explicit precision, {} and {:f} use up to 15 fractional digits and remove trailing zeros. Explicit precision is limited to 18 fractional digits.

The f placeholder requires a floating-point value; it does not convert an integer to a float.

docs.title: 2.9.3.6 Text: {:s}
docs.text:
Use {:s} or {} for text. The same formats accept the other supported string types and ^char. Here, t contains ten characters.

var s : rostr = "Amy"
var t : rostr = "abcdefghij"

PrintLn("{:s}", [s])     // = "Amy"
PrintLn("[{:8s}]", [s])  // = "[     Amy]": right alignment is the default
PrintLn("[{:<8s}]", [s]) // = "[Amy     ]": left-aligned text column
PrintLn("[{:>8s}]", [s]) // = "[     Amy]": explicit right alignment
PrintLn("[{:^8s}]", [s]) // = "[  Amy   ]": centered text
PrintLn("[{:8s}]", [t])  // = "[abcdefghij]": longer text is not truncated

The s kind is optional: {:8} and {:8s} both reserve a right-aligned field at least eight Unicode code points wide. Width never truncates longer text.

docs.title: 2.9.3.7 Booleans: {}
docs.text:
Use {} or {:?} for bool; there is no separate Boolean format letter.

var b : bool = true

PrintLn("{}", [b])     // = "true"
PrintLn("{}", [not b]) // = "false"
PrintLn("[{:6}]", [b]) // = "[  true]"

docs.title: 2.9.3.8 Characters: {:s}
docs.text:
Default formatting and {:s} write a character. Explicit numeric formats write its code.

var c : char  = 'A'
var w : wchar = '€'

PrintLn("{}", [c])     // = "A"
PrintLn("{}", [w])     // = "€"
PrintLn("{:s}", [w])   // = "€"
PrintLn("{:d}", [c])   // = "65"
PrintLn("{:u}", [w])   // = "8364"
PrintLn("{:04X}", [c]) // = "0041"

A char writes one byte; a wchar is encoded as UTF-8. A char16 value is converted to wchar before formatting. A UTF-16 surrogate pair is not combined automatically when its two code units are passed as two arguments. Convert UTF-16 text with StrFromUtf16() first. An invalid Unicode character value, including an isolated surrogate, produces �.

docs.title: 2.9.3.9 Pointers: {:p}
docs.text:
Use {:p} or {} for an address in hexadecimal with a leading ^. %i takes the address of i. The output below uses an example address; the actual address varies between runs.

var i  : int = 42
var p  : ^int = %i
var z  : pointer = nil
var pc : ^char = "abc"

PrintLn("{:p}", [p])           // = "^7FFC1234ABCD": address of i
PrintLn("{}", [p])             // = "^7FFC1234ABCD": same address with default formatting
PrintLn("{:p}", [z])           // = "^0": nil pointer
PrintLn("{}", [pc])            // = "abc": ^char is treated as text
PrintLn("{:p}", [pointer(pc)]) // = "^401234": convert to pointer to print the address

docs.title: 2.9.3.10 Null Values: {}
docs.text:
A null anyvalue prints null, which differs from the ^0 output of a nil pointer. Initialize a null value with .SetNull().

var v : anyvalue
v.SetNull()

PrintLn("{}", [v]) // = "null"

docs.title: 2.9.3.11 Literal Braces and Escaping
docs.text:
Double each brace in a format string to print one literal brace. Escaped braces do not consume arguments. In a double-quoted string literal, escape embedded double quotes as \":

var s : rostr = "Amy"

PrintLn("{{{}}}", [s])              // = "{Amy}"
PrintLn("{{\"name\":\"{}\"}}", [s]) // = '{"name":"Amy"}': escaped double quotes
PrintLn('{{"name":"{}"}}', [s])     // = '{"name":"Amy"}': single outer quotes avoid internal escaping
PrintLn("{{}}", [])                 // = "{}": just the literal braces
PrintLn("{}")                       // = "{}": no doubling need at non-formatting print

docs.title: 2.9.4 Width, Fill, Sign, Precision
docs.text:
The type-specific examples above show the common combinations. The supported option order is:

{: [alignment] [sign] [0] [width] [.precision] [kind] }

Spaces and square brackets in this diagram are explanatory; do not write them in the placeholder. Each bracketed part is optional.

Option Example Meaning < {:<8s} Left-align within the field > {:>8s} Right-align within the field ^ {:^8s} Center within the field + {:+d} Show + for a non-negative signed number or float - {:-d} Show a sign only for negative values; this is the default Space {: d} Use a leading space for a non-negative signed number or float 0 {:06d} Use zeros for right-aligned numeric padding Width {:8s} Reserve a field at least eight Unicode code points wide Precision {:.2f} Write two digits after the decimal point

Width and alignment work with text, characters, numbers, Boolean values, null, and pointers. DQ defaults to right alignment for every value type. < pads on the right, > pads on the left, and ^ divides padding between both sides. If centering needs an odd number of spaces, the extra space goes on the right.

Width is a minimum, not a maximum: longer values are never truncated to fit. Width counts Unicode code points, not UTF-8 bytes. For example, € counts as one code point even though its UTF-8 encoding uses three bytes, and café counts as four:

var w : wchar = '€'
var s : rostr = "café"

PrintLn("[{:>5s}]", [w]) // = "[    €]": four spaces plus one code point
PrintLn("[{:>6s}]", [s]) // = "[  café]": right alignment
PrintLn("[{:<6s}]", [s]) // = "[café  ]": left alignment
PrintLn("[{:^6s}]", [s]) // = "[ café ]": centered text

Combining marks count separately. Width does not measure visual character groups or terminal display columns.

A negative sign is written automatically. + also requests a sign for non-negative signed numbers and floating-point values. A space sign option reserves a sign position without writing +. The - option requests the default sign behavior; use < for left alignment.

Zero padding applies to right-aligned numbers and is written after the sign or pointer prefix. Left and center alignment use spaces even if 0 is present. Text and character output also use spaces.

Write alignment first, followed by the sign, zero fill, and width. For example, {:^+8d} centers a signed number, and {:+08d} enables zero fill with a sign. The former zero-before-sign spelling {:0+8d} is no longer supported.

docs.title: 2.9.5 Formatting APIs and Destinations
docs.text:
The same placeholders and []anyvalue argument syntax work with each API:

API Destination Availability Print(fmt, args) / PrintLn(fmt, args) Standard output use print Format(fmt, args) A new str Implicit sys; requires dynamic-string support .AddFmt(fmt, args) on str Appends to a dynamic string Requires dynamic-string support .AddFmt(fmt, args) on embstr Appends to a fixed buffer Works without dynamic-string support Exception(fmt, args) Exception message Requires exception support

The fmt parameter is strslice: literals, str, rostr, embstr, and existing slices can be passed directly. Even a substring can be used as the format:

var i : int = 42
var s : rostr = "{} ignored"

PrintLn(s[0:2], [i]) // = "42": only the "{}" slice is parsed

docs.title: 2.9.5.1 Print and PrintLn
docs.text:
Print(text : strslice)
Print(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue)
PrintLn()
PrintLn(text : strslice)
PrintLn(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue)

Print writes without adding a newline. PrintLn adds a newline, and PrintLn() writes a blank line.

Print("Hello, {}", [s]) // = "Hello, Amy": without a newline
PrintLn("!")            // = "!": followed by a newline
PrintLn()               // = "": a blank line

The one-argument form writes its text literally, without interpreting placeholders or escaped braces. Supplying the second argument selects the formatting overload:

PrintLn("{}")       // = "{}"
PrintLn("{{}}")     // = "{{}}"
PrintLn("{{}}", []) // = "{}"

docs.title: 2.9.5.2 Format
docs.text:
Format(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue) -> str

Use Format() when the result should be stored or returned rather than immediately printed. Format() is included in the implicit sys, which means it is available without a use declaration.

var s : str = Format("item-{:04d}", [i]) // = "item-0042": contents of s

Format() is also useful when passing formatted text to a function that does not support formatting itself. For example, a database connection's .Execute(sql) method takes a complete SQL statement. Here, dbconn is an open database connection and items is a table with one integer column:

var i : int = 42
dbconn.Execute(Format("INSERT INTO items VALUES ({:d})", [i]))

docs.title: 2.9.5.3 .AddFmt
docs.text:
.AddFmt(fmt : strslice, args : []anyvalue)

.AddFmt() appends to the existing contents of the str or embstr.

str and embstr(n) declarations without initializers initialize the string variables empty, so .AddFmt() can be called immediately (calling.Clear() before is not necessary):

var ds : str
ds.AddFmt("Order {}: {} items", [i, n]) // = "Order 42: 255 items": contents of s
var es : embstr(32)
es.AddFmt("mask = {:04X}", [n]) // = "mask = 00FF": contents of s

A str grows as needed by re-allocating its storage memory. An embstr(N) keeps its fixed buffer, including space for the terminating zero, so formatting can truncate the result:

var es : embstr(8)
es.AddFmt("{}", ["abcdefghij"]) // = "abcdefg": contents of s; seven bytes plus the terminator fit

Repeated .AddFmt() calls can assemble a larger message. Reserve space with .Reserve() first when the expected size of a dynamic string is known. This avoids repeated buffer growth and can reduce heap fragmentation.

The following example reserves 50000 bytes, enough for the numbers 1 through 10000, each followed by a space:

use print

func AppendNumbers(s : ref str):
    for i : int = 1 to 10000:
        s.AddFmt("{:d} ", [i])
    endfor
endfunc

func *Main():
    var s : str
    s.Reserve(50000)
    AppendNumbers(s)
    PrintLn("String length: {}", [s.length]) // = "String length: 48894"
endfunc

docs.title: 2.9.5.4 Exception Messages
docs.text:
The text formatting can be used at rising exceptions too:

var i : int = -42
if i < 1:
    raise Exception("invalid count: {}", [i]) // = "invalid count: 42"
endif

See Exceptions and Error Handling for raising, catching, and inspecting exceptions.

docs.title: 2.9.6 Argument and Error Rules
docs.text:
Formatting uses the stored value's type. For example, {:f} requires a float, while {:d} expects an integer or a character code. Convert the value explicitly before formatting when another category is needed:

PrintLn("{:.2f}", [float(i)])     // = "42.00"
PrintLn("{:d}", [StrToInt("42")]) // = "42"

A type/format mismatch produces a diagnostic marker instead of throwing a formatting exception:

PrintLn("{:f}", [i]) // = "<i-f!>": an integer with a float placeholder
PrintLn("{:d}", [s]) // = "<s-f!>": text with a numeric placeholder
PrintLn("{:d}", [b]) // = "<b-f!>": a Boolean with a numeric placeholder

docs.title: 2.9.6.1 Low-Level Formatter Flags
docs.text:
Format(), .AddFmt(), and the print helpers do not return a formatting status. For direct control, rtl/textformat exposes OTextFormatter, which writes through an OTextSink such as OTextSinkEmbStr, OTextSinkStr, or OTextSinkStdOut. Its .flags records DQFMT_FMT_ERROR for malformed braces or unsupported format options, and DQFMT_ARG_ERROR for incompatible value types or invalid Unicode characters. Each formatting call resets the flags.

With use rtl/textformat, let t be an OTextFormatter connected to the desired sink:

t.Format("{:f}", [i]) // = "<i-f!>": sets t.flags to DQFMT_ARG_ERROR

The runtime also defines DQFMT_TRUNCATED and DQFMT_SINK_ERROR, but the current built-in sinks do not set them when a fixed buffer fills. Keep the destination capacity in mind when complete output is required.

docs.title: 2.10. Arrays and Slices
docs.text:
An array keeps several values of the same type together, such as a list of names, a byte buffer, or a week's temperature readings. Use a fixed array when the number of values is known in advance, or a dynamic array when you need to add and remove values. A slice lets you work with part of an array without copying its elements.

Here is a small program that builds a shopping list of strings and prints it:

use print

func PrintList(list : []str):
    for item :? in list:
        PrintLn("{}", [item])
    endfor
endfunc

func *Main():
    var shopping : [*]str = ["bread", "milk"]
    shopping.Append("apples")
    shopping.Append(["potatoes", "tomatoes"])
    var i : int = shopping.IndexOf("potatoes")
    if i >= 0:
        shopping[i] = "rice"
    endif
    PrintList(shopping)
endfunc

This prints:

bread
milk
apples
rice
tomatoes

docs.title: 2.10.1 Array Forms
docs.text:
In the types below, T stands for the element type (e.g. int, float, str etc.), N is the number of elements in a fixed array.

Form Meaning When to use it [N]T A fixed array of N elements The size is known in advance, such as seven daily readings. [?]T A fixed array whose size comes from its initial values You want the compiler to count the values for you. []T A slice that borrows existing elements You want to pass an array or part of it to a function. [*]T A dynamic array that can grow or shrink You collect values as the program runs.

Every form has a .length property that returns the number of the array elements.

docs.title: 2.10.2 Array Properties and Methods
docs.text:
Use this table to find an operation, then follow its link for examples. D means dynamic arrays, F means fixed arrays, and S means slices. A result of — means the method returns no value; T is the element type.

Property or method Types Result Purpose .Append(value).Append(values) D — Add one or more elements at the end. .AppendSlice(values) D — Append the elements of another array or slice. .capacity D int Space available before more storage is needed. .Clear(free_storage = false) D — Remove everything; optionally release storage. .Clone() D [*]T Make an independent copy. .Compact() D — Reduce capacity to match the length. .Delete(index, count = 1) D — Remove one or more elements. .IndexOf(value) D, F, S int Find the first matching element, or return -1. .Insert(index, value).Insert(index, values) D — Add one or more elements before a position. .InsertSlice(index, values) D — Insert the elements of another array or slice. .length D, F, S int Number of elements. .Pop() D T Remove and return the last element. .PopFirst() D T Remove and return the first element. .Prepend(value).Prepend(values) D — Add one or more elements at the beginning. .refcount D int Number of references sharing the array. .Reserve(capacity) D — Make room for later additions. .SetCapacity(capacity) D — Set storage size, removing excess elements if needed. .SetLength(length) D — Change the number of elements.

docs.title: 2.10.3 Fixed Arrays
docs.text:
Use a fixed array when the number of elements will stay the same. Write the size inside brackets before the element type:

var readings : [7]float = {}              // seven readings, initially all zero
var header : [3]byte = [0x44, 0x51, 0x01] // exactly three bytes
var colors : [?]str = ["red", "green", "blue"] // the compiler infers [3]str

[?]T needs an array literal as its initializer so the compiler can count the elements. The length is part of a fixed array's type: [3]int and [4]int are different types. You can replace individual elements, but cannot add or remove any.

Assigning a fixed array to another compatible fixed array copies its elements:

var original : [3]float = [18.5, 21, 19.5]
var copy : [3]float = original
copy[0] = 22.5 // original[0] is still 18.5

Fixed arrays store their elements directly with the variable or containing structure. For arrays of autofree elements, assignment first frees the destination's previous objects, then transfers each source element and sets the source elements to nil. Assigning an array to itself leaves it unchanged. See the automatic cleanup rules.

docs.title: 2.10.4 Dynamic Arrays
docs.text:
Use [*]T when the number of elements can change. Dynamic arrays are initialized empty at the declaration, you can append elements using the .Append() method:

var names : [*]str
names.Append("Amy")
names.Append("Lin")
names.Append("Sam") // names is ["Amy", "Lin", "Sam"]

Assigning a dynamic array to another variable shares the same array. Changes to the elements, length, or capacity are visible through both variables. Use .Clone() when you need a separate copy:

var names : [*]str = ["Amy", "Lin"]
var shared : [*]str = names
shared[0] = "Sam"     // names is now ["Sam", "Lin"]
shared.Append("Jo")   // names is now ["Sam", "Lin", "Jo"]

var copy : [*]str = names.Clone()
copy[0] = "Alex"      // names[0] is still "Sam"

Assigning a different array to shared changes which array that variable uses; it does not make names use the new array.

Dynamic arrays allocate their element storage as needed and manage its lifetime automatically. An empty array can exist without allocating any storage.

Arrays of managed types, such as str, need extra runtime handling when elements are copied or removed. The compiler adds this handling automatically.

docs.title: 2.10.5 Indexing
docs.text:
Use array[index] to read or replace one element. Positions start at zero: the first element is at 0, the second at 1, and so on.

var names  : [*]str = ["Amy", "Lin", "Sam"]
var first  : str = names[0]    // "Amy"
var second : str = names[1]    // "Lin"
names[1] = "Jo"                // names is now ["Amy", "Jo", "Sam"]
var last : str = names[$last]  // "Sam"

$last means length - 1, the position of the last element. $end means length, the position just after it. Use $end for a slice bound or to insert at the end; it does not select an existing element.

Make sure the array is nonempty before using $last, and keep element indices between 0 and length - 1. Negative indices do not count backward from the end: use array[$last] or array[$end - 1] for the last element. Indexing does not adjust an invalid index to fit the available range.

Dynamic arrays report a runtime range error for invalid indices. Fixed arrays and slices currently omit runtime bounds checks for speed. An invalid access can read unrelated memory, corrupt data, or crash the program.

docs.title: 2.10.6 Slices
docs.text:
A slice is a view of existing elements. Use one to process just part of an array or to pass arrays of different sizes to the same function. Write []T for its type and array[start:end] to select a range. Slicing works on fixed arrays, dynamic arrays, and existing slices, with the same range rules as strings.

The start position is included and the end position is excluded. For example, data[1:3] selects elements 1 and 2:

var data   : [*]byte = [0x10, 0x20, 0x30, 0x40]
var middle : []byte  = data[1:3]  // [0x20, 0x30]
middle[0] = 0xFF                  // data is now [0x10, 0xFF, 0x30, 0x40]

Changing a slice element changes the original array because no elements were copied. A slice has its own length, but cannot add or remove elements from its source array.

Omit a bound to select from the beginning or through the end. Use :: instead of : when you want to include the element at the end position:

var data : [*]byte = [0x10, 0x20, 0x30, 0x40]
var all  : []byte = data[:]         // [0x10, 0x20, 0x30, 0x40]
var head : []byte = data[:2]        // [0x10, 0x20]
var tail : []byte = data[2:]        // [0x30, 0x40]
var last_two  : []byte = data[$end - 2:] // [0x30, 0x40]
var inclusive : []byte = data[1::3] // [0x20, 0x30, 0x40]

Slice bounds are limited to the available range: a negative bound becomes zero and a bound past the end becomes length. Negative slice bounds do not count backward from the end. If the resulting end is before the start, the slice is empty.

var data   : [4]int = [10, 20, 30, 40]
var all    : []int  = data[-5:100] // [10, 20, 30, 40]
var empty  : []int  = data[3:1]  // no elements
var at_end : []int  = data[$end:] // no elements
var negative_end : []int  = data[:-1] // no elements; -1 becomes zero

A slice borrows its source; it does not keep that source alive. Keep the original array alive while using the slice. Adding or removing elements, resizing, or releasing a dynamic array's storage can make existing slices and element pointers invalid. Create a new slice after such a change, even if the change seems to affect another part of the array. You also cannot keep a slice of a temporary array that disappears before the slice does.

docs.title: 2.10.7 Function Parameters
docs.text:
Use a slice parameter, []T, when a function needs to read or update elements without resizing the array. The caller can pass a fixed array, a dynamic array, or a slice with a compatible element type. Passing an array automatically gives the function a view of all its elements:

func Sum(values : []float) -> float:
    result = 0
    for value :? in values:
        result += value
    endfor
endfunc

func *Main():
    var fixed   : [3]float = [18.5, 21, 19.5]
    var growing : [*]float = [20.5, 22]
    var total   : float = Sum(fixed)     // 59
    var other   : float = Sum(growing)   // 42.5
    var part    : float = Sum(fixed[1:]) // 40.5
endfunc

A slice parameter can also change the caller's elements, just like the middle slice in the previous section. For a function that adds or removes elements, use a dynamic array passed by reference:

func AddName(names : ref [*]str, name : str):
    names.Append(name)
endfunc

func *Main():
    var names : [*]str = ["Amy", "Lin"]
    AddName(names, "Sam") // names is now ["Amy", "Lin", "Sam"]
endfunc

Dynamic-array parameters require a reference mode; names : [*]str by value is not supported. A ref parameter can resize the array or replace the caller's array variable. Other parameter modes and their read/write restrictions are explained in Functions.

docs.title: 2.10.8 Iteration
docs.text:
Use for ... in to work with each element in order. :? asks the compiler to infer the loop variable's type:

var readings : [*]float = [18.5, 21, 19.5]
var total    : float = 0
for reading :? in readings:
    total += reading
endfor
// total is 59

The ordinary loop variable receives each element's value. Use ref when you want to change the array elements themselves:

var readings : [*]float = [18.5, 21, 19.5]
for reading : ref in readings:
    reading += 0.5
endfor
// readings is now [19, 21.5, 20]

A ref loop variable refers directly to the current array element and has its exact type. Do not add or remove elements or otherwise resize the dynamic array while using that reference: the element may move or disappear.

When the array stores autofree elements, an ordinary loop variable refers to each object without removing it from the array or freeing it after the iteration. Use a ref loop variable to replace an element in place; this automatically frees the previous object. Elements can be nil, so check before using their fields or methods. See Dynamic Array autofree Elements.

docs.title: 2.10.9 Array Properties
docs.text: Properties let you inspect an array. They are read-only; use methods such as .SetLength() and .Reserve() to change its size or storage.

docs.title: 2.10.9.1 .length
docs.text:
.length counts elements, not bytes. Use it to check whether an array is empty or to find out how many values a slice contains. It works on every array form.

var data   : [4]int = [10, 20, 30, 40]
var middle : []int = data[1:3]
var total  : int = data.length   // 4
var count  : int = middle.length // 2
var empty  : [*]int
var is_empty : bool = empty.length == 0 // true

docs.title: 2.10.9.2 .capacity
docs.text:
.capacity tells you how many elements fit in a dynamic array's current storage. It is at least as large as .length. Extra capacity is spare room for future additions; it does not create extra elements that you can index.

var scores : [*]int = [10, 20, 30]
scores.Reserve(100)
var count : int = scores.length         // 3
var has_room : bool = scores.capacity >= 100 // true

When growth exceeds the capacity, the array obtains more storage automatically. An empty array with no allocated storage has capacity zero.

docs.title: 2.10.9.3 .refcount: Reference Count
docs.text:
.refcount is mainly useful for checking how many references share a dynamic array. Assigning it to another variable adds a reference; creating a slice does not. Temporary values can also add references. An array with no allocated storage has reference count zero.

var scores : [*]int = [10, 20, 30]
var shared : [*]int = scores
var references : int = scores.refcount // 2

docs.title: 2.10.10 Dynamic Array Methods
docs.text:
See Array Properties and Methods for a quick overview.

Call these methods on a dynamic array, such as names.Append("Amy"). Methods that change the array affect every variable sharing it. .Clone() returns a separate array, and .Pop() and .PopFirst() return the element they remove. The other methods return no value.

The prototypes below use T for the array's element type: for [*]str, T means str. A values : []T parameter accepts a fixed array, a dynamic array, or a slice with a compatible element type. These prototypes describe the built-in methods; you do not need to declare them yourself.

You can pass part of the same array as the source for an append or insert. The method preserves the source values even if it needs to move the array's storage:

var values : [*]int = [10, 20, 30]
values.Append(values[:2]) // [10, 20, 30, 10, 20]

After a method changes the array's size or storage, previously created slices for this array might become invalid; see Slices. Arrays of autofree elements have additional move and copy restrictions; see Dynamic Array autofree Elements.

docs.title: 2.10.10.1 .Append and .Prepend
docs.text:
.Append(value : T)
.Append(values : []T)
.AppendSlice(values : []T)
.Prepend(value : T)
.Prepend(values : []T)

Use .Append() to build a list one value at a time or add a whole group at once. Use .Prepend() to put values at the beginning. When adding several elements, both methods keep their original order.

var names : [*]str = ["Lin"]
names.Append("Sam")            // ["Lin", "Sam"]
names.Prepend(["Amy", "Jo"])   // ["Amy", "Jo", "Lin", "Sam"]
names.AppendSlice(["Alex"])    // ["Amy", "Jo", "Lin", "Sam", "Alex"]

.AppendSlice() explicitly adds the source's elements. This is useful for arrays whose elements are themselves arrays, where .Append() may instead add the source as one element.

Prepending moves the existing elements to make room. For a large list built one element at a time, appending usually does less work.

docs.title: 2.10.10.2 .Insert and .InsertSlice
docs.text:
.Insert(index : int, value : T)
.Insert(index : int, values : []T)
.InsertSlice(index : int, values : []T)

Use .Insert() to put values before an existing position. Elements at that position and after it move to make room. .InsertSlice() explicitly inserts all the source elements, like the range form of .Insert().

var stops : [*]str = ["home", "office"]
stops.Insert(1, ["bakery", "school"]) // ["home", "bakery", "school", "office"]
stops.Insert($end, "park")           // ["home", "bakery", "school", "office", "park"]

$end inserts after the last element, like .Append(). A negative insertion position inserts at the beginning, and a position past the end inserts at the end. Inserting near the beginning of a large array moves more elements than inserting near its end.

docs.title: 2.10.10.3 .Delete
docs.text:
.Delete(index : int, count : int = 1)

Use .Delete(index) to remove one element, or supply count to remove several. The elements after the removed range move to close the gap and keep their order.

var scores : [*]int = [10, 20, 30, 40]
scores.Delete(1, 2) // [10, 40]: remove elements at positions 1 and 2
scores.Delete(1)    // [10]
scores.Delete(100)  // [10]: nothing at this position

A negative position starts deleting at the beginning. A count larger than the remaining length removes everything from that position onward. A non-positive count or a position at or past the end leaves the array unchanged.

docs.title: 2.10.10.4 .Pop and .PopFirst
docs.text:
.Pop() -> T
.PopFirst() -> T

Use .Pop() to take the last element, for example when treating an array as a stack. Use .PopFirst() to take the first element, such as the next job in a small queue. Both remove the element and return its value.

var jobs : [*]str = ["download", "resize", "save"]
var next : str = jobs.PopFirst() // "download"; jobs is ["resize", "save"]
var last : str = jobs.Pop()      // "save"; jobs is ["resize"]

Check .length before popping if the array might be empty: both methods raise a runtime error on an empty array. .PopFirst() moves all remaining elements toward the beginning, so repeatedly using it on a large queue can be expensive.

docs.title: 2.10.10.5 .SetLength
docs.text:
.SetLength(length : uint)

Use .SetLength() when you know how many elements you need, for example before filling a byte buffer by index. Growing adds initialized elements: new numbers are zero and new strings are empty. Shrinking removes elements from the end but keeps the spare storage for later use.

var packet : [*]byte
packet.SetLength(3) // [0, 0, 0]; length and capacity are 3
packet[0] = 0x44
packet[1] = 0x51
packet[2] = 0x01
packet.SetLength(2) // [0x44, 0x51]; capacity stays 3

The requested length must be non-negative. If it exceeds the current capacity, .SetLength() allocates space for exactly that many elements. Existing spare capacity is retained when the requested length already fits.

When you append an element to an array with no spare space, the runtime doubles its allocated capacity, leaving room for later additions. Appending to an array with no allocated storage starts with room for one element.

docs.title: 2.10.10.6 .Reserve
docs.text:
.Reserve(capacity : uint)

Use .Reserve() before collecting many values when you can estimate the final size. It makes room for at least that many elements, which can avoid repeatedly moving the array into larger storage. It does not add elements, change existing values, or reduce capacity.

var readings : [*]float
readings.Reserve(100) // still empty, with room for at least 100 readings
readings.Append(18.5)
readings.Append(21.5) // [18.5, 21.5]; the reserved space is being used

Capacity must be non-negative. You can keep appending beyond the reserved amount; the array will grow automatically.

docs.title: 2.10.10.7 .SetCapacity and .Compact
docs.text:
.SetCapacity(capacity : uint)
.Compact()

Use .Compact() after building an array if you want to release its unused space. It reduces capacity to the current length without removing elements.

.SetCapacity() gives you direct control over the storage size. If the requested capacity is smaller than the length, elements at the end are removed to fit. Increasing capacity leaves the elements and length unchanged.

var values : [*]int = [10, 20, 30]
values.SetCapacity(2) // [10, 20]; length and capacity are 2
values.Reserve(100)
values.Compact()      // [10, 20]; capacity is 2 again

Capacity must be non-negative. Use .Reserve() when you only want to make room for later additions without risking removal of existing elements.

docs.title: 2.10.10.8 .Clear
docs.text:
.Clear(free_storage : bool = false)

Use .Clear() to empty a list before filling it again. It keeps the storage so later additions can reuse it. Pass true when you also want to release the storage. Both forms leave the array empty.

var messages : [*]str = ["Connected", "Ready"]
messages.Clear()             // length is 0; capacity is retained
messages.Append("Restarted") // ["Restarted"]: reuse the existing storage
messages.Clear(true)         // length and capacity are 0

docs.title: 2.10.10.9 .Clone
docs.text:
.Clone() -> [*]T

Use .Clone() to keep an independent copy before changing an array. Assigning the result to a new variable lets you edit that copy without changing the original array's elements.

var names : [*]str = ["Amy", "Lin", "Sam"]
var saved : [*]str = names.Clone()
names[0].Append(" Lovelace") // saved[0] is still "Amy"

For str elements, later edits to a string in either array leave the other array's string unchanged, as shown above.

Cloning copies the elements according to their types. Object references still point to the same objects, and nested dynamic arrays still share their inner arrays. Clone those inner arrays too if you need separate copies at every level. Cloning arrays of autofree elements is not supported; see Dynamic Array autofree Elements.

docs.title: 2.10.11.1 .IndexOf
docs.text:
.IndexOf(value : T) -> int

Use .IndexOf() to find an element in a fixed array, dynamic array, or slice. It returns the first matching position, starting at zero, or -1 if the value is absent. Check for -1 before using the result as an index.

var scores : [*]int = [10, 20, 30, 20]
var position : int = scores.IndexOf(20) // 1: the first match
if position >= 0:
    scores[position] = 25              // [10, 25, 30, 20]
endif
var missing : int = scores.IndexOf(99) // -1

For a slice, the result counts from the start of that slice:

var data : [4]int = [10, 20, 30, 40]
var middle : []int = data[1:3]          // [20, 30]
var position : int = middle.IndexOf(30) // 1, rather than 2

For str elements, .IndexOf() compares the text contents, just like ==. The comparison is case-sensitive and works on fixed arrays, dynamic arrays, and slices of str. Separate strings containing the same text match:

var names : [*]str = ["Amy", "Lin", "Sam", "Lin"]
var wanted : str = "Lin"
var position : int = names.IndexOf(wanted) // 1: the first matching name
var missing : int = names.IndexOf("lin")  // -1: case matters

For other element types, the search compares the bytes stored for each element. This works directly for values such as integers and bytes. Object references match only when they point to the same object; the search does not compare object contents. For structures, floating-point values, or other types that need a custom comparison, use a loop with the comparison you want. Structure padding and different floating-point bit patterns can otherwise affect the result.

docs.title: 2.10.11.2 Equality
docs.text:
For dynamic arrays and array slices, == [] checks whether the length is zero and <> [] checks whether there are any elements:

var jobs : [*]str
var empty : bool = jobs == [] // true
jobs.Append("download")
var has_jobs : bool = jobs <> [] // true

var pending : []str = jobs[:]
var has_pending : bool = pending <> [] // true
var finished : []str = jobs[1:]
var all_done : bool = finished == [] // true

To compare the contents of two arrays, compare their lengths and then their elements in a loop. General array equality is not provided automatically.

docs.title: 2.10.12 Multidimensional Arrays
docs.text:
An array can contain other arrays. Use this to represent a grid or table. For example, [2][3]int has two rows, each containing three integers:

var matrix : [2][3]int = [ [1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6] ]
var value : int = matrix[1][2] // 6: second row, third column
matrix[0][1] = 20             // first row is now [1, 20, 3]

You can also nest dynamic arrays when rows need to grow separately. Each row has its own storage. Cloning the outer array copies the row references, so the copy still shares those rows; see .Clone().

docs.title: 2.10.13 Dynamic Array autofree Elements
docs.text:
Use an element type such as autofree OTask when the array should automatically free the objects stored in it. Replacing an element frees its previous object. Removing elements with .Delete(), .Clear(), or a smaller length or capacity also frees the removed objects. Any remaining objects are freed when the last reference to the dynamic array is released. Assigning the array to another variable still shares the same array, rather than copying its objects.

New autofree elements start as nil, including those added by .SetLength(). Assigning nil to an element frees its current object and leaves that position empty, without changing the array's length. A nil element has nothing to free.

Assigning an autofree variable to an array element transfers the object and sets the source variable to nil. Single-element .Append(), .Prepend(), and .Insert() do the same:

object OTask:
    name : str
    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var tasks : [*]autofree OTask
    tasks.SetLength(2) // [nil, nil]

    var task = new autofree OTask('download')
    tasks[0] = task    // task is now nil; tasks[0] refers to the object
    tasks[0] = nil     // frees the object; tasks is [nil, nil], length still 2

    tasks.Append(new OTask('list'))
    var next : autofree OTask = tasks.Pop() // removes the object without freeing it
endfunc // next is freed automatically

.Pop() and .PopFirst() remove an element without freeing its object. They return an ordinary object reference: assign it to an autofree variable, as above, or explicitly delete it when finished. Popping a nil element returns nil; popping an empty array is still an error. Likewise, check for nil before accessing an element's fields or calling its methods.

Copying a range of autofree elements and calling .Clone() are not supported, because two separate arrays must not automatically free the same objects. See the automatic cleanup rules for more details.

docs.title: 2.11. Enumerations
docs.text:
An enumeration, or enum, gives names to a set of choices. Use one for values such as an order's status, a traffic light's color, or a game's difficulty. Each choice is called an enumerator.

Enum type names conventionally start with a capital N, as in NOrderStatus.

Here is a small program that changes an order's status:

use print

enum NOrderStatus = (pending, shipped, delivered)

func *Main():
    var status : NOrderStatus = pending
    status = shipped
    if status == shipped:
        PrintLn("Your order is on its way.")
    endif
