endfunc

This prints Your order is on its way.. The enum makes the choices clear and prevents an unrelated number or a value from another enum being assigned to status.

docs.title: 2.11.1 Declaration
docs.text:
Write enum, a type name, and the choices in parentheses:

enum NColor = (red, green, blue)

The choices have integer values behind the scenes. By default, the first is zero and each following choice adds one: red is 0, green is 1, and blue is 2. You normally work with the names rather than these numbers.

docs.title: 2.11.1.1 Explicit Values and Storage
docs.text:
In the declaration, assign an integer value with = after a choice's name. You can also select the storage type with : type after the enum type name:

enum NState : uint16 = (
    idle = 0,
    running = 10,
    stopped = 20,
)

enum NSigned : int8 = (negative = -1, zero, positive)

Explicit values must be compile-time integer constants. After an explicit value, the next implicit value is one higher: NSigned.zero is 0 and NSigned.positive is 1. Values must be unique and increase in declaration order; a later explicit value cannot move backward.

Only declared values belong to the enum. For example, NState has values 0, 10, and 20; 11 is not an enum member. Explicit values are useful when matching a file format or an external interface.

The default storage type is uint8. You can select int8, uint8, int16, uint16, int32, uint32, int64, or uint64 to fit the required range. For example, NState above occupies two bytes, while NSigned occupies one byte and allows negative values. Every choice, including an implicit value, must fit the storage type. The enum remains a separate type from the integer used to store it.

docs.title: 2.11.2 Naming and Lookup
docs.text:
When the expected enum type is clear, use the choice's name directly. You can also include the enum type name:

var color : NColor = green
color = NColor.blue
var is_blue : bool = color == blue // true

The shorter form works in assignments, function arguments, return values, and comparisons when the compiler can identify one expected enum type. Write NColor.green when that context is missing or the name could be ambiguous.

docs.title: 2.11.3 Type Safety
docs.text:
Compare values of the same enum with ==, <>, <, <=, >, or >=. Ordering follows their integer values, so red < blue when both are used as NColor values.

Enums do not support arithmetic or automatic conversion to integers. For example, assigning 1 to an NColor variable is an error even though green has that integer value. Use the conversion helpers below when reading numbers from a file or another program.

docs.title: 2.11.4 Ordinal Conversion
docs.text:
Use the read-only .ord property or Ord(value) to get a choice's integer value:

var color : NColor = green
var code : uint8 = color.ord // 1

To turn a number into an enum, use the enum type's methods. These methods check that the number belongs to a declared choice:

Method Use it when NColor.FromOrd(number) The number must be valid; an unknown value raises a runtime error. NColor.FromOrd(number, fallback) An unknown value should use a fallback choice. NColor.TryFromOrd(number, output) You want to check success before using the result.

For example, decode a saved color with a fallback:

var saved_code : int = 99
var color : NColor = NColor.FromOrd(saved_code, red) // red: 99 is unknown

if NColor.TryFromOrd(2, color):
    // color is now blue
endif

TryFromOrd returns true and updates output for a valid number. Otherwise it returns false and leaves output unchanged. Use this method or a fallback when a file or message might contain choices added by a newer program.

docs.title: 2.12. Structures and Unions
docs.text:
A structure keeps related values together. For example, a point has an x and a y coordinate, and a measurement might have a reading and a timestamp. Each named value inside a structure is a field.

Structure type names conventionally start with a capital S, as in SPoint.

use print

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

func *Main():
    var point : SPoint = {x: 10, y: 20}
    var copy : SPoint = point
    copy.x = 30
    PrintLn("{} {}", [point.x, copy.x])
endfunc

This prints 10 30. Assigning a structure copies its fields, so changing copy.x leaves point.x unchanged.

A union lets several fields share the same storage. It is useful for binary formats and C interfaces, and is covered after the structure examples.

docs.title: 2.12.1 Structures
docs.text:
Declare fields between struct Name: and endstruct. Use a dot to read or change a field:

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

var point : SPoint
point.x = 10
point.y = 20
point.y += 5 // point is now {x: 10, y: 25}
var origin : SPoint = {} // both coordinates are zero

A structure stores its fields directly in the variable that contains it.

Structures cannot contain managed strings, dynamic arrays, object references, embedded objects, or aggregates with managed fields. Use an object when you need those fields.

For short text stored inside a structure, use a fixed-storage embedded string:

struct SProduct:
    name : embstr(32)
    price : float
endstruct

var product : SProduct = {}
product.name = "Bread"
product.price = 2.5

Each structure declaration defines a separate type: two structures with the same fields are still different types.

docs.title: 2.12.1.1 Structure Initialization
docs.text:
A local structure variable declared without an initializer starts uninitialized. Reading it immediately produces a VarNotInit compiler error. Use = {} to explicitly initialize all fields to their zero/default values:

func Example():
    var point : SPoint       // uninitialized local variable
    var origin : SPoint = {} // x and y are zero
    point = {10, 20}         // initialize before reading
endfunc

Global structure variables and structure fields embedded in objects are zero-initialized by default when no initializer is supplied.

docs.title: 2.12.1.2 Structure Initializer Literals
docs.text:
A brace literal supplies the initial field values. You can name the fields or list values in field declaration order:

var named : SPoint = {x: 10, y: 20}
var positional : SPoint = {10, 20}
named = {y: 40, x: 30} // named fields may appear in either order

Use a final ? to give all remaining fields their default values:

var point : SPoint = {x: 10, ?} // y is zero
var origin : SPoint = {}       // all fields use their defaults

Without ?, supply every field exactly once. {?} also initializes the whole structure to its defaults. The ? fill marker always have to be the last.

The compiler checks and interprets the structure literals according the expected structure type supplied by a variable or function argument.

Nested initialization literals can be used for structures containing structure fields. Here, start and finish are both SPoint fields, so each inner pair of braces creates an SPoint:

struct SLine:
    start : SPoint
    finish : SPoint
endstruct

var line : SLine = {start: {0, 0}, finish: {10, 20}}

You can initialize a fixed array of structures with a single literal:

var points : [2]SPoint = [{0, 0}, {10, 20}]

You can mix positional and named structure entries. After a named entry, the next positional entry fills the field following it in declaration order:

var point : SPoint = {x: 10, 20} // x is 10; y is 20

A structure literal is a temporary value and cannot be passed directly to a reference parameter; put it in a variable first. Structure literals may also initialize compile-time constants, including public constants imported from another module. Union constants are not supported.

docs.title: 2.12.2 Storage Size with SizeOf()
docs.text:
SizeOf(Type) returns a type's storage size in bytes. You can also pass a variable name as SizeOf(variable). Both forms produce a compile-time integer constant:

const POINT_SIZE : int = SizeOf(SPoint)
var point : SPoint = {}
var bytes : int = SizeOf(point) // same as SizeOf(SPoint)

For a structure, the size includes all fields and any padding between or after them. For a union, it is the size of the shared storage, including any padding. Alignment and [[packed]] can affect the result; see Structure Field Alignment and Padding.

docs.title: 2.12.3 Field Offsets with OffsetOf()
docs.text:
OffsetOf(Type, field) returns the number of bytes from the start of a structure to the named field. Pass the type name and the field name without quotes. The result is a compile-time integer constant; no structure variable is needed:

struct SHeader [[packed]]:
    kind : uint8
    length : uint32
endstruct

const KIND_OFFSET : int = OffsetOf(SHeader, kind)     // 0
const LENGTH_OFFSET : int = OffsetOf(SHeader, length) // 1

Here, length starts one byte after the start of the structure. OffsetOf() includes any padding before a field, so removing [[packed]] may change the result. See Structure Field Alignment and Padding for alignment and padding rules.

Use OffsetOf() when checking a binary layout or matching an external record. OffsetOf() also accepts union types, where every field has offset zero.

docs.title: 2.12.4 Structure Methods
docs.text:
A method is a function that belongs to a type. Use one to perform an operation on the structure's fields:

struct SSize:
    width : int
    height : int

    func Area() -> int:
        return width * height
    endfunc
endstruct

var size : SSize = {width: 4, height: 3}
var area : int = size.Area() // 12

Inside the method, fields are available by name. Methods can also be declared inside the structure and defined later with a qualified name, such as func SSize.Area() -> int:.

Structure methods do not have the virtual dispatch described for objects.

docs.title: 2.12.5 Structure Inheritance
docs.text:
A structure can inherit fields and methods from one base structure:


struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

struct SPoint3D(SPoint):
    z : int
endstruct

var point : SPoint3D = {x: 10, y: 20, z: 30}

When inintializing a derived structure base fields come first, followed by derived fields.

docs.title: 2.12.6 Storage Unions
docs.text:
A union provides several ways to interpret the same bytes. Declare it with union Name: and endunion:

union UWord:
    raw : uint32
    bytes : [4]byte
endunion

var word : UWord = {raw: 42}
var number : uint32 = word.raw // 42

All fields begin at the same address. Writing word.raw also changes the bytes seen through word.bytes. Which byte comes first depends on the target's byte order.

Initialize a union with exactly one field, or use {} to zero all its storage. Storage beyond the chosen field receives default initialization. Assignment copies the complete union storage.

A union must contain at least one field. Unions do not support inheritance, methods, properties, field initializers, automatic conversion to a field's type, or union-valued constants. Each union declaration defines a distinct type.

docs.title: 2.12.6.1 Nested Union Fields
docs.text:
A structure or object can contain a named union field. For example, a measurement may store an integer reading or a floating-point reading:

struct SReading:
    kind : int
    union data:
        integer : int32
        real : float32
    endunion
endstruct

var reading : SReading = {kind: 1, data.integer: 42}
var value : int32 = reading.data.integer // 42

Here, the program can use kind to remember which form it stored. DQ does not maintain this field automatically. data.integer: 42 is a shorter spelling of data: {integer: 42}. Select only one alternative for each union field in an initializer; alternatives may themselves contain nested structures or unions.

docs.title: 2.12.7 Structure Field Alignment and Padding
docs.text:
Fields are stored in declaration order. Each field normally starts at an offset that satisfies its type's alignment requirement. For example, an uint32 field starts at an offset divisible by four. The compiler inserts unused bytes, called padding, between fields when needed.

A structure's alignment is the largest alignment required by any of its fields or its base structure. For example, if that alignment is four bytes, the structure must start at an address divisible by four.

Its size must also be a multiple of four in that example. If the fields and the padding between them take 10 bytes, the compiler adds 2 unused bytes at the end, making the size 12 bytes. In an array, the next structure then starts 12 bytes later, again at an address divisible by four.

docs.title: 2.12.7.1 Packed Structures
docs.text:
Put [[packed]] after the structure name, before the colon, to store fields consecutively without adding padding between them or after the last field. A packed structure has one-byte alignment:

struct SRecord:
    tag : byte
    count : uint32
    code : uint16
endstruct

struct SPackedRecord [[packed]]:
    tag : byte
    count : uint32
    code : uint16
endstruct

On a target where uint32 has four-byte alignment and uint16 has two-byte alignment, these declarations have the following layouts:

Query Normal structure Packed structure OffsetOf(Type, tag) 0 0 OffsetOf(Type, count) 4 1 OffsetOf(Type, code) 8 5 SizeOf(Type) 12 7

Packing an outer structure does not change the internal layout of a nested structure field. That field retains its own size and any internal padding. Packed fields may have unaligned addresses; this matters when passing their addresses to external code or hardware.

docs.title: 2.12.7.2 Explicit Field Alignment
docs.text:
Use [[align(n)]] after a field declaration to request a larger alignment in bytes:

struct SAlignedRecord:
    tag : byte
    value : uint16 [[align(8)]]
endstruct

Here, value starts at offset 8, the structure has eight-byte alignment, and its size is 16 bytes. A smaller alignment request does not reduce a field's natural alignment. In a packed structure, field alignment attributes are ignored.

A union uses the strictest alignment required by any field and is large enough for its largest field, rounded up to that alignment. [[packed]] is not supported on unions.

Use fixed-width fields and check SizeOf and OffsetOf when matching a C record or hardware interface. These queries, member access, and address-taking also work with unions. See Attributes and C Interoperability.

docs.title: 2.13. Pointers
docs.text: A pointer stores a memory address, which identifies a location in memory.

docs.title: 2.13.1 Pointer Basics
docs.text:
For a data type T, write ^T to create the corresponding pointer type, such as ^int or ^float.

When working with pointers, it is important to distinguish between address operations and pointed-data operations.

Address operations work on the memory address stored in the pointer. DQ works on the address when neither ^ nor . is written after the name of the pointer variable or constant: ptr = address

Pointed-data operations work on the data at the address stored in the pointer. DQ works on that data when ^ or . is written after the name of the pointer variable or constant. This is also called dereferencing: ptr^ = value

A simple example using the % to get the address of a variable:

var u32value : uint32       // an ordinary variable whose storage is managed by the compiler
u32value = 0x04030201       // assigns a value to the variable

var byteptr : ^byte         // declares a pointer variable of type `^byte`
byteptr = ^byte(%u32value)  // points to the memory location where `u32value` is stored
byteptr^ = 0x55             // updates the first byte at that address

PrintLn('u32value = 0x{:08X}', [u32value])  // = "u32value = 0x04030255"

On a little-endian system, the first byte is the least significant byte of u32value, so the example prints the result shown above.

Pointers are widely used and can improve performance significantly.

Using pointers also can be dangerous. There are many ways to end up with an invalid pointer (one that points to an invalid memory location). Accessing data through an invalid pointer can return invalid data or cause the application to crash.

Pointers are useful when working with C libraries, raw buffers, or hardware. For an ordinary function that updates a caller's variable, a ref parameter is usually simpler.

For a more practical example for using pointers see the Example: Processing a Sensor Packet.

docs.title: 2.13.2 Pointer Variables
docs.text:
Assigning a pointer variable sets its pointing address. A pointer variable can be re-assigned to point a different address:

var first  : int = 10
var second : int = 20
var curptr : ^int

curptr = %first    // setting the address of the pointer
curptr^ = 15       // first is now 15; current^ also reads 15
curptr = %second   // redirects curptr to second
curptr^ = 25       // second is now 25; first remains 15

var otherptr : ^int = current // assignment between two pointer variables

docs.title: 2.13.3 Typed Pointers and Casting
docs.text:
A pointer's type tells the compiler how to access the data at its address: how many bytes to read or write, which structure fields are available, and how far to move during pointer arithmetic.

The type after ^ describes the pointed-to value. For example, ^byte accesses a single byte, ^int32 accesses a 4-byte signed integer, and ^float accesses a floating-point number occupying 4 or 8 bytes, depending on the target. (The size of the pointer itself is the same for all three types, either 4 or 8 bytes depending on the target CPU architecture.)

The pointed-to type also determines the step size of pointer arithmetic and indexing: adding 1 to a ^byte moves by 1 byte, while adding 1 to a ^uint32 moves by 4 bytes.

Casting converts a value from one type to another, or tells the compiler to treat a value as a different type.

For pointers, casting usually changes the pointer type without changing the address stored in the pointer. The same memory address is then interpreted as pointing to a different data type.

The cast tells the compiler how to interpret the address; it does not check the actual value stored there.

Sometimes an address comes from an API without type information, or the same memory needs to be accessed through a different pointer type. An explicit cast supplies the required type.

Write ^T(address) to cast an address to a pointer to T. A pointer cast does not read, copy, or convert the data stored there.

For example, ^byte, ^int32, ^float, and ^uint64 pointers can all point to the beginning of the same eight-byte buffer. Use % to take its address and a trailing ^ to read or write through each pointer:

use print

var buffer : [8]byte [[align(8)]]

func ShowBuffer(acaption : strslice):
    Print("{:<28} at {:p}:", [acaption, %buffer[0]])
    for i : int = 0 count buffer.length:
        Print(" {:02X}", [buffer[i]])
    endfor
    PrintLn()
endfunc

func *Main():
    var byteptr  : ^byte   = %buffer[0]
    var intptr   : ^int32  = ^int32(%buffer[0])
    var floatptr : ^float  = ^float(%buffer[0])
    var u64ptr   : ^uint64 = ^uint64(%buffer[0])

    ShowBuffer("Initial")

    for i : int = 0 count buffer.length:
        byteptr[i]^ = 0xD0 + i
    endfor
    ShowBuffer("Set Pattern")

    byteptr^ = 42    // writes 1 byte
    ShowBuffer("byteptr^ = 42")

    intptr^ = -1000  // writes 4 bytes
    ShowBuffer("intptr^ = -1000")

    floatptr^ = 1.5  // writes SizeOf(float) bytes
    ShowBuffer("floatptr^ = 1.5")

    u64ptr^ = 0x0102030405060708 // writes 8 bytes
    ShowBuffer("u64ptr^ = 0x0102030405060708")
endfunc

Example output on Linux x64 (the address varies between runs):

Initial                      at ^555512345678: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
Set Pattern                  at ^555512345678: D0 D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6 D7
byteptr^ = 42                at ^555512345678: 2A D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6 D7
intptr^ = -1000              at ^555512345678: 18 FC FF FF D4 D5 D6 D7
floatptr^ = 1.5              at ^555512345678: 00 00 00 00 00 00 F8 3F
u64ptr^ = 0x0102030405060708 at ^555512345678: 08 07 06 05 04 03 02 01

ShowBuffer prints the starting address followed by all eight bytes in memory order. The global buffer starts with zeroes.

The "Set Pattern" loop writes the pattern using pointer indexing through byteptr[i]^, without changing byteptr.

The following byteptr^ = 42 changes only the first byte of that pattern. The int32 write changes the first 4 bytes to the two's-complement representation of -1000, leaving D4 D5 D6 D7 unchanged. Almost all current CPU architectures use little-endian byte order, with the least significant byte first. The floating-point write uses 8 bytes and shows the float64 representation of 1.5. On targets with a 4-byte float, that write changes only the first 4 bytes. The final 0x0102030405060708 uint64 write always uses 8 bytes: 08 07 06 05 04 03 02 01 in little-endian byte order.

The global buffer has eight-byte alignment, requested by [[align(8)]], so it can hold any of these values at its starting address, as some CPU architectures cannot read/write multi-byte data types from unaligned addresses.

%buffer[0] takes the address of its first byte. The casts ^int32(%buffer[0]), ^float(%buffer[0]), and ^uint64(%buffer[0]) take the same address and give it different pointer types.

As all four pointers access the same storage, each write overwrites the bytes used by that type, and each read interprets those bytes according to the pointer's type. Reading through intptr^ after the floating-point write would interpret the low 4 bytes of the floating-point representation as an integer (=0); it would not convert 1.5 to an integer.

docs.title: 2.13.4 The nil Value
docs.text:
nil is the special pointer value meaning no target. It is also called a null-pointer and represents address zero. Both typed pointers, such as ^int, and generic pointer variables can be assigned nil.

A nil pointer is always invalid for accessing data. Dereferencing it to read or write data, either with ptr^ or through a structure field such as ptr.field, usually causes the program to crash with a Segmentation Fault. The exact failure depends on the target system; never dereference nil.

Assigning, copying, and comparing nil are safe address operations. Use == or <> to check whether a pointer has a target before accessing its data:

var value : int = 10
var ptr   : ^int = nil // no target yet

if ptr == nil:
    ptr = %value      // give the pointer a valid target
endif

if ptr <> nil:
    ptr^ += 1         // value is now 11
endif

ptr = nil             // clear the pointer; value remains 11

Setting a pointer to nil clears its stored address; it does not change or free the pointed-to data, unless it is an autofree pointer.

docs.title: 2.13.5 Pointers as Function Parameters
docs.text:
Typed pointers can also be function parameters. A pointer may be nil, meaning it has no target, so a function that accepts an optional target must check before dereferencing it:

func Increment(target : ^int):
    if target <> nil:
        target^ += 1
    endif
endfunc

func *Main():
    var count : int = 10
    Increment(%count) // count is now 11
    Increment(nil)    // no target, so nothing is changed
endfunc

A non-nil pointer must still refer to a live value of the correct type. Copying a pointer does not copy its target or keep that target alive. DQ does not generally check raw addresses for you.

docs.title: 2.13.6 Structure Pointers
docs.text:
Pointers tor structures are very useful to manipulate memory structures at arbitrary positions in the memory. Fields of the pointed structure can be accessed either with ^. or . only.

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

var point   : SPoint = {x: 10, y: 20}
var address : ^SPoint = %point
address^.x = 30 // changes point.x
address.x  = 30 // changes point.x, `.` dereferences automatically

docs.title: 2.13.7 Generic Pointers
docs.text:
A generic pointer carries no information about the data it points to. Generic pointers do not support typed element arithmetic until converted to a suitable typed pointer.

Cast it to a typed pointer before accessing that data:

var value  : uint32 = 0x01020304
var rawptr : pointer = %value

^byte(rawpr)^ = 0x55 // value is now 0x01020355

Here, ^byte(rawptr) produces a pointer of type ^byte, so the ^byte(rawpr)^ expression manipulates the lowest byte of the 4-byte value.

docs.title: 2.13.8 Pointer Size and Memory Addresses
docs.text:
A pointer variable is either 32 bits (4 bytes) or 64 bits (8 bytes) wide, depending on the target CPU architecture. This is the size of the stored address; the data it points to can have a different size. For example, ^byte and ^uint64 have the same size on a given target.

In DQ, int and uint always have the same size as a pointer: SizeOf(pointer), SizeOf(int), and SizeOf(uint) are equal.

Target Pointer size int uint ARM_M (Arm Cortex-M) 32 bits (4 bytes) int32 uint32 Linux x64 (x86_64-linux) 64 bits (8 bytes) int64 uint64

Memory addresses are usually written in hexadecimal, where each digit represents 4 bits. A full-width 32-bit address has 8 hexadecimal digits, while a full-width 64-bit address has 16. Leading zeroes are often omitted.

For example, addresses might look like this:

Target Example address Meaning ARM_M 0x20001234 A location in the SRAM region ARM_M 0x40001000 A location in the peripheral region Linux x64 0x0000555512345678 A location in a process's virtual address space Linux x64 0x00007FFC1234ABCD Another possible user-space virtual address

On ARM_M, addresses refer directly to memory or hardware registers. The Cortex-M memory map defines regions such as SRAM and peripherals; the exact locations available depend on the microcontroller.

On Linux x64, an ordinary program uses virtual addresses, which the operating system maps to physical memory. Addresses can vary between runs. A pointer still occupies 8 bytes even when its address uses fewer than 16 hexadecimal digits; the CPU and operating system do not make every possible 64-bit address usable. You can see the Linux x64 memory map for more details.

DQ's PrintLn displays pointer addresses in hexadecimal with a leading ^ instead of 0x:

var value   : int = 42
var address : ^int = %value
PrintLn("{:p}", [address])

Example output could be ^20001234 on ARM_M or ^7FFC1234ABCD on Linux x64. These are illustrative addresses; the actual address depends on where value is stored.

docs.title: 2.13.9 Pointer Arithmetic and Indexing
docs.text:
Pointer arithmetic counts elements of the pointed-to type. For a pointer ptr : ^T, adding n moves the address by n * SizeOf(T) bytes.

Operation Meaning Changes ptr? ptr + n Address n elements forward No ptr - n Address n elements backward No ++ptr / --ptr Move forward / backward by one element Yes ptr += n / ptr -= n Move forward / backward by n elements Yes ptr[n] Same address as ptr + n No

Pointer indexing returns a pointer, so ptr[n]^ reads or writes the selected value. For a structure pointer, use ptr[n]^.x to access a field of the selected structure.

docs.title: 2.13.9.1 Stepping Through the Same Buffer
docs.text:
This example uses a fixed [16]byte buffer. It first advances a byte pointer, then casts its current address to ^uint32 and continues in 4-byte steps. The structure writes start at byte offset 8. Here, SPoint uses int16 coordinates so that each point occupies 4 bytes on both 32-bit and 64-bit targets.

Pointer type Element size Bytes moved by one ++ Byte offset selected by [1] from the start ^byte 1 byte 1 1 ^uint32 4 bytes 4 4 ^SPoint 4 bytes 4 4

The same 16 bytes can therefore hold 16 bytes, four uint32 values, or four SPoint values. These are different views of the same storage; writes through any of the pointers change buffer.

The uint32 writes below use unaligned addresses, so run this example on a target that supports them, such as Linux x64.

use print

struct SPoint:
    x : int16
    y : int16
endstruct

var buffer : [16]byte [[align(8)]]

func ShowBuffer(caption : strslice):
    Print("{:<18}:", [caption])
    for i : int = 0 count buffer.length:
        Print(" {:02X}", [buffer[i]])
    endfor
    PrintLn()
endfunc

func *Main():
    var byteptr  : ^byte   = %buffer[0]
    for i : int = 0 count buffer.length:
        byteptr[i]^ = i // indexing leaves byteptr at the start
    endfor
    ShowBuffer("Initial")

    byteptr^ = 0xAA // writes 1 byte at offset 0
    ++byteptr       // moves 1 byte: now at buffer[1]
    byteptr^ = 0xBB // writes 1 byte at offset 1
    ++byteptr       // moves 1 byte: now at buffer[2]
    ShowBuffer("After ++byteptr")

    var u32ptr : ^uint32 = ^uint32(byteptr) // keeps byte offset 2
    u32ptr^ = 0xD1D2D3D4 // writes 4 bytes at offsets 2..5
    ++u32ptr             // moves 4 bytes: now at buffer[6]
    u32ptr^ = 0xE1E2E3E4 // writes 4 bytes at offsets 6..9
    ++u32ptr             // moves 4 bytes: now at buffer[10]
    ShowBuffer("After ++u32ptr")

    // Start at offset 8 so that two 4-byte points fit in the buffer.
    var pointptr :? = ^SPoint(%buffer[8])
    pointptr.x = 11 // writes 2 bytes at offsets 8..9
    pointptr.y = 21 // writes 2 bytes at offsets 10..11
    ++pointptr      // moves 4 bytes: now at buffer[12]
    pointptr.x = 12 // writes 2 bytes at offsets 12..13
    pointptr.y = 22 // writes 2 bytes at offsets 14..15
    ShowBuffer("After ++pointptr")

    // Reset all three pointers to the beginning before comparing indexing.
    byteptr  = %buffer[0]
    u32ptr   = ^uint32(%buffer[0])
    pointptr = ^SPoint(%buffer[0])

    byteptr[2]^ = 0xCC       // byte offset 2
    u32ptr[1]^ = 0xA1A2A3A4  // byte offset 4: the second uint32
    pointptr[2]^.x = 0x5353  // writes 2 bytes at offsets 4..5: the second point's x
    pointptr[2]^.y = 0x5252  // writes 2 bytes at offsets 6..7: the second point's y
    ShowBuffer("Indexed writes")

    PrintLn("Second point: ({}, {})", [pointptr[1]^.x, pointptr[1]^.y])

    var fourth : ^SPoint = pointptr + 3 // byte offset 12: the fourth point
    PrintLn("Distance: {} points, {} bytes",
        [fourth - pointptr, ^byte(fourth) - ^byte(pointptr)])
endfunc

Example output on Linux x64 (little-endian):

Initial           : 00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F
After ++byteptr   : AA BB 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F
After ++u32ptr    : AA BB D4 D3 D2 D1 E4 E3 E2 E1 0A 0B 0C 0D 0E 0F
After ++pointptr  : AA BB D4 D3 D2 D1 E4 E3 0B 00 15 00 0C 00 16 00
Indexed writes    : AA BB CC D3 A4 A3 A2 A1 53 53 52 52 0C 00 16 00
Second point: (41892, 41378)
Distance: 3 points, 12 bytes

Each ++ changes only the pointer's address; the assignments through the pointers change the buffer. Casting byteptr to ^uint32 keeps its current byte offset, 2; the subsequent ++u32ptr operations step to offsets 6 and 10. The structure writes at offsets 8..15 overwrite the last two bytes of the previous uint32 write as well as the remaining initial bytes.

After the reset, the [] expressions leave all three pointers at the beginning. For example, u32ptr[1]^ writes the same four bytes as (u32ptr + 1)^. pointptr[1]^.x selects the second point, dereferences it, and accesses its x field. The indexed SPoint writes replace the same four bytes at offsets 4..7 that were just written through u32ptr[1]^.

Subtracting two pointers of the same type gives their distance in elements. The two point addresses above are three SPoint elements apart. Casting both to ^byte before subtracting gives the distance in bytes: 12.

The buffer starts at an address aligned with [[align(8)]], but offsets 2 and 6 are still unaligned for uint32. On targets that require aligned accesses, start those writes at offsets divisible by 4. A cast alone does not provide alignment or make more storage available. Unlike array indexing, pointer indexing carries no length information and does not check bounds. Keep each entire value you read or write within the buffer. You may form a pointer just past the last element, but must not dereference it; subtract pointers only within the same allocation or its one-past-end position.

docs.title: 2.13.10 Allocation and Lifetime
docs.text:
Use new when the pointed-to value needs separately allocated storage, and initialize it before reading it. Use delete when finished:

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

var point : ^SPoint = new SPoint
point^ = {x: 10, y: 20}
delete point = nil // release the allocation and clear this variable

Other pointers to the same allocation become invalid after delete; they are not cleared automatically. To release an allocation automatically when leaving a scope, use autofree ^T. See Memory Management and Autofree.

Pointers into local variables or fixed arrays are valid only while that storage exists. Resizing a dynamic array or growing or changing a string's storage can also invalidate pointers into it. Obtain a fresh pointer after such a change. Never return a pointer to a function's local variable.

docs.title: 2.13.11 Dangling Pointers
docs.text:
A non-nil address does not always guarantee that a pointer is valid: it might refer to memory that has already been freed or to a variable that has gone out of scope, like a local variable. Such pointers are called dangling pointers.

Using SPoint from the allocation example above:

var point : ^SPoint = new SPoint
point^ = {x: 10, y: 20}
var borrowed : ^SPoint = point // both pointers refer to the same allocation

delete point = nil          // free the allocation and clear point
// borrowed is still non-nil, but is now dangling:
// borrowed.x = 30          // invalid: the target has already been freed
borrowed = nil              // clear the dangling pointer

Never dereference nil or dangling pointers.

docs.title: 2.13.12.1 A Linked List with First and Last Pointers
docs.text:
A linked list stores each value in a node with a pointer to the next node. The nodes can be allocated separately. Unlike an array, the list is traversed by following next, rather than by incrementing a pointer.

SList keeps two addresses: first selects the first node and last selects the final node. Both are nil for an empty list. Keeping last lets Append add a node without walking through all the existing nodes. The last node's next is always nil.

use print

struct SNode:
    value : int
    next  : ^SNode
endstruct

struct SList:
    first : ^SNode
    last  : ^SNode

    func Append(value : int):
        var node : ^SNode = new SNode
        node.value = value
        node.next = nil

        if last == nil:
            first = node // adding the first node to an empty list
        else:
            last.next = node
        endif
        last = node
    endfunc

    func PopFirst(value : ref int) -> bool:
        if first == nil:
            return false
        endif

        var node : ^SNode = first
        value = node.value
        first = node.next // save the next address before releasing the node
        if first == nil:
            last = nil // removing the only remaining node empties both ends
        endif
        delete node
        return true
    endfunc

    func Clear():
        var value : int = 0
        while PopFirst(value):
        endwhile
    endfunc
endstruct

func *Main():
    var list : SList = {} // both first and last start as nil
    list.Append(10)
    list.Append(20)
    list.Append(30)
    PrintLn("First: {}, last: {}", [list.first.value, list.last.value])

    Print("Values:")
    var current : ^SNode = list.first
    while current <> nil:
        Print(" {}", [current.value])
        current = current.next // follow the link; nodes need not be adjacent
    endwhile
    PrintLn()

    var value : int = 0
    while list.PopFirst(value):
        PrintLn("Removed: {}", [value])
    endwhile
    PrintLn("Empty: {}", [list.first == nil and list.last == nil])

    list.Append(40) // the emptied list can be used again
    PrintLn("Reused: first={}, last={}", [list.first.value, list.last.value])
    list.Clear() // release every node still owned by the list
    PrintLn("Cleared: {}", [list.first == nil and list.last == nil])
endfunc

Example output:

First: 10, last: 30
Values: 10 20 30
Removed: 10
Removed: 20
Removed: 30
Empty: true
Reused: first=40, last=40
Cleared: true

When appending to an empty list, the new node becomes both first and last. Otherwise, last.next links the old tail to the new node, and last moves to that node. Appending changes links, without moving any existing nodes.

PopFirst returns false for an empty list. Otherwise, it copies the first node's value into the caller's variable, advances first to node.next, and then deletes the removed node. It clears last when the last remaining node is removed, so a later Append correctly starts a new list. Both appending and removing the first node take a constant number of pointer operations.

The list owns its allocated nodes. Clear reuses PopFirst to release all of them; deleting one node does not automatically follow and delete its next. Call Clear before the list leaves scope if it still contains nodes. Copying an SList structure copies only its two addresses, so it does not create an independent list and must not create a second owner of the same nodes. Any borrowed pointer to a removed node becomes invalid when that node is deleted.

docs.title: 2.13.12.2 Processing a Sensor Packet
docs.text:
This is a longer, somewhat practical example demonstrating using pointers.

Suppose a sensor station sends a binary packet containing a header followed by measurement records. The header tells us the format version, measurement time, location, and number of records. Each record identifies a measurement type and channel, and stores a measured value. In this example, measurement type 1 means temperature in degrees Celsius and type 2 means relative humidity in percent.

A file or network API may supply this packet as a buffer address and a byte count. Pointers let us read the header and records directly in that buffer, without copying each record into a separate variable.

For safer data handling structures are used in practice. Here two structures are used to group the data fields: SDataHeader and SDataRec. The SDataHeader describe the 32-byte header and the SDataRec the 8-byte data records.

Byte offset:  0                  32             40              48
              | SDataHeader      | SDataRec      | SDataRec      |
              | version, count,  | type, channel,| type, channel,|
              | time, location,  | pad, value    | pad, value    |
              | reserved space   |               |               |

The sender must use the same field layout, byte order as the receiver.

The _pad fields in this example align the data fields manually and/or reserve space for future expansions. The _pad fields initialized with zeroes.

Here, Main builds a packet in memory with that layout so the program can run without a file or network connection. SExamplePacket only supplies the sample storage; PrintData uses the address and byte count and can handle any number of records that fits.

use print
use time

struct SDataHeader:
    version  : uint32     // format identifier
    reccount : uint32     // data record count
    mtime    : float64    // measurement time: @time.Time()
    location : uint32     // measurement location
    _pad     : [3]uint32  // reserved bytes for future expansion
endstruct

struct SDataRec:
    mtype      : byte  // measurement type: 1 = temperature, 2 = humidity
    channel    : byte  // one station can have multiple sensors
    _pad       : [2]byte
    value      : float32  // measurement value
endstruct

func PrintData(data : pointer, size : int):
    if data == nil or size < SizeOf(SDataHeader):
        PrintLn("Incomplete header")
        return
    endif

    var header :? = ^SDataHeader(data)
    if header.version <> 1:
        PrintLn("Unsupported data version")
        return
    endif

    var capacity : int = (size - SizeOf(SDataHeader)) div SizeOf(SDataRec)
    if header.reccount > capacity:
        PrintLn("Incomplete records")
        return
    endif

    PrintLn("Location {}, time {}, record count: {}",
        [header.location, FormatTime1('yyyy-mm-dd hh:nn:ss', header.mtime), header.reccount])

    // header[1] points just past the header, where the records begin.
    var record :? = ^SDataRec(header[1])
    for i : uint32 = 0 count header.reccount:
        PrintLn("  mtype={}, channel={}, value={:.1f}",
            [record.mtype, record.channel, record.value])
        ++record
    endfor
endfunc

// Supplies an aligned buffer containing a header and two records.
struct SExamplePacket:
    header  : SDataHeader
    records : [2]SDataRec
endstruct

func *Main():
    var packet : SExamplePacket = {
        header: {version: 1, reccount: 2, location: 7, ?},
        records: [
            {mtype: 1, channel: 0, value: 21.5, ?},
            {mtype: 2, channel: 0, value: 45, ?}
        ]
    }
    // The structure literal can contain constants only. This is not a constant:
    packet.header.mtime = Time()

    PrintData(%packet, SizeOf(packet))
endfunc

Example output (the time varies because Time() supplies the current time):

Location 7, time 2026-10-31 19:30:00, record count: 2
  mtype=1, channel=0, value=21.5
  mtype=2, channel=0, value=45.0

In var header :? = ^SDataHeader(data), the cast converts the generic buffer address to ^SDataHeader, and :? tells the compiler to infer header's type from that expression. This allows header.version and header.reccount to access the header's fields. The cast does not read or copy the whole header.

To find the records, header[1] selects the address one header past header, equivalent to header + 1. Because header has type ^SDataHeader, this moves by SizeOf(SDataHeader), or 32 bytes. Pointer indexing returns a pointer, so header[1] does not read a second header; it only computes the address where the records begin.

Similarly, var record :? = ^SDataRec(header[1]) converts that address to ^SDataRec and infers that pointer type for record, letting us read a record's fields. Then ++record advances by one record, or 8 bytes. Both operations use the pointed-to type's size: header[1] skips a header, while record[1] would point to the next record.

Before accessing records, the function divides the remaining byte count by SizeOf(SDataRec) to find how many complete records fit. It checks the announced count against that capacity. Dividing the available space avoids multiplying an unchecked record count, which could overflow. Try passing SizeOf(packet) - 1 to PrintData: it prints Incomplete records without reading either record.

The caller must still supply a valid buffer of at least size bytes; the function cannot verify that an arbitrary address refers to that much memory. The pointers borrow packet's storage and are used only during the call, while packet is alive. No allocation or delete is needed. A binary format with a different byte order or floating-point representation needs explicit decoding rather than these direct pointer casts.

docs.title: 2.13.12.3 Double Pointers and an argv-Style Dynamic List
docs.text:
A double pointer, such as ^^char, points to a variable or array element that itself holds a ^char. This is useful for a list of pointers, such as a C-style argument table (argv): each entry points to a zero-terminated string. The strings can have different lengths and do not need to be adjacent in memory.

This example builds the strings in a dynamic array, then builds a separate dynamic array of pointers to their text. It passes the address of the first pointer slot as ^^char, together with an argument count (argc). A final nil entry also allows traversal without using the count.

use print

func PrintArgs(argc : int, argv : ^^char):
    for i : int = 0 count argc:
        var text : rostr = argv[i]^ // read a ^char from the pointer table
        PrintLn("argv[{}] = {}", [i, text])
    endfor

    var cursor : ^^char = argv
    Print("First characters:")
    while cursor^ <> nil:
        var textptr : ^char = cursor^
        Print(" {}", [textptr^])
        ++cursor // advance to the next ^char slot, not the next character
    endwhile
    PrintLn()
endfunc

func *Main():
    var arguments : [*]str = ["demo", "--color"]
    arguments.Append("blue")

    var pointers : [*]^char
    for i : int = 0 count arguments.length:
        pointers.Append(arguments[i].pchar)
    endfor
    pointers.Append(nil) // the final slot marks the end of the list

    var argv : ^^char = %pointers[0]
    PrintArgs(arguments.length, argv)

    var replacement : str = "green"
    argv[2]^ = replacement.pchar // replace a pointer in the table
    var selected : rostr = pointers[2]
    PrintLn("After replacement: {}", [selected])
    PrintLn("Original string: {}", [arguments[2]])
endfunc

Example output:

argv[0] = demo
argv[1] = --color
argv[2] = blue
First characters: d - b
After replacement: green
Original string: blue

There are two levels of storage between argv and a character:

Expression Type Meaning argv ^^char Address of the first pointer slot argv[i] ^^char Address of pointer slot i argv[i]^ ^char String address stored in slot i textptr^ char One character at the selected string address

++cursor moves by SizeOf(^char): one pointer slot, or 4 or 8 bytes depending on the target. It does not move through the string's characters. To do that, increment the inner ^char pointer instead.

Assigning argv[2]^ replaces the pointer stored in pointers[2]. It does not copy text, modify the string "blue", or replace arguments[2]. The rostr variables borrow the selected zero-terminated text so PrintLn can print it as a string rather than as an address.

The dynamic arrays manage their own storage. The pointer table borrows the strings; it does not own them. Keep arguments and replacement alive while their text pointers are used, and obtain fresh .pchar values after changing the source strings. Finish building pointers before taking %pointers[0]: resizing it can invalidate argv and cursor. The function expects argc valid string pointers followed by a nil slot; a raw double pointer does not carry the table's length.

docs.title: 2.13.12.4 Using Double Pointers for Return Values
docs.text:
A function can return a value normally and supply another result through a pointer parameter. To return a ^SList this way, the parameter must be ^^SList: the address of the caller's pointer variable.

For example, CollectHighReadings builds a list of temperature readings at or above a threshold. It returns the number of matching readings and writes the new list's address through its last parameter, outlist.

Reuse SNode and SList from A Linked List with First and Last Pointers, and replace that example's Main with the following code:

func CollectHighReadings(readings : []int, threshold : int, outlist : ^^SList) -> int:
    if outlist == nil or outlist^ <> nil:
        return -1 // require an output pointer whose current value is nil
    endif

    var list : ^SList = new SList
    list^ = {} // initialize first and last to nil
    var count : int = 0
    for reading : int in readings:
        if reading >= threshold:
            list.Append(reading)
            ++count
        endif
    endfor

    outlist^ = list // update the caller's pointer variable
    return count
endfunc

func *Main():
    var readings : [?]int = [22, 31, 24, 35]
    var alerts : ^SList = nil
    var count : int = CollectHighReadings(readings, 30, %alerts)
    if count < 0:
        PrintLn("Invalid output pointer")
        return
    endif

    PrintLn("High readings: {}", [count])
    var current : ^SNode = alerts.first
    while current <> nil:
        PrintLn("Reading: {}", [current.value])
        current = current.next
    endwhile

    alerts.Clear()      // release the list's nodes
    delete alerts = nil // release the SList itself and clear the pointer
endfunc

Example output:

High readings: 2
Reading: 31
Reading: 35

alerts has type ^SList, so %alerts has type ^^SList. Inside the function, outlist^ accesses the caller's alerts variable. Assigning outlist^ = list therefore changes alerts itself. A parameter of type ^SList would only receive a copy of its address; reassigning that parameter would not update the caller's pointer.

The caller must initialize alerts to nil. The function returns -1 without changing it if the output parameter is nil or the pointer slot is already occupied, avoiding overwriting an existing list. On success, the caller owns the new list and its nodes, even when no readings match and the list is empty. Call Clear before deleting the list, because deleting an SList alone does not free its nodes.

docs.title: 2.14. Objects and Properties
docs.text:
An object keeps data and the functions that work on it together. Its data is stored in fields (variables that belong to the object), and its functions are called methods. Use objects for things that have their own state and behavior, such as a counter, a document, a sensor, or a network connection.

Object type names conventionally start with a capital O, as in OCounter.

use print

object OCounter:
    value : int = 0

    func Increment():
        value += 1
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var counter <- OCounter()
    counter.Increment()
    counter.Increment()
    PrintLn("{}", [counter.value])
endfunc

This prints 2. The arrow <- creates an embedded object named counter (an object allocated directly in the local function rather than separately on the heap), and OCounter() creates and initializes it. When Main finishes, the object is cleaned up automatically.

Objects differ from structures in several important ways:

Feature Structure Object Assignment Copies the fields Copies the reference; both variables point to the same object Allowed fields Plain data only Any type, including str, [*]T, and other objects Setup and cleanup None Constructor (*Create), destructor (*Destroy), automatic field cleanup Methods Plain methods Supports virtual methods and properties Type testing No Can test the actual type at runtime with is

docs.title: 2.14.1 Fields and Methods
docs.text:
An object declaration defines two things between object Name: and endobject: - Fields: variables that belong to the object and hold its data. - Methods: functions that belong to the object and can read or update its fields.

A field can have an initial value (such as lives : int = 3), which is given to every newly created object. Fields without an initializer start with their zero or empty value: numeric fields start at zero, strings and dynamic arrays start empty, and object references start as nil (referring to no object).

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

object OPlayer:
    name     : str        // starts empty
    scores   : [*]int     // dynamic array, starts empty
    position : SPoint     // all fields zero
    lives    : int = 3
    rival    : OPlayer    // object reference, starts nil

    func AddScore(points : int):
        scores.Append(points)
    endfunc

    func Total() -> int:
        result = 0
        for points : int in scores:
            result += points
        endfor
    endfunc
endobject

Use a dot (.) to access a field or call a method:

var player <- OPlayer()
player.name = "Lin"
player.AddScore(10)
player.AddScore(25)
var total : int = player.Total() // 35

Inside a method, the object's own fields and methods can be used directly by name—no special prefix is needed.

If an object needs to refer to itself—for example, to pass itself as an argument to another function—it uses the special name self, as in engine.Create(self).

DQ checks code from top to bottom. This means a method must be declared before other methods in the same object can call it. If method A calls method B, write B above A, or declare the method first and define its body later.

To call a function outside the object from inside a method, use a module prefix: @.PrintLn(...) reaches PrintLn imported into the current module, while @print.PrintLn(...) names the print module explicitly. Compiler built-ins such as SizeOf() need no prefix. The full lookup rules and method-local use are covered under Organizing Object Code.

docs.title: 2.14.2 Object References
docs.text:
An object variable holds a reference (a handle pointing to the object in memory), rather than containing a separate copy of the fields. Assigning an object variable to another variable makes both refer to the same object:

var counter <- OCounter()
var alias : OCounter = counter
alias.Increment()
// counter.value is now 1: counter and alias refer to the exact same object

This is different from structures: copying a structure copies all of its data, so changing one copy leaves the other unchanged.

The same applies when passing objects to functions. An ordinary object parameter receives a reference to the caller's object, so the function can read and modify the object directly without needing a ref parameter:

func GiveBonus(player : OPlayer):
    player.AddScore(5) // modifies the caller's player object
endfunc

An ordinary reference such as alias or player only borrows the object: it can use the object, but it does not own it and is not responsible for destroying it.

docs.title: 2.14.2.1 The nil Reference
docs.text:
An object reference can be nil, meaning it currently points to no object at all. Like any other local variable in DQ, an object variable must be initialized before it is read (for example, initialized to nil).

Always check whether a reference might be nil before using it:

var selected : OPlayer = nil
// ...
if selected <> nil:
    selected.AddScore(1)
endif

Accessing a field or calling a method through a nil reference is invalid and stops the program with an error (a segmentation fault).

docs.title: 2.14.3 Creating and Destroying Objects
docs.text:
Every object needs memory to hold its fields. DQ provides three ways to store and manage an object, depending on how long it needs to exist:

Form How it works When to use it counter <- OCounter() Embedded object: stored directly in a function's local storage, the global data segment, or a containing object. Use for local objects, global objects, or fields without a separate heap allocation. Local objects and fields are destroyed automatically; globals are not. var counter = new autofree OCounter() Auto-free object: lives in dynamic memory (the heap). The variable owns it and releases it automatically. The object needs to outlive a single function, but you still want automatic cleanup without calling delete. var counter = new OCounter() Manually managed heap object: lives on the heap. You must destroy it yourself with delete. You want full manual control over when the object is destroyed.

docs.title: 2.14.3.1 Embedded Objects (<-)
docs.text:
An embedded object declared with <- has its storage directly in the context where it is declared:

  • Inside a function, it lives in local storage (the stack) and is destroyed automatically when its scope ends, including on an early return or when an exception leaves the scope.
  • At module scope, it lives in the global data segment. Global embedded objects are not destroyed automatically when the program finishes.
  • As a field of another object, it lives inside the containing object and is destroyed with it.

An embedded object cannot be redirected to point to another object, and it cannot be passed to delete.

For an embedded field, the constructor call can be delayed: write field <- OType .., without (), and call field.Create(...) explicitly from the containing object's constructor. See Embedding Objects in Fields for an example.

docs.title: 2.14.3.2 Constructors and Destructors
docs.text:
A constructor is a special method named *Create. It runs automatically when a new object is being created, allowing you to initialize fields and accept arguments from the caller.

A destructor is a special method named *Destroy. It runs automatically when the object is being destroyed, allowing you to perform any final cleanup (such as closing a file or releasing an external system resource).

The asterisk * marks them as special functions. When calling them explicitly or referring to them, write their names without *.

use print

object OConnection:
    host : str

    func *Create(ahost : strslice):
        host = ahost
        @.PrintLn("Connected to {}", [host])
    endfunc

    func Send(message : strslice):
        @.PrintLn("{} <- {}", [host, message])
    endfunc

    func *Destroy():
        @.PrintLn("Disconnected from {}", [host])
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var connection <- OConnection("example.com")
    connection.Send("hello")
endfunc

Output:

Connected to example.com
example.com <- hello
Disconnected from example.com

In OConnection("example.com"), the argument "example.com" is passed to *Create. If an object does not declare a constructor, you create it with empty parentheses: OType().

docs.title: 2.14.3.3 Heap Objects and Autofree Variables (new and autofree)
docs.text:
The heap is general memory where values can live independently of any single function call. Using new allocates memory for the object on the heap.

Adding autofree gives the variable an autofree type. An autofree variable destroys its heap object automatically when the variable goes out of scope, when it is set to nil, or when a new object is assigned to it. The variable is responsible for releasing the object, so it is also called its owner:

var counter = new autofree OCounter()
counter.Increment()
counter = new OCounter() // destroys the first counter before taking the new one
counter = nil            // destroys the second counter

Without autofree, you must manually pair new with delete:

var counter = new OCounter()
counter.Increment()
delete counter = nil // destroys the object, releases its storage, and clears the variable

Forgetting to call delete leaves the object stranded in memory (a memory leak). On the other hand, calling delete while other variables still point to the object leaves those variables pointing to invalid memory, which is dangerous (see dangling pointers).

Global objects are not destroyed automatically when the program finishes. See Memory Management and Autofree for details on transferring ownership, autofree array elements, and ref autofree parameters.

docs.title: 2.14.3.4 Automatic Field Initialization and Cleanup
docs.text:
Fields are initialized before the constructor body runs, so the constructor can safely use them immediately.

When an object is destroyed, the destructor body runs first. After that, DQ automatically cleans up the object's fields in reverse declaration order: - Managed strings (str) and dynamic arrays release their allocated storage. - Embedded objects are destroyed. - Autofree fields destroy the heap objects they hold.

Because of this automatic cleanup, you only need to write a *Destroy method when you have custom cleanup work to do, such as closing external handles or logging a message. Ordinary object references in fields are just borrows, so the objects they point to are not destroyed.

If an error or exception occurs inside a constructor, the object creation fails. Any fields and base parts that were already set up are cleaned up in reverse order, so half-constructed objects are never left behind. See Exceptions and Error Handling.

docs.title: 2.14.3.5 Overloaded Constructors
docs.text:
You can provide more than one constructor by adding the [[overload]] attribute to each. This gives callers different ways to create the object. One constructor can also call another constructor to reuse setup code:

object OColor:
    red   : byte
    green : byte
    blue  : byte

    func *Create(ared : byte, agreen : byte, ablue : byte) [[overload]]:
        red = ared
        green = agreen
        blue = ablue
    endfunc

    func *Create(gray : byte) [[overload]]:
        Create(gray, gray, gray) // calls the three-argument constructor
    endfunc
endobject

var orange <- OColor(255, 165, 0)
var gray <- OColor(128) // red, green, and blue are all 128

docs.title: 2.14.3.6 Embedding Objects in Fields
docs.text:
Just as a structure can contain another structure, an object can contain another object as one of its fields. Declare the embedded object with <- to construct it as part of the containing object and destroy it with that object:

object OEngine:
    power : int

    func *Create(apower : int):
        power = apower
    endfunc
endobject

object OCar:
    engine <- OEngine(120) // created with every OCar, destroyed with it
endobject

Sometimes the embedded object needs arguments that are only available when the outer object's constructor runs. In that case, omit the parentheses and write .. after the type name (engine <- OEngine ..). This reserves the storage without calling the constructor. Call Create explicitly inside the outer constructor:

object OCar:
    engine <- OEngine .. // reserves storage; constructed in OCar.Create

    func *Create(apower : int):
        engine.Create(apower)
    endfunc
endobject

An embedded object must be constructed before code attempts to use it. Its storage belongs entirely to the containing object, so never pass an embedded object to delete. The composed objects example shows how to use this pattern to give an embedded object a reference back to its container.

docs.title: 2.14.4 Member Visibility
docs.text:
By default, all members of an object (its fields, methods, and properties) are public, meaning any code that uses the object can access them.

You can restrict access using visibility labels:

Label Who can access the members that follow public Any code. This is the default. protected Only methods of this object and of objects derived from it. private Only methods of this specific object.

Visibility labels act like section headers inside the object: all members declared below a label share that visibility until another label appears.

Use visibility labels to protect an object's internal data from unauthorized or accidental changes. In the following example, callers can inspect the balance, but can only change it through Deposit, which ensures invalid amounts are rejected:

object OAccount:
private
    balance : int = 0
public
    func GetBalance() -> int:
        return balance
    endfunc

    func Deposit(amount : int) -> bool:
        if amount <= 0:
            return false
        endif
        balance += amount
        return true
    endfunc
endobject

Code using an OAccount can call account.GetBalance(), but cannot touch balance directly. The next section introduces properties, which let callers read a value with field syntax while keeping the underlying field private.

docs.title: 2.14.5 Properties
docs.text:
A property looks and acts like a regular field to anyone using the object, but behind the scenes it can use methods to read or write the value.

Properties give you the best of both worlds: clean, natural syntax (such as volume.value = 80) combined with the ability to validate input, compute values on demand, or expose read-only data while keeping internal fields private.

docs.title: 2.14.5.1 Field-Backed Properties
docs.text:
The simplest property reads from or writes to a private field directly. Omitting write makes it a read-only property:

object OTimer:
private
    elapsed : int = 0
public
    property seconds : int read elapsed // read-only for outside callers

    func Tick():
        elapsed += 1
    endfunc
endobject

Outside callers can read timer.seconds, but attempting to assign to it (timer.seconds = 0) is caught at compile time with an error.

docs.title: 2.14.5.2 Computed Properties
docs.text:
A getter method computes the value each time the property is read, without needing to store it in a separate field:

object OTemperature:
public
    celsius : float = 20
private
    func GetFahrenheit() -> float:
        return celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
    endfunc
public
    property fahrenheit : float read GetFahrenheit
endobject

var temp <- OTemperature()
temp.celsius = 25
var f : float = temp.fahrenheit // computes 77 dynamically

No fahrenheit field is stored in memory; it always calculates the temperature from the current celsius value.

docs.title: 2.14.5.3 Checking New Values with Setters
docs.text:
A setter method receives the new value and checks or adjusts it before storing it:

use print

object OVolume:
private
    level : int = 50

    func SetLevel(value : int):
        if value < 0:
            level = 0
        elif value > 100:
            level = 100
        else:
            level = value
        endif
    endfunc
public
    property value : int read level write SetLevel
endobject

func *Main():
    var volume <- OVolume()
    volume.value = 150 // SetLevel limits it to 100
    volume.value -= 10 // reads 100, then calls SetLevel(90)
    PrintLn("{}", [volume.value])
endfunc

This prints 90.

docs.title: 2.14.5.4 Property Accessor Rules
docs.text:
The methods used to read and write a property are called accessors: - read specifies the field or getter method that supplies the value. A getter takes no parameters and returns the property type. - write specifies the field or setter method that updates the value. A setter takes the new value as its only parameter and returns nothing.

Accessor methods must belong to the same object and must be declared before the property that uses them.

A property needs at least one accessor: - Omit write for a read-only property. - Omit read for a write-only property. - Compound assignment operators such as += or -= read the current value, modify it, and write it back, so they require both read and write.

docs.title: 2.14.5.5 Indexed and Default Properties
docs.text:
An indexed property lets callers use square bracket syntax ([]), similar to an array. Its getter receives the index; its setter receives the index followed by the new value:

object OScores:
private
    values : [3]int

    func GetScore(index : int) -> int:
        return values[index]
    endfunc

    func SetScore(index : int, value : int):
        values[index] = value
    endfunc
public
    property score : [index : int]int default read GetScore write SetScore
endobject

var scores <- OScores()
scores.score[0] = 10
scores[1] = 20 // the default keyword lets you omit .score

Indices are accessor parameters and are not restricted to integers. For example, OStrStrMap in collections/strstrmap declares its item property with a string key:

property item : [akey : str]str default read GetItem write SetItem

Callers can use a string with either the property name or the default syntax:

use collections/strstrmap, print

func *Main():
    var settings <- OStrStrMap()
    settings.item["theme"] = "dark"
    PrintLn("{}", [settings["theme"]]) // prints dark
endfunc

An indexed property can accept more than one index, which is useful for grids and tables:

property cell : [row : int, col : int]int read GetCell write SetCell

Callers can use this with multiple indices: grid.cell[1, 2] = 5.

Putting default after the indexed property type allows callers to use brackets directly on the object itself (such as scores[1] instead of scores.score[1]). When an object and its base types declare several default properties, the one declared latest is selected.

docs.title: 2.14.5.6 Property Restrictions
docs.text:
A property is not an actual variable stored at a single memory address: reading it calls a getter or reads a field, and writing it calls a setter. Because of this:

  • A property cannot be passed to a ref, refin, or refout parameter. To pass a property's value to a function that modifies it through ref, copy the value into a temporary local variable, pass that variable, and assign the updated value back to the property:
var level : int = volume.value
Adjust(level) // func Adjust(value : ref int)
volume.value = level
  • You cannot take the memory address of a property using %.

Values returned by a property behave normally; for example, a property that returns an object reference can be followed immediately by member access, as in window.current_button.Click().

docs.title: 2.14.6 Inheritance
docs.text:
Inheritance allows a new object type to build on an existing object type: - The existing type is called the base object (or parent). - The new type is called the derived object (or child).

The derived object automatically inherits all fields and methods from the base object and can add its own new fields and methods. In DQ, an object can inherit from one base object, written in parentheses after its name:

object OAnimal:
    name : str

    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
    endfunc
endobject

object ODog(OAnimal):
    tricks : int = 0

    func Learn():
        tricks += 1
    endfunc
endobject

var dog <- ODog("Rex") // uses the inherited OAnimal constructor
dog.Learn()
var animal : OAnimal = dog // a derived object can be assigned to a base reference

A derived object can be used wherever its base type is expected, as shown in the assignment var animal : OAnimal = dog. When viewed through an animal reference, only the members declared in OAnimal are accessible.

docs.title: 2.14.6.1 Constructors and Inheritance
docs.text:
When an object inherits from a base type, the base part must be initialized:

  • If the derived object does not declare a constructor of its own, it automatically inherits the base constructor (as ODog("Rex") does above).
  • If the derived object declares its own constructor, it must call the base constructor using inherited Create(...):
object OGuideDog(ODog):
    owner : str

    func *Create(aname : strslice, aowner : strslice):
        inherited Create(aname) // initialize the base OAnimal/ODog part first
        owner = aowner
    endfunc
endobject

If the base constructor takes no parameters, calling inherited Create() is optional; DQ calls it automatically if you omit it. If the base constructor requires parameters, the derived constructor must call it explicitly. The compiler prevents calling the base constructor more than once.

Object setup runs from base to derived, and cleanup runs in reverse order: when an object is destroyed, the derived destructor runs first, and then the base destructor runs automatically. A destructor may call inherited Destroy() explicitly if the base cleanup must happen at a specific point during destruction.

docs.title: 2.14.6.2 Virtual Methods
docs.text:
Normally, when you call a method through an object reference, the compiler decides which method to run based on the declared type of the variable. For example, if a variable is declared as var animal : OAnimal, calling animal.Sound() would normally call OAnimal.Sound(), even if the variable currently holds an ODog.

A virtual method changes this: it tells DQ to inspect the actual object in memory at runtime and run that specific object's version of the method instead.

  • In the base object, mark the method with [[virtual]] to allow derived objects to customize it.
  • In the derived object, mark the replacement method with [[override]].
use print

object OAnimal:
    name : str

    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
    endfunc

    func Sound() -> str [[virtual]]:
        return "..."
    endfunc

    func Speak():
        @.PrintLn("{} says {}", [name, Sound()])
    endfunc
endobject

object ODog(OAnimal):
    func Sound() -> str [[override]]:
        return "Woof"
    endfunc
endobject

object OCat(OAnimal):
    func Sound() -> str [[override]]:
        return "Meow"
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var dog <- ODog("Rex")
    var cat <- OCat("Tom")
    var animals : [2]OAnimal = [dog, cat]
    for animal :? in animals:
        animal.Speak()
    endfor
endfunc

Output:

Rex says Woof
Tom says Meow

Speak is declared only in OAnimal, yet its call to Sound() runs the derived implementation for each animal. Without [[virtual]], both lines would print ....

The override must have the exact same parameters and return type as the virtual base method. The compiler reports an error if [[override]] is used on a method that has no matching virtual method in the base type, or if a derived method has the same name as a virtual method but forgets [[override]].

Accessor methods can be virtual. A derived object can override an inherited accessor method to customize how the property behaves.

A destructor cannot call virtual methods, because derived parts of the object may already have been torn down.

docs.title: 2.14.6.3 Calling the Base Implementation
docs.text:
Inside an overriding method, inherited calls the base type's version of that method. This lets you extend the base behavior rather than replacing it entirely:

object OLoudDog(ODog):
    func Sound() -> str [[override]]:
        var base : str = inherited Sound()
        return base + "!!!" // "Woof!!!"
    endfunc
endobject

Use the explicit call syntax, inherited Sound(), when you need the return value or want to pass different arguments. A bare inherited statement calls the base method with the current arguments and ignores any return value.

docs.title: 2.14.6.4 Abstract and Final Methods
docs.text:
An abstract method has a header but no body. It acts as a requirement: the base object declares that every derived object must provide its own version of this method. Declare it with [[virtual, abstract]] and two dots .. instead of a body:

object OShape:
    func Area() -> float [[virtual, abstract]] ..
endobject

Because an abstract object type has incomplete methods, you cannot create an object directly from an abstract type (writing new OShape() or <- OShape() is an error). You can only create objects from derived types that have implemented all abstract methods.

A final method, marked with [[virtual, final]], prevents any further derived types from overriding it.

docs.title: 2.14.7.1 Runtime Type Tests and Casts
docs.text: When you hold a reference of a base type (such as var animal : OAnimal), it might point to an ODog, an OCat, or another derived object. DQ provides two tools to check and convert references safely at runtime:

docs.title: 2.14.7.1.1 Testing Types with is
docs.text:
The is operator tests whether an object reference points to an object of a particular type or one of its derived types. It returns true or false, and safely returns false if the reference is nil:

var dog <- ODog("Rex")
var animal : OAnimal = dog
if animal is ODog:
    // true: animal refers to an ODog
endif

docs.title: 2.14.7.1.2 Converting References with TryCast()
docs.text:
To access fields or methods that exist only on the derived type, you must convert the base reference to the derived type. This conversion is called a type cast.

Because the object might not actually be of that type, use TryCast(TargetType, source) for a safe, checked conversion. Local variables can be declared in any of these three forms:

  • var specific : ODog = TryCast(ODog, animal)
  • var specific :? = TryCast(ODog, animal)
  • var specific = TryCast(ODog, animal)

The last two forms infer the variable's type from the target type passed to TryCast. All three forms check the actual object at runtime:

  • If the object is an ODog (or a type derived from ODog), the new variable receives a reference to that object.
  • If the object is something else (such as an OCat), or if animal is nil, the new variable receives nil instead of crashing.
var asdog = TryCast(ODog, animal) // the ODog, or nil
var ascat = TryCast(OCat, animal) // nil: animal is not an OCat
if asdog <> nil:
    asdog.Learn()
endif

Converting a reference only changes how the compiler views the object. It does not copy the object, and it does not transfer ownership.

docs.title: 2.14.7.2 Object Type Variables and Type Names
docs.text:
In DQ, variables can hold data values, but they can also hold types. A type of OBase variable can store the type OBase or any type derived from it. This allows a program to choose at runtime which kind of object to construct:

func MakeAnimal(cat : bool, name : strslice) -> OAnimal:
    var animaltype : type of OAnimal = ODog
    if cat:
        animaltype = OCat
    endif
    return new animaltype(name) // creates an ODog or OCat using the OAnimal constructor
endfunc

Calling new on the type variable constructs an object of whichever type was stored in it. The selected type must accept the constructor arguments of the base type. Unrelated types, abstract types, and types with incompatible constructors are rejected by the compiler. The returned heap object still needs an autofree variable or an explicit delete.

docs.title: 2.14.7.2.1 Querying Type Names
docs.text:
TypeName(Type) returns the name of a type as text. When passed an object reference, TypeName(reference) returns the actual runtime type of the object if it is non-nil, or the variable's declared type if it is nil:

var animal : OAnimal = MakeAnimal(true, "Tom")
PrintLn("{}", [TypeName(animal)]) // prints "OCat"
delete animal

Use TypeName for debugging and logging rather than as a permanent identifier in file formats or network protocols.

docs.title: 2.14.8 Object Method References
docs.text:
DQ allows you to store a function in a variable so it can be called later (a function reference). Because a method belongs to a specific object instance, storing a method requires an object method reference, written as func(...) of object.

An object method reference bundles two things together:

  1. The method to call.
  2. The specific object instance to call it on.

When you assign a virtual method to an object method reference, DQ resolves the method implementation for that specific object at the time of assignment. The reference only borrows the object—it does not keep the object alive. See Object Method References for a complete example.

docs.title: 2.14.9 Organizing Object Code
docs.text: As objects grow, method bodies can be defined separately from their declarations. Forward declarations let object types refer to each other, and explicit module prefixes or method-local use control access to outside names.

docs.title: 2.14.9.1 Declaring Methods Separately
docs.text:
Every method has two parts:

  1. The declaration (the header): tells the compiler the method's name, its parameters, and what type it returns.
  2. The definition (the body): the actual lines of code that run when the method is called.

Both parts can be written together directly inside the object ... endobject block. However, when an object has many methods or long code, keeping everything inside the object can make it difficult to read. DQ lets you separate them:

  • Put just the declaration inside the object, followed by .. (two dots) to indicate that the body will be provided later.
  • Write the full definition (the body) outside the object, prefixing the method name with the object type name, such as func OButton.Click():.
object OButton:
    caption : str

    func Click() ..
    func *Create(acaption : strslice) ..
endobject

func OButton.*Create(acaption : strslice):
    caption = acaption
endfunc

func OButton.Click():
    @.PrintLn("{} clicked", [caption])
endfunc

The definition outside the object must match the declaration's parameters, return type, and attributes. Inside the separated method body, all fields and methods of the object are available directly by name, exactly as if the method were written directly inside the object block.

docs.title: 2.14.9.2 Forward Declarations
docs.text:
The DQ compiler reads source files from top to bottom. If two object types reference each other (for example, OParent has a field pointing to OChild, and OChild has a field pointing to OParent), one of them must be introduced before its full description is written.

A forward declaration introduces the name of an object type using .. so other declarations can refer to it:

object OParent .. // forward declaration: introduces OParent

object OChild:
    parent : OParent // allowed because OParent was introduced above
endobject

object OParent:
    child : OChild
