endobject

The full definition of the object must be supplied before any code creates the object, accesses its fields, or calls its methods.

docs.title: 2.14.9.3 Accessing Variables and Functions Outside of the Object
docs.text:
Inside an object method, bare names always refer to the object's own members (its fields, methods, and properties). Variables, constants, and functions outside of the object scope are not directly available by their bare names. This restriction applies to:

  • Global variables and constants declared in the same module.
  • Functions declared in the same module.
  • Symbols from imported modules, including the runtime's built-in sys module (such as MemSet, MemCopy, or MemAlloc).

This scope separation prevents accidental naming conflicts—an object's field (such as count, status, or length) can never be confused with an outside variable or library function with the same name.

The exception to this rule is compiler internal built-ins, such as SizeOf(), OffsetOf(), and TypeName(), as well as language types (such as int, float, str, rostr, or SPoint). These are built into the language itself and are always available everywhere without any prefix.

To access outside variables, constants, or functions from inside a method, you normally prefix them with @:

  • @module.Name (fully qualified): names the imported module and the symbol, such as @print.PrintLn, @sys.MemSet, or @socket.AF_INET.
  • @..Name (current module only): refers to a symbol that is defined in the current module (until this source code position)
  • @.Name (full outside scope): the short form. It reaches everything available in the current module at that source code position, including its own global variables and constants, as well as imported functions.
use print

var greeting_count : int = 0

object OGreeter:
    name : str = "Lin"

    func Greet():
        @print.PrintLn("Hello, {}!", [name]) // fully qualified module reference
        @.greeting_count += 1                // short form for a module variable
        @.PrintLn("Greetings so far: {}", [@.greeting_count])
    endfunc
endobject

Writing PrintLn(...) or greeting_count without a prefix inside Greet is a compile error (ObjVsInModuleNs), and the compiler error message suggests the prefixed form.

docs.title: 2.14.9.4 Method-Local Use
docs.text:
While prefixing outside symbols with @. or @module. works well for occasional calls, practical code often uses many outside definitions at once. For example, low-level networking, file I/O, or system routines frequently rely on dozens of constants, types, and functions from modules such as socket or sys. Writing @socket.AF_INET, @socket.libc_htons(...), and @sys.MemSet(...) on every single line quickly becomes verbose and clutters the code.

To solve this, DQ provides the method-local use statement. Placing a use statement at the very beginning of a method body opens outside namespaces for direct, unqualified access inside that specific method:

func ONanoDatagram.SetRemoteAddr(aaddr : rostr, aport : uint16):
    use socket, sys
    MemSet(%remote_addr, 0, SizeOf(remote_addr))
    remote_addr_len = SizeOf(remote_addr)
    remote_addr.sin_family = AF_INET
    remote_addr.sin_port = libc_htons(aport)

    if libc_inet_pton(AF_INET, aaddr, %remote_addr.sin_addr) <> 1:
        raise ENanoNet('Invalid Host IP address: {}', [aaddr])
    endif
endfunc

In this method:

  • SizeOf(remote_addr) needs no prefix because SizeOf() is a compiler internal function available everywhere.
  • MemSet comes from the sys module, while AF_INET, libc_htons, and libc_inet_pton come from socket.
  • The use socket, sys statement makes all of them accessible directly by their bare names throughout the method body.

docs.title: 2.14.9.4.1 Forms of Method-Local use
docs.text:
Method-local use supports the following forms:

  • use module1, module2: Opens one or more specific imported module namespaces for direct access (as shown with use socket, sys above).
  • Using an imported alias: If a module was imported at the file level with an alias (such as use libc/stdio as cstdio), you must use that alias name in the method-local statement: dq func OLogger.Log(msg : strslice): use cstdio // refers to libc/stdio via its module alias printf("%s\n", msg.pchar) endfunc
  • use . (local module definitions): Makes all declarations belonging to the current module itself (its global variables, constants, and functions) directly available without @. prefixes.
  • use * (make everything available): Makes all symbols visible at the current module level directly available inside the method, including the current module's own declarations and all imported modules.

docs.title: 2.14.9.4.2 Scope and Rules
docs.text:
• Method-local use only affects name lookup inside that specific method body. It does not affect any other methods in the same object or file.
  • It does not load new modules from disk; it only opts already imported module namespaces into unqualified lookup within the method.
  • Object members always take precedence: if an object field has the same name as an outside symbol brought in by use, using that name inside the method accesses the object's field. To reach the outside symbol in that case, use an explicit @module.Name or @.Name prefix.

docs.title: 2.14.10.1 A Short Object Demo
docs.text:
This example combines inheritance, a read-only property, an embedded helper, and autofree variables. OChild changes a protected field and extends a virtual method, while OBase manages the helper's construction and cleanup.

use print

object OBase ..

object OHelper:
    base : OBase

    func *Create(abase : OBase) ..
    func *Destroy() ..
endobject

object OBase:
protected
    intval : int = 1
public
    name   : embstr(64)
    helper <- OHelper ..

    property value : int  read intval

    func PrintExtra()  [[virtual]]:
        @.Print(' value={}', [value])
    endfunc

    func *Create(aname : rostr):
        name = aname
        helper.Create(self)
    endfunc

    func *Destroy():
        @.PrintLn('"{}" destroyed', [name])
    endfunc

    func Print()  [[virtual]]:
        @print.Print('{}:', [name])
        PrintExtra()
        @.PrintLn()
    endfunc
endobject

func OHelper.*Create(abase : OBase):
    base = abase
    @.PrintLn('Helper for "{}" created', [base.name])
endfunc

func OHelper.*Destroy():
    @.PrintLn('Helper for "{}" destroyed', [base.name])
endfunc


object OChild(OBase):
    flval : float

    func *Create(aname : rostr, aflval : float):
        inherited Create(aname)
        intval = 2
        flval = aflval
    endfunc

    func PrintExtra()  [[override]]:
        inherited
        @.Print(' flval={}', [flval])
    endfunc
endobject

func Manipulate(aobj : ref autofree OBase):
    aobj = new OChild('Child3-heap', 7 / 3)
    aobj.Print()
endfunc

func ErrorTest():
    PrintLn('Error test')
    try:
        var obj = new autofree OChild('ErrChild-heap', 8.3)
        raise Exception('Some error happened!')
    except Exception as e:
        PrintLn('ERROR: {}', [e.message])
        e.PrintBacktrace()
    endtry
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn('DQ Objects Demo')

    var ob = new autofree OBase('Base-heap')
    ob.Print()

    if true:
        var oc1 <- OChild('Child1-stack', 3 / 2)
        oc1.Print()
    endif

    ErrorTest()

    PrintLn('reassigning autofree type')
    ob = new OChild('Child2-heap', 3.14)
    ob.Print()

    PrintLn('Autofree type as argument')
    Manipulate(ob)

    PrintLn('nil-ing autofree type')
    ob = nil

    PrintLn('Test finished.')
endfunc

Source: dq_intro_3.dq.

This test outputs:

DQ Objects Demo
Helper for "Base-heap" created
Base-heap: value=1
Helper for "Child1-stack" created
Child1-stack: value=2 flval=1.5
"Child1-stack" destroyed
Helper for "Child1-stack" destroyed
Error test
Helper for "ErrChild-heap" created
"ErrChild-heap" destroyed
Helper for "ErrChild-heap" destroyed
ERROR: Some error happened!
Backtrace =
  #0 ErrorTest @ /workvc/dq-lang/examples/dq_intro_3.dq:75
  #1 Main @ /workvc/dq-lang/examples/dq_intro_3.dq:93
reassigning autofree type
"Base-heap" destroyed
Helper for "Base-heap" destroyed
Helper for "Child2-heap" created
Child2-heap: value=2 flval=3.14
Autofree type as argument
"Child2-heap" destroyed
Helper for "Child2-heap" destroyed
Helper for "Child3-heap" created
Child3-heap: value=2 flval=2.333333333333334
nil-ing autofree type
"Child3-heap" destroyed
Helper for "Child3-heap" destroyed
Test finished.

OChild can change the protected intval field, while outside callers can only read it through the inherited value property. Calling Print() runs OBase.Print, whose virtual call to PrintExtra() selects the child's override. The bare inherited in that override prints the base value before the child adds flval.

helper.Create(self) gives the embedded helper a borrowed reference to its container. The helper's method bodies appear after the full OBase definition so they can access base.name. The name uses embstr(64), keeping its text storage inside the object. Because helper is declared after name, it is destroyed first and can still read the name during cleanup.

ErrorTest shows that the local autofree variable destroys its object before the exception handler runs. The handler then calls e.PrintBacktrace(); its frames depend on the build and source location. The rest of Main demonstrates autofree variable replacement, replacement through a ref autofree OBase parameter, and early destruction by assigning nil.

docs.title: 2.14.10.2 A Temperature Log with Properties
docs.text:
OTemperatureLog keeps a limited number of recent temperature readings. Its internal storage is private; callers interact with it exclusively through properties and methods:

Property Kind Purpose count read-only, computed Current number of stored readings average read-only, computed Average of all stored readings capacity field-backed read, validated setter Maximum number of readings; lowering it discards the oldest extra readings reading indexed, default Reads or updates a stored reading by index 
use print

object OTemperatureLog:
private
    readings : [*]float
    limit    : int = 5

    func GetCount() -> int:
        return readings.length
    endfunc

    func GetAverage() -> float:
        result = 0
        for value : float in readings:
            result += value
        endfor
        if readings.length > 0:
            result /= readings.length
        endif
    endfunc

    func SetCapacity(value : int):
        limit = iif(value < 1, 1, value)
        while readings.length > limit:
            readings.Delete(0) // drop the oldest readings
        endwhile
    endfunc

    func GetReading(index : int) -> float:
        return readings[index]
    endfunc

    func SetReading(index : int, value : float):
        readings[index] = value
    endfunc

public
    property count    : int   read GetCount
    property average  : float read GetAverage
    property capacity : int   read limit write SetCapacity
    property reading  : [index : int]float default read GetReading write SetReading

    func Add(value : float):
        if readings.length == limit:
            readings.Delete(0)
        endif
        readings.Append(value)
    endfunc

    func Print():
        @.Print("count {}:", [count])
        for i : int = 0 count count:
            @.Print(" {}", [reading[i]])
        endfor
        @.PrintLn(", average {:.2f}", [average])
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var log <- OTemperatureLog()
    log.Add(21.5)
    log.Add(22)
    log.Add(35)
    log.Add(22.5)
    log.Print()

    log[2] = 23 // corrects a wrong reading through the default property
    log.reading[0] += 0.5
    log.Print()

    log.capacity = 2 // keeps only the two newest readings
    log.Print()

    log.capacity = -5 // SetCapacity limits it to a minimum of 1
    log.Add(24)
    log.Print()
    PrintLn("Capacity: {}", [log.capacity])
endfunc

Output:

count 4: 21.5 22 35 22.5, average 25.25
count 4: 22 22 23 22.5, average 22.38
count 2: 23 22.5, average 22.75
count 1: 24, average 24.00
Capacity: 1

count and average do not have dedicated storage fields; their getters compute fresh values directly from the readings array each time they are read. capacity reads the private limit field directly, but writes go through SetCapacity, which enforces a minimum value of 1 and trims excess elements.

log[2] = 23 invokes SetReading(2, 23) through the default property. log.reading[0] += 0.5 exercises both accessors: it calls GetReading(0), adds 0.5, and then passes the result to SetReading(0, 22). Inside Print, properties are accessed naturally by name, such as count and reading[i].

Because readings is private, external code cannot modify the array directly or bypass the validation logic in Add and SetCapacity.

docs.title: 2.14.10.3 Shapes in an Array with Autofree Elements
docs.text:
This example builds a shape hierarchy. OShape declares an abstract Area method, and each derived shape provides its own calculation. A dynamic array of autofree references owns the shapes, so they are destroyed automatically when they are removed from the array or when the array leaves scope.

use print

object OShape:
    name : str

    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
    endfunc

    func Area() -> float [[virtual, abstract]] ..

    func Describe() [[virtual]]:
        @.PrintLn("{}: area {:.2f}", [name, Area()])
    endfunc

    func *Destroy():
        @.PrintLn("Released {}", [name])
    endfunc
endobject

object ORectangle(OShape):
    width  : float
    height : float

    func *Create(awidth : float, aheight : float):
        inherited Create("rectangle")
        width = awidth
        height = aheight
    endfunc

    func Area() -> float [[override]]:
        return width * height
    endfunc
endobject

object OSquare(ORectangle):
    func *Create(aside : float):
        inherited Create(aside, aside)
        name = "square"
    endfunc
endobject

object OCircle(OShape):
    radius : float

    func *Create(aradius : float):
        inherited Create("circle")
        radius = aradius
    endfunc

    func Area() -> float [[override]]:
        return 3.14159 * radius * radius
    endfunc

    func Describe() [[override]]:
        inherited // prints the name and the area
        @.PrintLn("  radius: {}", [radius])
    endfunc
endobject

func TotalArea(shapes : []autofree OShape) -> float:
    result = 0
    for shape : OShape in shapes:
        result += shape.Area() // calls the Area method of the actual shape type
    endfor
endfunc

func *Main():
    var shapes : [*]autofree OShape // the array owns the shapes
    shapes.Append(new ORectangle(4, 2.5))
    shapes.Append(new OSquare(3))
    shapes.Append(new OCircle(1.5))

    for shape : OShape in shapes:
        shape.Describe()
    endfor
    PrintLn("Total area: {:.2f}", [TotalArea(shapes)])

    var rectangles : int = 0
    for shape : OShape in shapes:
        if shape is ORectangle: // true for OSquare too
            ++rectangles
        endif

        var circle = TryCast(OCircle, shape) // nil for other shapes
        if circle <> nil:
            circle.radius *= 2
            PrintLn("Enlarged {}: area {:.2f}", [TypeName(circle), circle.Area()])
        endif
    endfor
    PrintLn("Rectangles: {}", [rectangles])

    shapes.Delete(0) // destroys the rectangle
    PrintLn("Remaining: {}", [shapes.length])
endfunc

Output:

rectangle: area 10.00
square: area 9.00
circle: area 7.07
  radius: 1.5
Total area: 26.07
Enlarged OCircle: area 28.27
Rectangles: 2
Released rectangle
Remaining: 2
Released square
Released circle

OSquare inherits from ORectangle and reuses its constructor and Area calculation, simply passing the same value for both width and height. OCircle overrides Describe and uses a bare inherited call to run the base shape description before printing its radius.

Inside the loop, shape has the base type OShape, yet each shape.Area() call selects the correct derived formula at runtime. shape is ORectangle is also true for the square, because OSquare derives from ORectangle. TryCast safely converts the reference to OCircle, returning nil for any other shape.

The loop variables and the TotalArea parameter only borrow the shapes. The shapes dynamic array owns them: shapes.Delete(0) immediately destroys the rectangle, and the remaining shapes are destroyed automatically when shapes goes out of scope at the end of Main.

docs.title: 2.14.10.4 Lifetime of Composed Objects
docs.text:
This example traces how objects are created and destroyed when objects are composed together. An OMachine contains an embedded OEngine, and the engine keeps an ordinary reference back to its machine. OPump inherits from OMachine and extends its Run method.

use print

object OMachine ..

object OEngine:
    machine : OMachine // back-reference; the engine does not own the machine

    func *Create(amachine : OMachine) ..
    func Start() ..
    func *Destroy() ..
endobject

object OMachine:
    name   : str
    engine <- OEngine .. // constructed later, in OMachine.Create

    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
        @.PrintLn("{}: created", [name])
        engine.Create(self)
    endfunc

    func Run() [[virtual]]:
        engine.Start()
    endfunc

    func *Destroy():
        @.PrintLn("{}: destroyed", [name])
    endfunc
endobject

func OEngine.*Create(amachine : OMachine):
    machine = amachine
    @.PrintLn("{}: engine created", [machine.name])
endfunc

func OEngine.Start():
    @.PrintLn("{}: engine running", [machine.name])
endfunc

func OEngine.*Destroy():
    @.PrintLn("{}: engine destroyed", [machine.name])
endfunc

object OPump(OMachine):
    rate : int

    func *Create(aname : strslice, arate : int):
        inherited Create(aname)
        rate = arate
    endfunc

    func Run() [[override]]:
        inherited
        @.PrintLn("{}: pumping {} l/min", [name, rate])
    endfunc
endobject

func ReplaceMachine(machine : ref autofree OMachine):
    machine = new OPump("pump-2", 40) // releases the caller's previous machine
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("-- embedded object in a block")
    if true:
        var local <- OPump("pump-1", 25)
        local.Run()
    endif

    PrintLn("-- autofree variable replacement")
    var current = new autofree OMachine("mixer")
    current.Run()
    ReplaceMachine(current)
    current.Run()

    PrintLn("-- exception")
    try:
        var temporary = new autofree OMachine("tester")
        raise Exception("power failure")
    except Exception as e:
        PrintLn("Error: {}", [e.message])
    endtry

    PrintLn("-- end of Main")
endfunc

Output:

-- embedded object in a block
pump-1: created
pump-1: engine created
pump-1: engine running
pump-1: pumping 25 l/min
pump-1: destroyed
pump-1: engine destroyed
-- autofree variable replacement
mixer: created
mixer: engine created
mixer: engine running
mixer: destroyed
mixer: engine destroyed
pump-2: created
pump-2: engine created
pump-2: engine running
pump-2: pumping 40 l/min
-- exception
tester: created
tester: engine created
tester: destroyed
tester: engine destroyed
Error: power failure
-- end of Main
pump-2: destroyed
pump-2: engine destroyed

OEngine needs to store a reference to its machine, but OMachine is declared further down in the file. The forward declaration object OMachine .. introduces the type name so OEngine can declare the machine : OMachine field. The engine's method bodies are defined after OMachine is fully declared because they access machine.name.

The engine cannot be constructed in its field declaration line because the machine's self reference is only available inside OMachine.Create. The .. in engine <- OEngine .. reserves the field's storage, delaying construction until engine.Create(self) is called.

Each machine's destructor runs before its fields are cleaned up, which is why destroyed appears before engine destroyed. Furthermore, fields are cleaned up in reverse declaration order, so engine is destroyed before name, ensuring machine.name remains valid while the engine's destructor runs.

The three sections illustrate the different ways objects are cleaned up: - local is destroyed when the if block ends. - ReplaceMachine replaces the caller's autofree variable via a ref autofree parameter, which automatically destroys "mixer" before assigning "pump-2". - temporary is destroyed when the exception escapes the try block, before the except handler begins executing. - Finally, current releases "pump-2" when Main returns.

docs.title: 2.15. Memory Management and Autofree
docs.text:
The earlier chapters introduced automatic string and array storage, borrowed pointers, and the three ways to create objects. This chapter brings those rules together and explains how autofree variables manage heap allocations as values pass between functions, objects, and collections.

An autofree type, such as autofree OTask or autofree ^SPoint, adds automatic cleanup to an object-reference or pointer type. A variable of that type releases its allocation when it is replaced or leaves scope. It is also called the allocation's owner: it is responsible for releasing that allocation. A borrow lets other code use the allocation without taking responsibility for its cleanup.

Keeping that responsibility clear prevents both memory leaks (storage that is never released) and dangling references (references to storage that no longer exists).

For object construction and destructors, see Creating and Destroying Objects. For the lifetime of an address, see Allocation and Lifetime.

docs.title: 2.15.1 Choosing Storage and Cleanup
docs.text:
Lifetime means how long a value's storage exists. Ownership means who is responsible for releasing it. Choose a form that fits how you use the value:

Form Lifetime and responsibility Number, fixed array, structure, fixed-storage embedded string Lives directly in its containing variable or object. str Manages its text storage; changing a shared string makes an independent value. [*]T Manages shared array storage; aliases see changes to the same array. var task <- OTask(...) Embedded object; lives with its scope or containing object. new OTask(...) Heap object; needs an explicit delete or an autofree variable. autofree OTask, autofree ^T, autofree pointer Autofree types; variables release their heap allocations automatically. Pointer, rostr, strslice, []T, ordinary object alias Borrows existing storage; does not keep it alive.

Keep borrowed storage alive for as long as you use it. For example, a slice of a local array cannot be returned for use after that local array has disappeared.

An object variable declared without autofree does not destroy the object automatically. Assigning it to another variable does not change that:

var task : OTask = new OTask("download")
var another : OTask = task

There is one task object, and both variables let you access it. The second declaration does not create a second object, and neither variable has an autofree type. When both variables leave scope, the object remains allocated. DQ does not find and release it for you.

For automatic cleanup, declare task with an autofree type. Otherwise, call delete when you are finished with the object. After it is destroyed, you must stop using it through either variable; having another variable refer to the object does not keep it alive.

Strings and dynamic arrays release their own storage automatically, but an array's storage is separate from any heap objects its elements refer to. For example, releasing a [*]OTask array does not destroy its task objects. Use [*]autofree OTask when the array should also destroy those objects during cleanup.

docs.title: 2.15.2 Explicit Allocation and Release
docs.text:
Allocate heap objects with new and raw byte buffers with MemAlloc. Use delete to release either allocation. The allocation stays in memory until you release it; leaving the function does not release it automatically.

This complete program demonstrates both forms. Each function releases its allocation when its work finishes normally. RunTask prints the supplied mode, but returns early if the mode is empty. ProcessData fills its buffer with fillvalue, which must be between 0 and 255 because each byte holds a value in that range. The early-return branches deliberately contain a mistake: they return before reaching the cleanup.

use print

object OTask:
    name : str

    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
    endfunc

    func *Destroy():
        @.PrintLn("Finished: {}", [name])
    endfunc
endobject

func RunTask(amode : rostr):
    var task : OTask = new OTask("download")
    if amode == "":
        PrintLn("Task mode must not be empty")
        return // mistake: skips delete, leaving the task allocated
    endif

    PrintLn("Working on {} in {} mode", [task.name, amode])
    delete task
endfunc

func ProcessData(fillvalue : int):
    var buffer : ^byte = ^byte(MemAlloc(256))
    if buffer == nil:
        PrintLn("Could not allocate buffer")
        return // no allocation was made, so there is nothing to release
    endif
    if fillvalue < 0 or fillvalue > 255:
        PrintLn("Invalid fill value: {}", [fillvalue])
        return // mistake: skips delete, leaving the buffer allocated
    endif

    MemSet(buffer, fillvalue, 256)
    PrintLn("First byte: {}", [buffer[0]^])
    delete buffer
    PrintLn("Buffer released")
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("-- normal completion")
    RunTask("fast")
    ProcessData(42)

    PrintLn("-- early return")
    RunTask("")
    ProcessData(300)
    PrintLn("Back in Main")
endfunc

Output when the allocations succeed:

-- normal completion
Working on download in fast mode
Finished: download
First byte: 42
Buffer released
-- early return
Task mode must not be empty
Invalid fill value: 300
Back in Main

On the normal path, delete task calls the task's destructor and releases its storage. delete buffer releases the byte buffer; there is no object destructor to call for it. These variables are not used again before their functions end, so there is no need to clear them. Other variables that refer to the same allocation must no longer be used to access it either. Never delete an embedded object created with <-.

When the mode is empty or the fill value is outside 0 to 255, return immediately leaves the function. It skips all remaining statements, including delete. For example, ProcessData(300) allocates its buffer before checking the value, then returns without freeing it. Notice that the second pair of calls prints neither Finished: download nor Buffer released. Both functions return to Main, but the task object and the 256-byte buffer from those calls are still allocated.

Their local variables disappear when the functions return, so the program no longer has a way to reach those allocations and release them. This is a memory leak. Repeating these calls would leave more memory allocated each time, even though no work was completed.

You could add the missing release before each early return. However, every additional exit path needs the same care, including exceptions. The next section introduces autofree variables, which release their allocations on both normal completion and early return, without a separate cleanup call on each path.

The implicit runtime also provides MemFree for releasing raw storage and MemFreeRef for releasing it and clearing a generic pointer variable in one call. External resources often have their own close or release function; match each resource to the operation its API requires.

docs.title: 2.15.2.1 Reusing a Variable After delete
docs.text:
For a variable without autofree, delete buffer releases the allocation but leaves the old address in the variable. That address is no longer valid. If the variable stays in scope, use delete buffer = nil to release the allocation and set the variable to nil in one statement:

var buffer : ^byte = ^byte(MemAlloc(256))
// use the buffer

delete buffer = nil // release the storage and mark the variable as empty

// Later, allocate a new buffer if there is none.
if buffer == nil:
    buffer = ^byte(MemAlloc(512))
endif
// use the new buffer

delete buffer // finished with this variable

Here, nil tells later code that the variable currently refers to no buffer. Without clearing it, buffer == nil would not detect that the first allocation has been released. The same applies to an object variable without autofree. Clearing one variable does not clear other variables that refer to the released allocation.

You can also assign a new allocation directly after delete; setting nil first is not required for reassignment. It is useful when later code needs to check whether the variable currently holds an allocation. Assigning nil alone to a variable without autofree does not release its allocation.

docs.title: 2.15.3.1 Declaring Autofree Variables
docs.text:
Use autofree for a heap allocation that should be released automatically. This complete program creates two task objects in Main and allocates a structure and a byte buffer in ProcessData. The task destructor prints a message so you can see when object cleanup happens:

use print

object OTask:
    name : str

    func *Create(aname : strslice):
        name = aname
    endfunc

    func *Destroy():
        @.PrintLn("Finished: {}", [name])
    endfunc
endobject

struct SPoint:
    x : int
    y : int
endstruct

func ProcessData(fillvalue : int):
    var point : autofree ^SPoint = new SPoint
    point.x = 10
    point.y = 20

    var buffer : autofree ^byte = ^byte(MemAlloc(256))
    if buffer == nil:
        PrintLn("Could not allocate buffer")
        return
    endif
    if fillvalue < 0 or fillvalue > 255:
        PrintLn("Invalid fill value: {}", [fillvalue])
        return
    endif
    MemSet(buffer, fillvalue, 256)

    PrintLn("Point: ({}, {})", [point.x, point.y])
    PrintLn("Buffer filled with {}", [fillvalue])
    PrintLn("Leaving ProcessData")

    // no manual free is required for point and buffer
endfunc

func *Main():
    var first = new autofree OTask("download")
    var second : autofree OTask = new OTask("resize")
    PrintLn("Tasks: {}, {}", [first.name, second.name])

    ProcessData(42)
    PrintLn("Back in Main")
endfunc

Output:

Tasks: download, resize
Point: (10, 20)
Buffer filled with 42
Leaving ProcessData
Back in Main
Finished: resize
Finished: download

first uses the new autofree shorthand. second declares its autofree type explicitly and assigns a newly created object to it. Both forms arrange for the object to be destroyed automatically.

point has type autofree ^SPoint and releases the structure's heap storage automatically. buffer has type autofree ^byte and releases its 256-byte allocation automatically. The cast ^byte(...) gives the raw allocation a byte-pointer type. MemSet(buffer, fillvalue, 256) fills all 256 bytes with the requested value.

When ProcessData returns, its local autofree variables release their allocations in reverse declaration order: first buffer, then point. This happens after Leaving ProcessData is printed and before Main prints Back in Main. Releasing these non-object allocations produces no destructor messages; their storage is already freed when execution returns to Main. If fillvalue is outside 0 to 255, the early return also releases both allocations automatically.

The task objects remain available until Main ends. Then second is destroyed before first, producing Finished: resize and Finished: download. No delete or MemFree calls are needed in either function.

An autofree variable must refer to a compatible heap allocation. Do not give it a local variable's address, an address inside another allocation, or an external resource handle such as a file handle.

When the initializer already determines the pointed-to type, you can use autofree ? to avoid writing that type twice:

var buffer : autofree ? = ^byte(MemAlloc(256))
var point : autofree ? = new SPoint

The compiler infers ^byte for buffer and ^SPoint for point. The autofree type attribute is never inferred: you must write it explicitly. Here, autofree ? combines an inferred pointer type with explicitly requested automatic cleanup. The new autofree shorthand used for first also specifies autofree explicitly.

docs.title: 2.15.3.2 Cleanup
docs.text:
An autofree variable releases its current allocation when it is overwritten or leaves its scope. Assigning nil releases it early:

var task = new autofree OTask("download")
task = new OTask("resize") // destroys download before taking the new object
task = nil                 // destroys resize; task is now empty

For objects, cleanup calls *Destroy and releases the heap storage. For autofree ^T and autofree pointer, it releases the allocation without calling an object destructor. An autofree variable set to nil has nothing to release.

delete also works on an autofree variable and leaves it nil:

var task = new autofree OTask("download")
delete task // task is now nil; leaving the scope will not delete it again

Local autofree variables start as nil, and local values are cleaned up in reverse construction order. Managed values, embedded objects, and autofree variables receive cleanup on normal block exit, return, loop transfers, and exception propagation. Autofree fields are cleaned up in reverse declaration order when their containing object is destroyed.

Global autofree variables start as nil. Replacing them releases their old values, but DQ does not automatically destroy globals at program shutdown. Release global resources explicitly.

docs.title: 2.15.3.3 Borrowing and Moving Ownership
docs.text:
Only one autofree variable should be responsible for a given allocation. Assigning one autofree variable to another moves ownership: the destination becomes responsible for releasing the allocation, and the source becomes nil:

var first = new autofree OTask("download")
var second : autofree OTask = first
// first is now nil; second owns the download task

Assigning an autofree variable to an ordinary reference instead borrows the object:

var task = new autofree OTask("download")
var borrowed : OTask = task
borrowed.name = "resize" // changes the same object; task still handles cleanup

The borrow becomes invalid when the autofree variable releases the object. Do not delete the borrowed reference separately or assign it to another autofree variable. DQ does not track every borrowed reference and clear it when the object is destroyed; a non-nil borrow can still be invalid.

Moving ownership does not move the object in memory. Existing borrows still refer to that object, but its lifetime now depends on the destination autofree variable. The source becomes nil, so check or replace it before using it again.

Source Assign to autofree T Assign to ordinary T Ordinary T Take ownership; the source remains an alias. Copy the reference. autofree T variable Move ownership; set the source to nil. Borrow; the source still handles cleanup.

Replacing an autofree variable first releases its previous allocation. Assigning an autofree variable to itself leaves it unchanged.

docs.title: 2.15.3.4 Autofree Variables and Functions
docs.text:
An ordinary object or pointer parameter borrows its argument, including when the caller passes an autofree variable. The call does not clear that variable or transfer responsibility for cleanup:

func Rename(task : OTask, name : strslice):
    task.name = name
endfunc

Calling Rename(task, "resize") changes the object's name while leaving ownership with the caller.

Use ref autofree T when the function needs to replace the caller's autofree variable:

func ReplaceTask(task : ref autofree OTask):
    task = new OTask("save") // releases the caller's previous task
endfunc

A ref autofree T parameter requires an autofree variable; a ref T parameter requires ordinary reference storage. Their autofree qualifications must match. To return a new object, use an ordinary object result and let the caller assign it to an autofree variable. autofree return types are not supported.

docs.title: 2.15.3.4.1 Returning a New Object
docs.text:
A factory is a function that creates a value for its caller. It can return a new heap object directly:

func CreateTask(name : strslice) -> OTask:
    return new OTask(name)
endfunc

func *Main():
    var task : autofree OTask = CreateTask("download")
    Rename(task, "resize")
    ReplaceTask(task)
    PrintLn("Working on {}", [task.name])
endfunc

Put this code after OTask, Rename, and ReplaceTask from the examples above. It prints:

Finished: resize
Working on save
Finished: save

Rename borrows the object. ReplaceTask changes the caller's autofree variable, destroying the renamed object before storing the new one. The final object is destroyed when Main ends.

The ordinary OTask result type does not say whether a function returns a new object or borrows an existing one. Document that distinction for callers. Never return a local embedded object, or an object still owned by a local autofree variable: local cleanup would destroy it before the caller could use it.

docs.title: 2.15.3.5 Autofree Fields
docs.text:
An object can take responsibility for another object through an autofree field:

object OWorker:
    current : autofree OTask
endobject

func *Main():
    var worker <- OWorker()
    var task = new autofree OTask("download")
    worker.current = task // moves ownership into the field; task becomes nil
    PrintLn("Working on {}", [worker.current.name])
endfunc

With the earlier OTask definition and use print, this prints Working on download followed by Finished: download. Destroying worker automatically cleans up current; OWorker needs no custom destructor. Use an ordinary OTask field for a borrowed link, such as a reference back to a containing object. Giving two fields ownership of the same allocation would cause both to attempt to release it.

docs.title: 2.15.3.6 Arrays
docs.text:
An array with an autofree element type automatically releases its objects:

var tasks : [*]autofree OTask
tasks.Append(new OTask("download"))
tasks.Append(new OTask("resize"))
tasks.Delete(0) // destroys download; resize remains in the array

Replacing or removing an element destroys its previous object. New empty elements are nil. Assigning a dynamic array to another variable still shares the same array; its remaining objects are destroyed when the last reference to that array is released.

Single-element .Append(), .Prepend(), and .Insert() take ownership of an ordinary reference or move a source of an autofree type. .Pop() and .PopFirst() remove an object without destroying it and return an ordinary reference. Assign the result to an autofree variable or delete it explicitly:

var tasks : [*]autofree OTask
tasks.Append(new OTask("download"))
var next : autofree OTask = tasks.Pop() // next now owns the removed task

Use for item : ref in tasks to replace array elements in place. The reference keeps the element's autofree type, so replacement frees the previous object. See Dynamic Array autofree Elements for more examples.

docs.title: 2.15.3.6.1 Array Copying Restrictions
docs.text:
Assigning a fixed array of autofree elements moves every element: each destination's previous value is released, and each source element becomes nil. Self-assignment leaves the array unchanged.

Dynamic arrays of autofree elements cannot use .Clone() or copy a range with .Append(), .Prepend(), .Insert(), or the slice variants. Copying those objects into separate autofree elements would duplicate ownership. Borrowed []autofree T views can still be indexed, iterated, and passed to read-only APIs. Single-element insertion can move an element from the same array even when the operation moves the array's storage.

docs.title: 2.15.3.7 Placement Restrictions and Type Inference
docs.text:
autofree can qualify an object type, a typed pointer, or pointer. It can be used for variables, object fields, fixed- or dynamic-array elements, and ref parameters. It cannot be used directly on numbers, booleans, characters, structures, unions, function references, or whole array types.

It is also not supported on embedded <- fields, structure or union fields, properties or their indices, function results, or refin and refout parameters. Type aliases may name autofree types, with the same placement rules.

Type inference never adds the autofree attribute. Use autofree ? to infer the underlying type while specifying automatic cleanup explicitly. Bare :? produces a type without autofree, even when the source is an autofree variable. For the new autofree T declaration shorthand, omit :? as in the examples above. The same distinction applies to inferred for ... in variables.

docs.title: 2.15.3.7.1 Inference Example
docs.text:
var task = new autofree OTask("download")
var borrowed :? = task           // inferred OTask; task is unchanged
var next : autofree ? = task     // inferred OTask, explicit autofree; task becomes nil

borrowed still refers to the same object, now owned by next. Prefer an explicit autofree type at a transfer point if it makes the responsibility easier to see.

docs.title: 2.16. Exceptions and Error Handling
docs.text:
An exception reports a failure, such as invalid input or an operation that cannot be completed. It stops the current work and looks for code that handles the problem. Use try and except to handle a failure without ending the whole program.

Custom exception type names conventionally start with a capital E, as in EInput.

use print

object EInput(Exception):
endobject

func RequirePositive(value : int):
    if value <= 0:
        raise EInput("expected a positive value, got {}", [value])
    endif
endfunc

func *Main():
    try:
        RequirePositive(0)
        PrintLn("Value accepted")
    except EInput as error:
        PrintLn("Error: {}", [error.message])
    endtry
    PrintLn("Ready for another value")
endfunc

This prints:

Error: expected a positive value, got 0
Ready for another value

raise reports the problem. Execution skips the remaining statements in the try block and enters the matching except handler. as error gives the handler a name for the exception, so it can read the message.

docs.title: 2.16.1 Three Ways to Handle File Errors
docs.text: Consider a function that logs three measurements: temperature, relative humidity, and pressure. Each version opens measurements.log in append mode and makes three separate writes, one per measurement. Each line includes the same Unix timestamp, in seconds, obtained from Time().

docs.title: 2.16.1.1 No Error Handling
docs.text:
This version calls libc directly and ignores all return values:

use time

func libc_fopen(filename : ^char, mode : ^char) -> pointer [[external('fopen')]] ..
func libc_fprintf(stream : pointer, fmt : ^char, ...) -> int32 [[external('fprintf')]] ..
func libc_fclose(stream : pointer) -> int32 [[external('fclose')]] ..

func LogMeasurements(temp : float, rh : float, pressure : float):
    var timestamp : float64 = Time()
    var f : pointer = libc_fopen("measurements.log", "a")
    libc_fprintf(f, "%.3f temp=%.2f\n", timestamp, temp)
    libc_fprintf(f, "%.3f rh=%.2f\n", timestamp, rh)
    libc_fprintf(f, "%.3f pressure=%.2f\n", timestamp, pressure)
    libc_fclose(f)
endfunc

The code is short, but it cannot tell the caller whether logging succeeded. If opening fails, f is nil, and passing it to libc_fprintf is invalid and may crash the program. If a write fails, the function still attempts the remaining writes and silently loses data.

docs.title: 2.16.1.2 Return-Value-Based Error Handling
docs.text:
With the same libc declarations, the function can check each result and return false on failure. libc_fopen returns nil on failure; libc_fprintf returns a negative value on failure. A successful open does not guarantee that any of the writes will succeed, so each write needs its own check.

use time
use print

func libc_fopen(filename : ^char, mode : ^char) -> pointer [[external('fopen')]] ..
func libc_fprintf(stream : pointer, fmt : ^char, ...) -> int32 [[external('fprintf')]] ..
func libc_fclose(stream : pointer) -> int32 [[external('fclose')]] ..

func LogMeasurements(temp : float, rh : float, pressure : float) -> bool:
    var timestamp : float64 = Time()
    var f : pointer = libc_fopen("measurements.log", "a")
    if f == nil:
        return false
    endif
    if libc_fprintf(f, "%.3f temp=%.2f\n", timestamp, temp) < 0:
        libc_fclose(f)
        return false
    endif
    if libc_fprintf(f, "%.3f rh=%.2f\n", timestamp, rh) < 0:
        libc_fclose(f)
        return false
    endif
    if libc_fprintf(f, "%.3f pressure=%.2f\n", timestamp, pressure) < 0:
        libc_fclose(f)
        return false
    endif
    return libc_fclose(f) == 0
endfunc

func *Main():
    if not LogMeasurements(21.5, 48, 1013.2):
        PrintLn("Could not log measurements")
    endif
endfunc

Every failure path after opening closes the file before returning. Closing also needs a check on the success path: libc buffers output, so a failure may only be reported when libc_fclose flushes the remaining data. After a write has already failed, the function returns false regardless of the close result. The caller must check the function's return value too; intermediate callers would need to pass that failure on explicitly.

docs.title: 2.16.1.3 Exception-Based Error Handling
docs.text:
The standard file package's OFile object raises EFileError when opening or writing fails. The logging function can therefore express the sequence of operations directly:

use file
use time
use print

func LogMeasurements(temp : float, rh : float, pressure : float):
    var timestamp : float64 = Time()
    var f <- OFile()
    f.Open("measurements.log", "a")
    f.WriteText(Format("{:.3f} temp={:.2f}\n", [timestamp, temp]))
    f.WriteText(Format("{:.3f} rh={:.2f}\n", [timestamp, rh]))
    f.WriteText(Format("{:.3f} pressure={:.2f}\n", [timestamp, pressure]))
endfunc

func *Main():
    try:
        LogMeasurements(21.5, 48, 1013.2)
    except EFileError as error:
        PrintLn("Could not log measurements: {}", [error.message])
    endtry
endfunc

Each WriteText checks for failure inside OFile. If opening or any write raises an exception, the remaining operations are skipped and the exception travels to the caller's handler. There is no error result to check or pass on in LogMeasurements.

The local f uses autofree ownership (<-), so its destructor closes the file both on normal return and during exception propagation. Currently, OFile.Close() does not report libc close errors, so this version cannot detect failures reported only when buffered output is flushed at close time.

None of these approaches makes the three writes atomic: if a later write fails, earlier lines may already have been written. Handling an error does not undo those writes.

docs.title: 2.16.2 Advantages of the Exception-Based Error Handling
docs.text:
The logging examples show several advantages of exceptions:

  • The normal sequence stays short and readable. Opening the file and writing the three measurements appear together, without repeated checks and early returns between them. Adding another write does not require another error branch in the logging function.
  • Error details travel with the failure. The boolean result only says that logging failed. An exception carries a type and message, and its backtrace helps locate the failure. Callers can distinguish error types without adding separate output parameters to every intermediate function.
  • Errors cannot be silently ignored. With return values, forgetting a check can let the program continue working with invalid or incomplete data. An exception automatically stops the failed operation, even when the programmer has not supplied an error handler. The program normally reports the unhandled exception with its message and backtrace, then terminates when no matching error handler provided.
  • Cleanup code does not need to be repeated. The common cleanup block - except or finally - makes the source code more maintainable and readable.

docs.title: 2.16.3 Raising and Matching Exceptions
docs.text:
Exception is supplied by the implicit runtime when exception support is enabled. Its constructor accepts a message, optionally with formatting arguments, just like PrintLn.

You can define your own exception types to distinguish failures. This example uses libc's scanf to read a number from the console. It raises Exception if no number can be read, or EInput if the number is greater than 100:

use print

func libc_scanf(fmt : ^char, ...) -> int32 [[external('scanf')]] ..

object EInput(Exception):
endobject

func *Main():
    try:
        PrintLn("Enter a number no greater than 100:")
        var value : float64 = 0
        if libc_scanf("%lf", %value) <> 1:
            raise Exception("Could not read a number")
        endif
        if value > 100:
            raise EInput("Number is too big: {}", [value])
        endif
        PrintLn("Number accepted: {}", [value])
    except EInput as error:
        PrintLn("Input problem: {}", [error.message])
    except Exception as error:
        PrintLn("Other problem: {}", [error.message])
    endtry
endfunc

For example, entering 42 prints Number accepted: 42, entering 150 prints Input problem: Number is too big: 150, and entering hello prints Other problem: Could not read a number.

The %lf conversion stores a float64 at the address %value. scanf returns 1 when it reads that number successfully. It reads a numeric prefix, so input such as 42abc also reads as 42; this example does not validate the entire line.

A handler for Exception also matches exceptions derived from it, including EInput. Placing the EInput handler first lets it handle the too-big case separately.

If a handler does not need the exception value, omit as error:

except EInput:
    // handle an input problem without reading its message

If no handler matches, the exception continues to the caller. Do not call delete on the handler's exception variable; the exception machinery manages that object.

docs.title: 2.16.3.1 Re-raising an Exception
docs.text:
A handler can report a failure or do some local work, then let its caller handle the same failure. Use raise without an argument inside the handler to re-raise the current exception:

use print

object EInput(Exception):
endobject

func RequirePositive(value : int):
    if value <= 0:
        raise EInput("Expected a positive value, got {}", [value])
    endif
endfunc

func ProcessValue(value : int):
    try:
        RequirePositive(value)
        PrintLn("Processing {}", [value])
    except EInput as error:
        PrintLn("Could not process value: {}", [error.message])
        raise
    endtry
endfunc

func *Main():
    try:
        ProcessValue(0)
    except EInput as error:
        PrintLn("Please try again: {}", [error.message])
    endtry
endfunc

Output:

Could not process value: Expected a positive value, got 0
Please try again: Expected a positive value, got 0

ProcessValue reports the problem, but its bare raise passes the exception on to the handler in Main. The Processing line is skipped. Re-raising preserves the original exception type, message, and backtrace, so the failure still points to RequirePositive. If no outer handler catches it, the exception reaches the default error handler.

docs.title: 2.16.4 Cleanup with finally
docs.text:
A finally block performs an action whenever execution leaves a try block. It runs after normal completion or a handled error, and also when an exception continues to the caller:

use print

func *Main():
    try:
        PrintLn("Starting work")
        raise Exception("Connection lost")
    except Exception as error:
        PrintLn("Error: {}", [error.message])
    finally:
        PrintLn("Work finished")
    endtry
endfunc

This prints Starting work, Error: Connection lost, and Work finished. You can also use try with finally alone when you want cleanup without handling the exception there.

finally also runs when return, break, or continue leaves the protected block. It is useful for an explicit action such as restoring a setting or releasing an external resource. For objects owned by your code, prefer automatic cleanup: local autofree variables, managed values, and embedded objects already clean themselves up during exception propagation.

docs.title: 2.16.4.1 Restoring State Without Handling the Error
docs.text:
A finally block is useful even when cleanup does not involve memory. This complete program temporarily changes a setting and restores it before a caller handles the error:

use print

var quiet : bool = false

func RunQuietly():
    var previous : bool = quiet
    quiet = true
    try:
        raise Exception("work failed")
    finally:
        quiet = previous
        PrintLn("Setting restored")
    endtry
endfunc

func *Main():
    try:
        RunQuietly()
    except Exception as error:
        PrintLn("Error: {}; quiet={}", [error.message, quiet])
    endtry
endfunc

Output:

Setting restored
Error: work failed; quiet=false

RunQuietly has no except handler, so the exception continues to Main. Its finally block runs first. Saving the previous setting also makes this work when quiet was already true before the call.

docs.title: 2.16.5 Messages and Backtraces
docs.text:
The exception's .message describes the problem. A backtrace shows the sequence of calls that led to it. If no handler catches the exception, the default error handler prints both and ends the program with a failure status.

Save this example as backtrace.dq. It calls through several functions and lets the exception reach the default error handler:

func CheckTemperature(temp : float):
    if temp > 100:
        raise Exception("Temperature is too high: {}", [temp])
    endif
endfunc

func LogTemperature(temp : float):
    CheckTemperature(temp)
endfunc

func ReadSensor():
    LogTemperature(150)
endfunc

func *Main():
    ReadSensor()
endfunc

Run it with dq-run backtrace.dq. Example output on Linux, with the source paths shortened to the filename:

UNCAUGHT EXCEPTION: Exception: Temperature is too high: 150
Backtrace =
  #0 CheckTemperature @ backtrace.dq:3
  #1 LogTemperature @ backtrace.dq:9
  #2 ReadSensor @ backtrace.dq:13
  #3 Main @ backtrace.dq:17

Read the backtrace from the failure outward: CheckTemperature raised the exception, called by LogTemperature, which was called by ReadSensor, which was called by Main. The source locations help you find each step in the code.

To get source code line info at the backtraces the executable must be compiled with -g. Code optimization might "scramble" the source code, so for clean source code info the optimization might need to be turned off with -O0. The dq-run uses -g -O0 by default to provide best error reporting. The dq-comp however uses -O1 by default for better performance.

The backtrace info is available on Windows and Linux, but might not be available on every target.

docs.title: 2.16.6 Cleanup Details and Limitations
docs.text:
Initialized local values are cleaned up in reverse construction order as an exception leaves their scope. If a constructor fails, already initialized autofree fields and base state are also cleaned up.

Catching an exception does not undo changes made before the failure. Restore or discard partially updated data as appropriate for the operation. If a finally block raises another exception, the new exception becomes the active failure. Calling an external process-exit function does not perform normal block-exit cleanup.

docs.title: 2.16.7 Zero-Cost Exception Handling
docs.text:
DQ uses zero-cost exception handling based on unwind tables on supported hosted targets. The compiler records which parts of a function are protected and where their cleanup code and exception handlers are located. These tables are stored in the executable; they do not need to be checked after each call.

Function calls inside a try block remain ordinary calls in the generated machine code. They are not wrapped in an extra error-checking function, and there is no hidden exception-result check after every call. When no exception is raised, execution follows the normal sequence of operations.

When an exception is raised, the runtime uses the unwind tables to walk back through the active function calls, run the required cleanup, and transfer control to a matching handler. This work happens on the error path.

“Zero-cost” refers to the absence of per-call exception checks during normal execution. It does not mean that raising an exception is free: finding a handler, capturing a backtrace, and running cleanup take time. The tables and handler code also increase executable size, and exception handling can affect compiler optimizations. Ordinary cleanup, including finally blocks, still runs wherever the program requires it.

docs.title: 2.16.8 Runtime Errors and Target Support
docs.text:
Runtime checks, such as range and encoding checks, can also report failures. Some targets convert hardware faults into exceptions: Linux runtimes and Windows x86-64 have fault handling, with recovery verified at -O0. Optimized fault recovery has backend/runtime limitations. Validate addresses before use; fault handling is not a portable way to make invalid memory access safe.

Exceptions normally default to enabled on hosted targets and disabled on bare targets. The compiler options --exceptions and --no-exceptions, or a project setting, select support. EXCEPTIONS is defined when that support is enabled. WASI does not support DQ exceptions.

Runtime checks still apply when exception handling is disabled, but failures cannot be recovered with DQ handlers in that configuration. See Compiler Directives and Runtime and Program Execution.

docs.title: 2.17. anyvalue
docs.text:
anyvalue holds one value that can be a number, text, a boolean, or another supported basic type. It remembers which kind of value it holds. Use it when a function needs to accept different kinds of input, as formatting functions do.

use print

func *Main():
    var value : anyvalue = 42
    PrintLn("{}", [value.AsInt(0)])

    value = "hello"
    PrintLn("{}", [value.AsStr("")])
endfunc

This prints 42 and then hello. The same variable first holds an integer, then text. The accessor methods, such as AsInt, let you read a value in the form you need. Unlike an ordinary int or str, an anyvalue does not have one fixed kind of content throughout its lifetime. Use a specific type when the kind is known in advance; use anyvalue at interfaces that need mixed values.

docs.title: 2.17.1 Checked Access
docs.text:
Use an Is... method to check the kind of value. Use an As... method to read it, supplying a default for values that cannot be converted:

var value : anyvalue = "hello"
var number : int = value.AsInt(-1) // -1: text is not converted to a number
var text : str = value.AsStr("")  // "hello"

The default is also a possible real value. If you need to distinguish a stored -1 from a failed conversion, check the kind first:

if value.IsInt():
    var number : int = value.AsInt(0)
    // use the stored integer
endif

Some accessors accept more than one related kind; for example, AsFloat can read an integer as a floating-point value. They do not perform arbitrary conversions such as parsing text into numbers.

docs.title: 2.17.2 Array Parameters
docs.text:
A []anyvalue parameter accepts a list containing different kinds of values. This is how PrintLn and Format receive their formatting arguments:

use print

func Log(format : rostr, values : []anyvalue):
    PrintLn(format, values)
endfunc

func *Main():
    Log("{}: {} items, ready={}", ["Shopping", 3, true])
endfunc

This prints Shopping: 3 items, ready=true. The bracketed list supplies a temporary array whose elements are converted to anyvalue. Log can pass that list to another function directly. Do not keep its slice for use after the call returns, because the temporary array will no longer exist.

docs.title: 2.17.3 Null
docs.text:
anyvalue can also represent null, meaning a missing value. Use SetNull to set it and IsNull to test it:

var reading : anyvalue = 21.5
reading.SetNull()
var missing : bool = reading.IsNull() // true

Null is different from zero, false, an empty string, and a nil pointer.

docs.title: 2.17.4 Supported Values
docs.text:
An anyvalue can hold these basic values:

Values Notes Signed and unsigned integers Integer width and signedness are recorded. Floating-point numbers float32, float64, and float. Booleans true or false. Characters char and wchar; char16 is stored as wchar. Text str, rostr, strslice, and embstr. Pointers Typed pointers and generic pointer values. Null A missing value, set with SetNull().

Objects, structures, function references, and arbitrary arrays cannot be stored as general values inside it. The temporary array in a []anyvalue call works because each supported element is converted separately.

docs.title: 2.17.5 Methods
docs.text:
Use this table to choose a check or accessor. def means the default value to return when the requested conversion is unavailable.

Method Meaning IsNull() / SetNull() test or set the null value IsNumber() true for integer or floating point values IsInt() / IsSInt() / IsUint() test integer kind AsInt(def) / AsUint(def) convert integer, float, or character code, otherwise return default IsChar() / AsChar(def) / SetChar(value) test, read, or set a byte character IsWChar() / AsWChar(def) / SetWChar(value) test, read, or set a Unicode character; setter also accepts char16 IsBool() / AsBool(def) test/read boolean IsPointer() / AsPointer(def) test/read pointer IsFloat() / IsFloat32() / IsFloat64() test floating point kind AsFloat(def) / AsFloat32(def) / AsFloat64(def) convert float or integer IsText() true for str, rostr, strslice, or embstr values IsStr() true only for dynamic str AsStr(def) return a dynamic string AsText(def) return a text view-style value

A helper can use these methods to produce a label for different kinds of data:

use print

func ToLabel(value : anyvalue) -> str:
    if value.IsNull():
        return "<missing>"
    elif value.IsText():
        return value.AsStr("")
    elif value.IsNumber():
        return Format("{}", [value])
    else:
        return "<value>"
    endif
endfunc

Add this entry point after ToLabel to try each branch:

func *Main():
    var value : anyvalue = 42
    PrintLn("{}", [ToLabel(value)])
    value = "hello"
    PrintLn("{}", [ToLabel(value)])
    value.SetNull()
    PrintLn("{}", [ToLabel(value)])
    value = true
    PrintLn("{}", [ToLabel(value)])
endfunc

This prints 42, hello, <missing>, and <value>, each on its own line. ToLabel checks the stored kind before choosing how to represent it. The final branch is this function's policy for values such as booleans, rather than a limitation of DQ's formatting functions.

Format is available through the implicit sys runtime interface. See String Functions.

docs.title: 2.17.6 Setters and Text Views
docs.text:
In addition to assignment, explicit setters choose what kind of value to store:

Methods Stored category SetInt(value), SetUInt(value) Signed/unsigned integer. SetBool(value), SetPointer(value) Boolean or raw address. SetFloat(value), SetFloat32(value), SetFloat64(value) Floating-point value. SetChar(value), SetWChar(value) Byte character or Unicode scalar. SetText(value), SetEmbStr(value) Borrowed text representation. SetStr(value) Managed dynamic string. SetNull() Missing value (null).

AsStrSlice(default) is the text-view alias of AsText(default). A borrowed text view returned by an accessor still depends on the stored/source value's lifetime. SetStr, AsStr, and IsStr require dynamic-string support. Method names are case-sensitive; in particular the unsigned setter is SetUInt, while its predicate and accessor are IsUint and AsUint.

docs.title: 2.17.7 Lifetime
docs.text:
Storing a managed str keeps its text alive. Storing borrowed text or a pointer does not keep the source alive. For example, a slice into a local buffer must not be used after that buffer has disappeared, even if stored in an anyvalue.

To retain text independently of a borrowed source, copy it into managed string storage before keeping it:

var buffer : embstr(32) = "ready"
var saved : anyvalue
saved.SetStr(buffer) // stores a managed string copy of the buffer's text
buffer = "changed"
// saved.AsStr("") is still "ready"

A view returned by AsText or AsStrSlice is also borrowed. Keep its source valid for as long as you use the view. Copying and destroying an anyvalue automatically performs the appropriate storage handling for its current kind.

docs.title: 2.17.8 Character Details
docs.text:
Characters have their own kind: IsNumber and IsInt return false for them. AsWChar can widen a stored char; AsChar returns its default for a stored wchar.

Formatting with {}, {:?}, or {:s} writes a char byte directly and encodes a wchar as UTF-8. The formats {:d}, {:u}, {:x}, and {:X} instead write the character code:

PrintLn('wchar="{}"', [wchar(0x20AC)]) // wchar="€"

An invalid Unicode scalar, including an isolated char16 surrogate, produces � and sets DQFMT_ARG_ERROR.

docs.title: 2.17.9 Runtime Type Information
docs.text: Internally, each value records a broad kind, a more specific representation, and its data. Use the public predicates and accessors rather than depending on the private memory layout. The methods are backed by the runtime's AnyVal... functions.

docs.title: 2.18. Modules and Packages
docs.text:
A module is a .dq source file. Split a program into modules to keep related code together and reuse it from other files. A package groups modules under a shared name, such as json or file.

Here is a complete two-file program. Put both files in the same directory.

math_extra.dq:

func Add(left : int, right : int) -> int ..

implementation

func Add(left : int, right : int) -> int:
    return left + right
endfunc

main.dq:

use print
use ./math_extra as math --

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [@math.Add(2, 3)])
endfunc

Run dq-run main.dq to compile both files and print 5. use imports the module, as math gives it a short name, and @math.Add calls its public function. The trailing -- keeps that module's names qualified.

The import connects two separate scopes. Add belongs to math_extra.dq; Main belongs to main.dq. The alias math is the name the importing file uses to reach the other module, not a rename of its source file.

docs.title: 2.18.1 Public and Private Declarations
docs.text:
Declarations before implementation are public: other modules can use them. Declarations after it are private, except for definitions of functions already declared in the public section.

Use this split when callers need only the public signature:

const PUBLIC_VALUE : int = 1
func PublicValue() -> int ..

implementation

const PRIVATE_VALUE : int = 2

func PublicValue() -> int:
    return PUBLIC_VALUE + PRIVATE_VALUE
endfunc

An importing module can use PUBLIC_VALUE and PublicValue, but cannot access PRIVATE_VALUE. A public function can also have its body directly in the public section; implementation is optional.

docs.title: 2.18.2 Basic Imports
docs.text:
Use a package name to import an installed module, or a relative path for a nearby source file. Omit the .dq extension:

use print
use ./helpers

By default, public names are available directly and through the module's namespace. For example, after use print, both PrintLn(...) and @print.PrintLn(...) are available. A namespace keeps names from different modules separate.

The compiler normally supplies the sys runtime interface automatically, so basic runtime functions do not need a separate use sys.

docs.title: 2.18.3 Aliases and Merge Control
docs.text:
as chooses a namespace name. Add -- to require that name at each use:

use ./math_extra as math --
var total : int = @math.Add(2, 3)

This helps when two modules have functions with the same name. You can instead choose which public names are available without qualification:

Import form Names available directly use ./helpers All eligible public names. use ./helpers -- None; use @helpers.Name. use ./helpers only(Read, Write) Only Read and Write. use ./helpers exclude(Debug) All eligible public names except Debug.

--, only, and exclude are alternatives; do not combine them on one import. Qualification through the namespace remains available. For example, only(Read) makes Read available by its short name, but does not make other public declarations private: they can still be reached as @helpers.Name. Use implementation in the defining module to hide a declaration from callers.

docs.title: 2.18.4 Relative and Root Paths
docs.text:
Use these forms to find files within your project:

Path Starting point use ./child The importing file's directory. use ../sibling Its parent directory. use ^/root_child The module or package root.

A path cannot go above the established root. To put a main file in a subdirectory while importing siblings from a shared project root, see Source Root Option.

For example, consider this project layout:

project/
    main.dq
    helpers.dq
    tools/
        report.dq

From main.dq, use ./helpers imports helpers.dq, and use ./tools/report imports report.dq. From tools/report.dq, use ../helpers reaches the same helper module, provided project is the established root. If report.dq is compiled as the main file itself, set #opt module_root_depth = 1 before its imports so that its parent directory is included in the root.

Bare imports such as use json search for installed packages. The root module conventionally has the package name, for example json/json.dq. use nanonet/nano_http selects another module inside a package.

docs.title: 2.18.5 Package Search
docs.text:
A package is a source directory containing a module tree. Build metadata is optional; it does not replace the source modules.

The compiler searches standard and installation directories, your user package directory, and directories supplied with --pkg-path. An explicit package path can override an installed package. If several --pkg-path options are given, the last takes precedence.

docs.title: 2.18.6 Namespace and Symbol Conflicts
docs.text:
If two imported modules expose the same name, qualify it or restrict which names they make available. Import order does not silently choose one meaning. Conflicting local declarations, aliases, selected names, and reexports are also checked.

@. explicitly selects the current module's global scope. Inside an object method, use it to call a module function rather than an object member.

docs.title: 2.18.7 Initialization
docs.text:
A module can define *ModuleInit() for setup that must happen before *Main:

use print

var greeting : str

func *ModuleInit():
    greeting = "Ready"
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [greeting])
endfunc

This prints Ready. A used module initializes before the module that uses it, and each module initializes once. Global embedded objects are also initialized before the application starts.

There is no automatic module/global finalization phase. Explicitly release long-lived resources when the application shuts down.

docs.title: 2.18.8 Reexports
docs.text:
reexport makes an imported module's public names available through your own module's public interface:

use ./leaf only(Value, Run) reexport

Use this to provide one convenient entry point for a group of modules. Selection and alias rules apply before reexporting, and conflicting names are reported as errors. Put a reexport in the public section, before implementation.

For example, a library can keep its work in reader.dq and writer.dq, and provide a single storage.dq entry point:

// storage.dq
use ./reader only(Read) reexport
use ./writer only(Write) reexport

A caller can then write use ./storage and use Read and Write without importing the two implementation modules separately. The functions still belong to their original modules; reexporting does not copy their code or run their initialization again. This fragment assumes the two companion modules provide those public functions.

docs.title: 2.18.9 Method-Local Use
docs.text:
Inside an object method, outside variables, constants, and functions (including those from the runtime sys module and imported modules) are not directly accessible by their bare names. Placing a method-local use statement at the start of a method body allows direct, unqualified access to outside symbols—such as use socket, sys, use ., or use *.

Because this feature specifically controls name resolution inside object methods, its full description, rules, and practical examples are documented in Objects and Properties.

docs.title: 2.18.10 Interface Loading and Cycles
docs.text:
Modules may refer to each other only when the compiler can resolve their public interfaces. A circular dependency that needs unavailable implementation details is an error; the diagnostic shows the dependency chain.

The compiler saves public information in .dqm_if files and compiled code in .o files. These are generated build artifacts, not files to import in source.

docs.title: 2.18.11 Package Root and Source Options
docs.text:
The compiler identifies each module by its package or module root and relative path. Importing the same module through another alias or reexport does not create another runtime instance. Two different source files cannot claim the same module identity with different contents. Repeated imports must also use consistent, unambiguous aliases and selections.

For a main file whose root needs to include parent directories, #opt module_root_depth = N selects how many parent levels form the root. Place it before imports that depend on the root. See Compiler Directives.

.dqbuild, .o, and .dqm_if files are generated caches and may change between compiler versions. For cache locations and rebuilding, see Build Process and Module Artifacts. The low-level --no-use-sys option disables the normally implicit runtime import.

docs.title: 2.18.12 Built-in Search Roots on Linux
docs.text:
The compiler adds these package search roots automatically. <compiler-dir> is the directory containing the dq-comp executable:

/usr/lib/dq/stdpkg
<compiler-dir>/../lib/dq/stdpkg
<compiler-dir>/../stdpkg
/usr/lib/dq/packages
<compiler-dir>/../lib/dq/packages
$HOME/.dq/packages

Package roots are checked from last to first. Therefore, a matching package in $HOME/.dq/packages takes precedence over the installation roots, and a root provided with --pkg-path takes precedence over all built-in roots. If several --pkg-path options are given, the last one takes precedence.

docs.title: 2.19. Attributes
docs.text:
An attribute gives the compiler extra instructions about a declaration. You have already seen examples such as [[overload]] for functions with the same name and [[virtual]] for object methods. Other attributes control optimization, memory layout, or access to external code. Most ordinary DQ code needs no attributes; add one when a declaration needs a specific behavior.

Write attributes inside [[...]] next to the declaration they affect:

use print

func Double(value : int) -> int [[inline]]:
    return value * 2
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [Double(21)])
endfunc

This prints 42. [[inline]] asks the compiler to consider putting the function's code directly at its call sites. It does not change how you call Double or the values it accepts.

docs.title: 2.19.1 Writing Attributes
docs.text:
An attribute belongs to the declaration beside it; it does not set a mode for the rest of the file. Function attributes go after the parameter list and optional result type, before : for a body or .. for a declaration. An attribute can also go before a declaration or in another supported trailing position, as the field and global examples below show.

Some attributes take arguments, such as the symbol name in [[external('puts')]]. Combine attributes in one list, separated by commas:

func DefaultHandler() [[weak, cexport]]:
    // fallback implementation
endfunc

docs.title: 2.19.2 Attribute Summary
docs.text:
Not every attribute applies to every declaration. Use the table to find the attribute for your task; less common details follow the examples.

Attribute Purpose and applicable declarations external, external('name') Bind a function or global variable to a native symbol. external('name', 'module') Select a WebAssembly function import module. export('name') Export a function or global value with an explicit native name. cexport Use the declaration name as its unmangled native export name. used Retain a function or global value whose references are invisible to the optimizer. section('name') Place a function or global value in a named native section. align(n) Request alignment for supported global storage or compound fields. packed Pack a structure/compound layout. overload Mark a function, method, or constructor as an overload. inline, always_inline, noinline Control inlining of functions. virtual, override, abstract, final Control object method dispatch and inheritance. asm Supply a function body in target assembly. weak Give a module-level function definition replaceable weak linkage. volatile, noread, nowrite Control direct low-level global/field access. regrw, regro, regwo Volatile register read/write, read-only, and write-only shorthands. nowarn Suppress warnings on supported declarations/statements.

docs.title: 2.19.3 Function Inlining
docs.text:
Inlining can avoid the cost of a function call, but can also increase program size. [[inline]] is a hint; [[always_inline]] makes a stronger request, and [[noinline]] prevents inlining. Normal [[inline]] is considered at -O1 and above.

Inlining across module boundaries requires full link-time optimization (--lto=full), which lets the optimizer see function bodies from other modules.

docs.title: 2.19.3.1 Optimization Levels
docs.text: At -O1, only functions marked inline or always_inline are eligible for inlining. Unmarked definitions receive LLVM's noinline attribute, including in full LTO builds. An explicit noinline still prevents inlining of a function marked inline. Higher optimization levels can also inline unmarked functions.

docs.title: 2.19.4 Linkage and Placement
docs.text:
Use [[external]] for a function or global variable supplied by native code. Use [[cexport]] to expose a DQ declaration under its own name, or [[export('native_name')]] to choose another name:

var counter : uint32 = 0 [[export('dq_counter'), align(4), used]]

func ReadCounter() -> uint32 [[cexport]]:
    return counter
endfunc

Native code can refer to dq_counter and ReadCounter using the corresponding C declarations. Match the types and calling convention described in C Interoperability.

[[used]] retains a function or global value even when ordinary DQ code does not refer to it. Use it for names reached through assembly, a linker script, or a hardware table. It preserves the definition through compilation and linking, including link-time optimization.

[[section('name')]] puts a function or global in a named native section. A linker script or other build setup may be needed to place it at a particular hardware address.

docs.title: 2.19.5 Layout Attributes
docs.text:
[[packed]] removes ordinary layout padding from a structure or compound type. [[align(n)]] requests alignment on supported global storage or fields:

struct SHeader [[packed]]:
    kind : uint8
    length : uint32
endstruct

Use packed layout only when the file format, hardware, or external declaration requires it. Packed fields may be unaligned. Check SizeOf and OffsetOf instead of assuming a particular layout, and choose alignment values supported by the target. See Structures and Unions.
