docs.title: 2.19.6 Volatile and Register Access
docs.text:
A hardware register is a memory location through which a program communicates with a device. Reading it may observe changing device state; writing it may start an operation. volatile tells the compiler to preserve those accesses even when ordinary memory optimizations could remove them.

Hardware registers often live at fixed memory addresses. Register attributes let a declaration say whether each register can be read, written, or both:

struct SDeviceRegisters:
    STATUS  : [[regro]] uint32
    CONTROL : [[regrw]] uint32
    COMMAND : [[regwo]] uint32
endstruct

This structure describes the register layout; declaring the type alone does not connect it to a device. Code for a particular board must obtain the correct base address before accessing its fields through a pointer.

The register attributes expand to the fundamental access attributes:

Register attribute Equivalent attributes Allowed operations [[regrw]] [[volatile]] read and write [[regro]] [[volatile, nowrite]] read only [[regwo]] [[volatile, noread]] write only

Reading [[noread]] storage or writing [[nowrite]] storage is a compile error. A modify-assignment such as |= reads and writes its target and therefore needs both operations to be allowed. noread and nowrite cannot be combined on the same declaration. These restrictions apply to direct global, field, and fixed-array-element access and are retained through module interfaces.

docs.title: 2.19.6.1 Access Limitations
docs.text: Volatile accesses are observable compiler operations, but they are not atomic and do not imply a CPU or compiler memory barrier. Taking an address or binding a reference currently discards noread and nowrite; this is an explicit low-level escape. Whole-structure initialization and copying also do not yet apply the access restrictions of individual fields.

docs.title: 2.19.7 Weak Attribute
docs.text:
[[weak]] provides a fallback function that native code can replace with a strong definition of the same linker name. Combine it with [[cexport]] when C or assembly code should use the function's plain DQ name:

func DefaultHandler() [[weak, cexport]]:
    // used unless another linked definition replaces DefaultHandler
endfunc

weak does not change the name by itself. It takes no arguments and applies only to module-level function definitions, not external declarations or methods.

docs.title: 2.19.8 Validity and Conflicts
docs.text:
Unknown, unsupported, or misplaced attributes produce warnings or errors. Resolve those diagnostics rather than relying on an attribute the compiler could not apply. An attribute cannot bypass a language rule: for example, an external function cannot also have a DQ body.

Some combinations have additional restrictions. weak requires a module-level definition; assembly functions have the combinations described in Assembly Functions. Access restrictions apply to reads and writes individually, so an operation such as += requires both.

For object method attributes, see Inheritance and Virtual Dispatch.

docs.title: 2.20. Compiler Directives
docs.text:
A compiler directive controls how source code is compiled. Use directives to enable optional logging, choose code for a target platform, include shared source, or link an external library. Directives are processed during compilation; they do not run each time the program runs.

For example, include a diagnostic message only when LOGGING is defined:

use print

#define LOGGING
#define BUFFER_SIZE = 256

func *Main():
    #ifdef LOGGING
        PrintLn("buffer size = {}", [BUFFER_SIZE])
    #endif
endfunc

This prints buffer size = 256. Remove #define LOGGING and compile again to leave out the print statement entirely. By comparison, an ordinary if chooses what to execute while the program is running.

docs.title: 2.20.1 Definitions and Namespaces
docs.text:
#define NAME defines a name with the value true. Add = expression to supply a constant boolean or integer value:

#define LOGGING
#define BUFFER_SIZE = 256
#define DOUBLE_BUFFER_SIZE = BUFFER_SIZE * 2

You can use earlier definitions in later ones. Definitions can also come from compiler options such as -DLOGGING or -DBUFFER_SIZE=512, project files, and target settings.

Definitions belong to the @def namespace and are normally available by their short names. Use @def.BUFFER_SIZE if a local declaration has the same name. DQ definitions provide constant values; they do not perform C-style textual macro substitution. For ordinary program constants, use const. Definitions are useful when the build configuration and conditional compilation need to refer to the same setting.

docs.title: 2.20.2 Conditional Compilation
docs.text:
#if tests a constant boolean expression. #ifdef tests whether a name exists. Use #else for an alternative and #endif to close the group:

use print

func *Main():
    #ifdef WINDOWS
        PrintLn("Running on Windows")
    #elifdef LINUX
        PrintLn("Running on Linux")
    #else
        PrintLn("Running on another platform")
    #endif
endfunc

Only the selected branch becomes part of the program. Other branches are skipped before normal DQ parsing, although their nested conditional directives must still balance. This lets a source file contain declarations or assembly instructions that are valid only for the selected platform.

Directive Effect #if expression Start a branch selected by a constant Boolean expression. #ifdef name / #ifndef name Start a branch if a visible name exists / does not exist. #elif expression Test another condition if no earlier branch was selected. #elifdef name / #elifndef name Test another name-existence condition. #else Select the remaining alternative. #endif Close the conditional group.

For a value comparison, use #if rather than #ifdef:

#define API_LEVEL = 4

#if API_LEVEL >= 3
    const HAS_NEW_API : bool = true
#else
    const HAS_NEW_API : bool = false
#endif

The condition must be a compile-time bool and can use only names already visible at that point. A variable whose value is known only at runtime cannot supply the condition.

docs.title: 2.20.3 Target and Feature Definitions
docs.text:
The compiler supplies names for the selected target and enabled features:

Definition Meaning LINUX, WINDOWS, WASI, BARE Effective platform/runtime selection. X86_FAMILY, X86, X64 x86 family and selected 32/64-bit architecture. ARM, ARM_M, ARM_A, ARMHF Applicable Arm profile/ABI markers. ARM64, AARCH64 AArch64 target markers. RISCV, RV32, RV64 RISC-V family and register width. WASM WebAssembly target. TARGET_32BIT, TARGET_64BIT Effective pointer width. PTRSIZE Pointer size in bytes. EXCEPTIONS DQ exception support is enabled. DYNSTRINGS Heap-backed dynamic strings are enabled.

Check the feature you need rather than assuming every target has it. Disabled features are normally absent, so use #ifdef EXCEPTIONS, for example, to test for exception support.

docs.title: 2.20.4 Include
docs.text:
#include inserts another file's source at that point:

#include "shared.dqi"

Single quotes are also accepted. Use an include for a source fragment; use use when you want a module with its own public interface and namespace.

Plain include paths search the current source file's directory and then the package search roots. ./ and ../ are relative to the source file; ^/ is relative to the module root.

docs.title: 2.20.4.1 Include-Once Fragments
docs.text:
Put #include_once at the start of an included fragment when it should be processed only once. Later inclusions skip the rest of that file. This is separate from use, which already imports a module as one shared instance. For example, save this fragment as shared.dqi beside your main file:

#include_once
const MAX_ITEMS : int = 16

The main file can include it more than once, directly or through other fragments, without declaring MAX_ITEMS twice. Included declarations appear in the scope where the include occurs; the fragment has no separate module namespace.

docs.title: 2.20.4.2 Separate Header Files
docs.text:
A module can keep its public declarations in a .dqh file with the same base name. For file.dq, this directive includes file.dqh:

#include header

Use it before implementation. It cannot be used from inside a .dqh file.

docs.title: 2.20.5 Link Libraries
docs.text:
#linklib asks the linker to use an external library. For example, the following declaration gets zlib's version string:

#linklib('z')

func zlibVersion() -> ^char [[external]] ..

The library must be installed and available to the target's linker. See C Interoperability for the full example and setup links.

docs.title: 2.20.6 Source Root Option
docs.text:
#opt module_root_depth sets how many parent levels above the main source file's directory form the module root:

#opt module_root_depth = 1

For project/src/main.dq, a value of 1 uses project as the root. A value of 0 uses project/src. This affects ^/ imports and includes. The value must be a nonnegative integer literal; place the option before paths that need the selected root.

docs.title: 2.20.7 Existence Tests and Defined
docs.text:
Existence tests find visible names, including local variables, parameters, object members, types, module declarations, merged imports, and definitions. Defined(NAME) provides the same test as a constant boolean expression:

#define LOGGING = false

#if Defined(LOGGING) and @def.LOGGING
    // included only if LOGGING exists and its value is true
#endif

A name can exist even when its value is false or zero. #ifdef LOGGING therefore succeeds for the definition above; it does not read that value.

Qualified names restrict lookup: @def.FEATURE checks definitions, @.MODULE_VALUE checks the current module, and @module.PUBLIC_VALUE checks that namespace. Names from inner or completed sibling scopes are not visible. Preprocessor definitions remain available to existence tests in methods even without a method-local use.

You may test whether an uninitialized local exists without reading it. This does not permit you to read the variable before assigning a value.

docs.title: 2.20.8 Optional Constants
docs.text:
FirstInt, FirstFloat, and FirstBool select the first available constant from optional names, with a required fallback at the end. This is useful for settings that a board or build configuration may supply:

const BUFFER_SIZE : int = FirstInt(BOARD_BUFFER_SIZE, DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE, 256)
const SCALE : float = FirstFloat(BOARD_SCALE, 1)
const LOGGING : bool = FirstBool(BOARD_LOGGING, false)

Missing names are skipped from left to right. The first name that exists must be a constant convertible to the required type. A variable or an incompatible constant is an error, rather than a reason to try the next name. The fallback must be valid even when it is not selected.

The results are int, float, and bool, respectively. These expressions always run during compilation and can be used in ordinary expressions or conditional directives. Optional candidates must be bare names, such as BOARD_SCALE, rather than qualified names or arbitrary expressions.

docs.title: 2.20.9 Directive Forms
docs.text:
An ordinary directive starts with # and ends at the physical line ending. For a directive embedded inside a source line, use #{...}:

#define FAST
var value : int = #{ifdef FAST} 1 #{else} 2 #{endif}

Directives accept // and /* ... */ comments. A line comment does not extend a directive onto the next line. Only supported directive names have meaning; there is no general #pragma or implied syntax from other languages.

docs.title: 2.20.10 Include Dependencies
docs.text:
If an implementation include affects the compiled module, declare it before implementation with #srcdep:

#srcdep "somefunc_impl.dqi"

func Calculate(value : int) -> int ..

implementation

#include "somefunc_impl.dqi"

Here somefunc_impl.dqi contains the body of Calculate. #include inserts that body where it belongs, while the earlier #srcdep tells the build system that a change to the fragment can require recompiling the module.

#srcdep records the dependency without inserting its contents there. It uses the same path lookup as #include and records only the named file; it does not parse that file or discover its dependencies.

Automatic include tracking covers directives directly in the main .dq file or its same-basename .dqh. Nested includes in .dqi files are still parsed, but their dependencies are not tracked automatically. Add explicit dependencies when needed for reliable rebuilding.

For build-option precedence and library search paths, see Compiler Usage and Options and Project Files.

docs.title: 2.21. C Interoperability
docs.text:
DQ can call functions from C libraries and let C code call DQ functions. This is useful for reusing existing libraries or working with an operating system's native APIs. There are two parts to calling a C function: declare its interface so DQ can compile the call, and link its implementation so the finished program can run it. Declare the function's name, parameter types, and result in DQ, then mark it [[external]].

For example, call the C library's puts function to print a line:

func c_puts(text : ^char) -> int32 [[external('puts')]] ..

func *Main():
    c_puts("hello from C")
endfunc

This prints hello from C. external('puts') connects the DQ name c_puts to the native function named puts. Normal hosted programs already link the C runtime; other libraries may need an explicit link request.

docs.title: 2.21.1 External Functions and Symbols
docs.text:
If the DQ and native names are the same, use plain [[external]]:

func puts(text : ^char) -> int32 [[external]] ..

The trailing .. ends the declaration without a DQ body. The implementation comes from the external library.

Match the library's actual declaration, usually found in its C header. The compiler checks your DQ code against the declaration you wrote; it cannot check that declaration against the library. A wrong signature may compile successfully and still fail at runtime.

The ABI, or application binary interface, includes details such as type sizes, memory layout, and how function arguments are passed. These must agree between DQ and the native code.

docs.title: 2.21.2 Match C Types Explicitly
docs.text:
Use fixed-width DQ types where the C declaration has a known width:

C-side concept Typical DQ declaration int, unsigned int on usual hosted ABIs int32, uint32 Fixed-width int8_t ... uint64_t Matching DQ fixed-width integer. size_t uint on supported pointer-sized hosted ABIs. float, double float32, float64 void *, opaque handle pointer Pointer to a known type ^T Zero-terminated byte string ^char or a compatible rostr argument. C record/union An explicitly matching struct/union layout.

DQ int is pointer-sized, so use int32 for the usual C int. C long also varies by platform: it has different widths on Windows x64 and Linux x64. Check the target's header rather than assuming similar type names match.

DQ objects, dynamic arrays, str, and unsized embstr are not automatically represented like a C library's objects, arrays, or strings. Pass the raw data in the form the library expects.

docs.title: 2.21.3 Strings, Buffers, and Borrowing
docs.text:
C string functions usually expect a pointer to bytes ending in a zero byte. A text literal or rostr can be passed directly to a ^char parameter:

use print

func strlen(text : ^char) -> uint [[external]] ..

func *Main():
    var text : rostr = "hello"
    PrintLn("{} bytes", [strlen(text)])
endfunc

This prints 5 bytes. DQ passes the underlying text address without copying it. Although the C parameter is written ^char, do not let C write through it when the source is read-only.

For a dynamic str or fixed-storage embstr(N), use .pchar to obtain a borrowed pointer to terminated text. A strslice may not end in a zero byte; copy it into a str or fixed-storage buffer before passing it to a C string function:

var message : str = "hello world"
var first_word : str = message[:5]
c_puts(first_word.pchar) // prints hello, using c_puts from the opening example

Keep the text or buffer alive while C uses its address. If the library stores the pointer for later, the source must remain valid for that entire period.

A C function that writes into a buffer must know its usable size. Do not let it write beyond the capacity or bypass DQ's string length and sharing rules. See Buffer and String Details before passing writable string storage.

docs.title: 2.21.4 Variadic Functions
docs.text:
A C function with ... accepts extra arguments. For example, printf uses its format string to interpret those arguments:

func printf(format : ^char, ...) -> int32 [[external]] ..

func *Main():
    var value : int32 = 42
    printf("value = %d\n", value)
endfunc

This prints value = 42. Here %d expects a C int, so the argument is int32. DQ cannot verify the types expected by a C format string. Extra arguments follow the target's C argument-promotion rules. DQ's own formatting instead uses a checked list of anyvalue values.

docs.title: 2.21.5 Callbacks
docs.text:
A callback is a function you give to a library for it to call. Use a plain function reference with the exact signature the C API expects. A bound of object method reference also stores its receiver, so it is not a plain C function pointer. Keep any callback context alive for as long as the library may use it.

For example, the C library's qsort function sorts a buffer by repeatedly calling a comparison function supplied by the caller:

use print

type FCompare = func(left : pointer, right : pointer) -> int32

func qsort(base : pointer, count : uint, size : uint,
    compare : FCompare) [[external]] ..

func CompareInts(left : pointer, right : pointer) -> int32:
    var a : int32 = ^int32(left)^
    var b : int32 = ^int32(right)^
    if a < b:
        return -1
    elif a > b:
        return 1
    endif
    return 0
endfunc

func *Main():
    var values : [4]int32 = [30, 10, 40, 20]
    qsort(%values[0], values.length, SizeOf(int32), CompareInts)
    for value : int32 in values:
        PrintLn("{}", [value])
    endfor
endfunc

This prints 10, 20, 30, and 40, each on its own line. qsort receives the address of the first element, the number of elements, and the size of each one in bytes. It passes two element addresses to CompareInts, which reads them as int32 values and returns a negative, zero, or positive C int. Explicit comparisons avoid the overflow that subtracting the values could cause.

qsort rearranges the caller's array during the call and does not retain its address afterward. The local array therefore lives long enough. This example uses plain fixed-width numbers; do not use raw C byte-copying operations to rearrange DQ values that require managed copying or cleanup.

docs.title: 2.21.6 Linking and Native Ownership
docs.text:
Use #linklib('name') when an external library needs to be linked explicitly. For example, this program prints the installed zlib version:

use print
#linklib('z')

func zlibVersion() -> ^char [[external]] ..

func *Main():
    var version : rostr = zlibVersion()
    PrintLn("zlib {}", [version])
endfunc

This requires zlib to be installed in the target linker's search path. Compiler options and project files can also provide native libraries and object files. Existing C declarations are available through modules such as use libc/stdio.

Release resources with the operation their API specifies. For example, close a native file using the library's close function. A returned pointer may be borrowed, or may need a library-specific release function; do not assume that delete or an autofree pointer is appropriate.

Linux setup and Windows setup explain native library installation and search paths.

docs.title: 2.21.7 Exporting DQ Functions
docs.text:
Use [[cexport]] to expose a function under its DQ name, or [[export('name')]] to choose its native name:

func Add(left : int32, right : int32) -> int32 [[cexport]]:
    return left + right
endfunc

The corresponding C declaration includes the header for fixed-width integers:

#include <stdint.h>

int32_t Add(int32_t left, int32_t right);

The C and DQ files must be compiled for the same target and linked together. The export attribute supplies the symbol name; it does not itself build a shared library or arrange runtime initialization for a C-owned entry point. See Attributes for exported globals and symbol retention.

Avoid letting a DQ exception cross a native call boundary unless that interface explicitly supports it. Handle failures within the DQ entry point when needed.

docs.title: 2.21.8 External Global Variables
docs.text:
A global variable may also come from native code:

var native_counter : int32 [[external('native_counter')]]

The linked native code must supply that symbol. Some C headers expose apparent globals through macros or functions instead. For example, do not assume errno is an exported integer variable; use the platform's real interface.

docs.title: 2.21.9 Structures, Unions, and Layout
docs.text:
When passing a C record or union, match its field types, order, padding, alignment, and calling convention. Check SizeOf and OffsetOf on the target. Use [[packed]] only when the corresponding C record is packed the same way; packing a normally aligned record changes its layout.

A union gives several fields the same storage without remembering which one was written. Ensure the selected field contains a valid value before reading it. See Structures and Unions and Attributes.

docs.title: 2.21.10 Buffer and String Details
docs.text:
embstr(N) has N storage bytes including its zero terminator, leaving room for at most N - 1 content bytes. A C writer must respect both that capacity and any runtime descriptor requirements. Raw writes into a dynamic str must not bypass its copy-on-write and length handling.

C termination-based APIs see only the text before the first zero byte. To pass binary data or text containing embedded zeros, use an API that takes a pointer and a length. DQ text operations preserve embedded zeros when the length is known.

rostr also converts to ^char in C variadic arguments, such as a %s argument to printf. Neither this conversion nor .pchar extends the source lifetime. See Conversions and Borrowed Lifetimes.

docs.title: 2.21.11 WebAssembly Imports
docs.text: For WebAssembly functions, [[external('name', 'module')]] can select both the import name and its module. The second argument applies only to function imports on that target, not to external global variables.

docs.title: 2.22. Assembly Functions
docs.text:
An assembly function lets you write machine instructions and call them like a DQ function. Use one when you need a specific processor instruction that DQ expressions or library functions do not provide. You will need to know the assembly language for your target processor.

Here is a complete x86-64 example that adds two numbers:

use print

func Add(left : int, right : int) -> int [[inline, asm]]:
    lea $result, [$left + $right]
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [Add(19, 23)])
endfunc

This prints 42. $left and $right stand for the function arguments, and $result stands for its return value. The compiler chooses the actual registers. For ordinary addition, use a DQ expression; this small example shows how an assembly operation connects to a normal function call.

There are two forms:

Attributes What you write [[inline, asm]] Instructions inserted at each direct call; the compiler connects arguments and results. [[asm]] A complete native function, including argument handling and return instructions.

Both use a colon body closed by endfunc. They do not accept a bodyless declaration or a brace body. Instructions and register names depend on the target; the x86-64 examples do not work unchanged on ARM or RISC-V.

docs.title: 2.22.1 Inline Assembly Functions
docs.text:
[[inline, asm]] is useful for a small operation that should become part of the caller's code. Declare its input and result types just as for an ordinary function, then use named operands in the instructions.

On x86-64, use Intel syntax. ARM, AArch64, and RISC-V use their native syntax. DQ does not translate instructions or reorder their operands.

docs.title: 2.22.1.1 Named Operands
docs.text:
Use $result for the return value and $parameter for a function parameter. The compiler replaces these names with the target assembly operands allocated for the call.

For example, ARM targets with the rbit instruction can reverse the bits of a 32-bit value:

func ReverseBits(value : uint32) -> uint32 [[inline, asm]]:
    rbit    $result, $value
endfunc

$result is valid only when the function has a return type. An unknown name is a compile error. A literal dollar sign in assembly text must be written as $$ because the underlying assembly template syntax reserves $.

By default, parameters are register inputs and the result is a register output. Use the hints below for constant operands, memory access, or additional effects. The input and output registers may overlap. Write instructions that remain correct if $result uses the same register as an input, and do not modify an input register unless that change is represented by an output or clobber.

docs.title: 2.22.1.2 Operand Hints
docs.text:
The compiler must know what your instructions read or change. Put one hint list immediately before endfunc to describe those effects. For example, this x86-64 function multiplies by a compile-time constant:

func MulImmediate(value : int32, factor : int32) -> int32 [[inline, asm]]:
    imul    $result, $value, $factor
    [[immediate(factor), clobber(flags)]]
endfunc

The hint list tells the compiler about the instructions; it is not assembly text. It supports these clauses:

Hint Meaning immediate(parameter, ...) Require compile-time integer-like arguments and use them as immediate operands memread(parameter, ...) Describe memory read through typed pointer or readable reference arguments memwrite(parameter, ...) Describe memory written through typed pointer or writable reference arguments memreadwrite(parameter, ...) Describe memory both read and written through typed pointer or read/write reference arguments clobber(resource, ...) Declare registers or other target resources modified by the assembly

A clause can name multiple operands. Clause and argument order do not affect the meaning. Each parameter may occur in at most one hint; parameters omitted from the list remain register inputs.

An immediate argument must be a compile-time constant at every call site. Its type must be an integer, Boolean, character, or enumeration type.

Memory operands must be typed pointers or references so that the compiler knows the accessed element type. The reference mode must permit the described access: refin can be read but not written, refout can be written but not read, and ref supports all three memory hints. The programmer remains responsible for passing a valid address.

A clobber names a register or other resource changed by the instructions. clobber(memory) is supported on every inline-assembly target. It acts as a compiler barrier, preventing memory operations from being moved across it:

func CompilerBarrier() [[inline, asm]]:
    [[clobber(memory)]]
endfunc

This does not emit a processor memory-barrier instruction.

clobber(flags) declares the condition-code state on x86, ARM, and AArch64 targets. It is not available on RISC-V. A physical register can also be named as a clobber, using its lowercase target name or a recognized conventional alias:

func AddOneThroughRax(value : int) -> int [[inline, asm]]:
    mov     rax, $value
    lea     $result, [rax + 1]
    [[clobber(rax)]]
endfunc

Declare every memory access and every modified resource that is not already an output. The optimizer can only account for effects described by the signature, memory hints, and clobbers.

docs.title: 2.22.2 Reading and Writing Memory
docs.text:
Use memory hints for instructions that access a pointed-to value. With these hints, $address means the memory at that address, rather than a register containing the pointer. These examples use x86-64 Intel syntax:

func Load32(address : ^int32) -> int32 [[inline, asm]]:
    mov     $result, $address
    [[memread(address)]]
endfunc

func Store32(address : ^int32, value : int32) [[inline, asm]]:
    mov     $address, $value
    [[memwrite(address)]]
endfunc

func AddTo32(address : ^int32, value : int32) [[inline, asm]]:
    add     $address, $value
    [[memreadwrite(address), clobber(flags)]]
endfunc

To try these three functions, place use print before them and add:

func *Main():
    var value : int32 = 10
    Store32(%value, 20)
    AddTo32(%value, 3)
    PrintLn("{}", [Load32(%value)])
endfunc

This prints 23. %value supplies the address of the local variable. memwrite describes the store, memreadwrite describes the addition, and memread describes the load. These hints tell the optimizer how the assembly interacts with the surrounding DQ code; the instructions perform the actual reads and writes.

An instruction may still require an explicit size qualifier when its other operands do not determine the access width:

func Inc32(address : ^int32) [[inline, asm]]:
    inc     dword ptr $address
    [[memreadwrite(address), clobber(flags)]]
endfunc

docs.title: 2.22.3 Complete Assembly Functions
docs.text:
Use [[asm]] when you need to control the whole native function. Unlike the inline form, its body must include the instruction that returns to the caller.

use print

func Return42() -> int [[asm]]:
    mov     eax, 42
    ret
endfunc

func *Main():
    PrintLn("{}", [Return42()])
endfunc

This prints 42 on x86-64 and uses Intel syntax. DQ uses the unified instruction destination, source operand order and does not support AT&T syntax.

The DQ signature determines the calling convention: the rules for passing arguments and returning values. The assembly implementation must read arguments from the correct registers or stack locations, place a return value in the correct location, preserve all required registers, and return to the caller. Parameter names and result are not available as operands in a complete assembly function.

The compiler emits an [[asm]] function as naked and non-inline. Consequently, it does not generate a prologue or epilogue (the instructions that normally set up and restore a function's stack and registers), or a DQ return operation. [[asm]] cannot be combined with [[external]], [[abstract]], or [[always_inline]].

docs.title: 2.22.4 Inline Assembly Restrictions
docs.text:
An inline assembly function does not produce a separately callable function. Every direct call emits the assembly template at the call site. It therefore cannot be converted to a function reference or have its address taken.

Inline assembly functions must be ordinary module-level functions. Methods and special functions such as *Main and *ModuleInit are not supported. They also cannot use [[external]], [[noinline]], [[weak]], [[section]], or native export attributes. [[overload]] is allowed, and inline assembly definitions in a module's public interface remain available to importing modules.

docs.title: 2.22.4.1 Operand Types and Registers
docs.text: Without an operand hint, each parameter is a register input. Integer, Boolean, character, enumeration, pointer, and floating-point scalar operands are supported. The result is always a register output and must also have a supported scalar type. Integer and pointer values use the target's general-purpose register class; floating-point values use its native floating-point register class. Availability of a particular floating-point register class may depend on the selected CPU features.

docs.title: 2.22.5 Source Processing
docs.text:
Assembly bodies participate in normal DQ source processing:

  • // and /* ... */ comments are removed;
  • compiler directives are processed, and inactive conditional branches are omitted;
  • endfunc closes the body only when it is active and outside a comment;
  • comments and skipped branches preserve the separation between assembly tokens and instructions.

This permits target-specific implementations selected with conditional compilation. This x86-64 example uses a build-supplied TARGET_HAS_PAUSE definition to choose the instruction:

func Pause() [[inline, asm]]:
    #ifdef TARGET_HAS_PAUSE
        pause
    #else
        nop
    #endif
endfunc

Inside an assembly body, # starts a DQ directive only when it is the first non-whitespace, non-comment character on a physical source line. After assembly text has started on the line, # remains target assembly syntax. For example, the immediate in mov r0, #1 is preserved. Keep an instruction and any line-leading immediate operand on the same physical line; a continuation line starting with # would be parsed as a directive.

Because DQ comments are removed before assembly is parsed, do not use // or /* ... */ when those characters are intended as target assembler syntax. A line-leading # likewise cannot be used as a target assembler comment. In a complete [[asm]] body, [[...]] has no special meaning. In an [[inline, asm]] body, a line beginning with [[ is parsed as the single trailing operand-hint list, after which only comments, whitespace, and endfunc may follow.

docs.title: 2.22.6 Supported Inline-Assembly Targets
docs.text:
Typed inline assembly is supported for these target identifiers:

  • x86-64: x86_64;
  • ARM: arm_m0, arm_m3, arm_m4, arm_m4f, arm_m33, arm_m7f, arm_m7fd, arm, and ARM-A identifiers beginning with arm_a;
  • AArch64: aarch64, arm64;
  • RISC-V 32-bit: riscv32, rv32i, rv32imac;
  • RISC-V 64-bit: riscv64, rv64g.

Complete [[asm]] functions are not restricted to this list. In either form, instructions must match the selected target and CPU features.

docs.title: 3. DQ Compiler and Tools
docs.text:
Install the tools for your host platform, then use dq-run for small programs or dq-comp and a project file for a repeatable application build.

  • Compiler and Tool Overview
  • Runtime and Program Execution
  • Linux Development Environment
  • Windows Development Environment
  • Compiler Usage and Options
  • Project Files
  • Build Process and Module Artifacts
  • Targets and Cross-Compilation
  • VSCode Setup and Debugging

Compiler contributors can continue with Building the Compiler from Source.

docs.title: 3.1. Compiler and Tool Overview
docs.text:
The DQ tools turn .dq source modules into native programs. The compiler uses LLVM to generate machine code and a Clang linker driver to combine that code with the DQ runtime and native libraries.

Tool Purpose dq-comp Compile a source module or .dqproj project and link an executable. dq-run Compile and run a single source file. dq-atrun Compile and execute the repository's autotests.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Install and Check the Tools
docs.text:
Use a DQ release package for your host platform. Keep its bin, stdpkg, and bundled toolchain directories together, since the tools discover supporting files relative to the compiler.

Follow Linux Development Environment or Windows Development Environment for installation. To work on the compiler itself, see Building the Compiler from Source.

dq-comp --version
dq-comp --help
dq-run --help

docs.title: 3.1.2 Compile a Program
docs.text:
Save this as hello.dq:

use print

func *Main():
    PrintLn("Hello, DQ!")
endfunc

Run it directly:

dq-run hello.dq

Or keep the compiled executable:

dq-comp -g -O0 hello.dq
./hello

On Windows, the output is hello.exe; run it with .\hello.exe in PowerShell. *Main is the DQ program entry point. The selected runtime supplies the native startup code on hosted targets.

docs.title: 3.1.3 Choose a Workflow
docs.text:
Use dq-run for small examples. Compiler options go before the source filename; program arguments go after it, optionally separated by --:

dq-run -O2 hello.dq -- first second

When no compiler options are supplied, dq-run selects -g -O0. These flags provide source information for debugging and runtime backtraces.

Use dq-comp for explicit output names, reusable builds, and cross targets. A project file keeps a longer set of options together. Imported DQ modules and runtime modules are compiled as needed; you do not need to list every imported source file on the command line.

The next chapters describe program execution, compiler options, and the generated build artifacts.

docs.title: 3.2. Runtime and Program Execution
docs.text: The DQ runtime is written in DQ and lives in stdpkg/rtl. It supplies the services needed by generated code: managed storage, runtime checks, module initialization, and platform startup. The compiler builds the required runtime modules alongside your program.

docs.title: 3.2.1 Hosted Startup
docs.text:
On Linux, Windows, and WASI, the selected runtime supplies the native main entry point. Startup records the command-line arguments, initializes imported modules in dependency order, then calls the DQ func *Main() entry point. Each canonical module is initialized once.

Returning from *Main ends a normal hosted run. The implicit exit_code variable starts at zero; assign it to select the process result while allowing local scope cleanup to finish:

use print

func *Main():
    if ArgCount() < 2:
        PrintLn("Please supply a name")
        exit_code = 1
        return
    endif
    var name : rostr = ArgStr(1)
    PrintLn("Hello, {}!", [name])
endfunc

Run the saved program with dq-run hello.dq -- Alice. ArgCount() includes the program name at index zero. ArgStr(i) returns a borrowed zero-terminated pointer, or nil when the index is outside the argument list.

Exit(status) terminates a hosted process immediately through the C runtime. Use a normal return when local destructors and finally actions need to run. DQ does not currently perform automatic global/module finalization at shutdown; release resources explicitly when their shutdown actions matter.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Implicit Runtime Interface
docs.text:
Ordinary modules automatically receive the public names of rtl/sys. These include memory helpers, string helpers, and, on hosted targets, argument access. The exception interface is included when exceptions are enabled. The sys chapter lists the user-facing services.

--no-use-sys suppresses that implicit import. It is intended for bootstrap and low-level runtime modules that must control their own dependencies.

docs.title: 3.2.3 Runtime Features
docs.text:
Feature Hosted default Bare default Selection Exception handling Enabled, except on WASI Disabled --exceptions / --no-exceptions, or exceptions in a project. Dynamic strings Enabled Disabled --dynstrings / --no-dynstrings, or dynstrings in a project.

The compiler defines EXCEPTIONS and DYNSTRINGS only when the corresponding feature is enabled. Use conditional compilation for code that needs both configurations.

With exceptions disabled, try, except, finally, and raise are rejected. Runtime checks remain active and report failures through RuntimeError and its runtime error hook. Hosted defaults print the error and terminate the process.

With dynamic strings disabled, heap-owning str operations are rejected. Literals, rostr, strslice, and fixed-storage embstr remain available. See Project Files for feature settings.

docs.title: 3.2.4 Exceptions and Diagnostics
docs.text:
On exception-enabled hosted targets, an uncaught exception reaches the runtime's top-level reporter, which prints the message and backtrace and exits with failure. Compile with -g -O0 to retain useful source locations:

dq-comp -g -O0 app.dq
dq-run app.dq

The second command chooses those flags when no compiler options are supplied. See Exceptions and Error Handling for handlers and cleanup. Signal/access-violation conversion has platform and optimization limitations documented in Exceptions and Backtraces.

docs.title: 3.2.5 Bare-Metal Startup
docs.text:
Bare targets produce objects by default and do not supply a complete board startup environment. A board project provides its entry point, reset/startup code, memory layout, and linker script. Do not assume hosted argument access, process termination, or an operating-system exception reporter.

On bare targets, the default Exit implementation loops indefinitely and Errno() returns -1. Runtime integration belongs to the board support code. See Targets and Cross-Compilation and bare-metal project runtimes.

docs.title: 3.3. Linux Development Environment
docs.text: This chapter sets up a Linux computer for developing DQ applications. The package commands below use Ubuntu; other distributions may use different package names and installation commands.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Download and Extract DQ
docs.text:
Download the Linux compiler archive for your CPU architecture from the DQ releases page. For an x86_64 computer, the full package is named dq-VERSION-x86_64-linux-full.tar.gz, where VERSION is the release number.

The full package includes the DQ tools, standard packages, examples, and the Clang/LLVM toolchain used to link programs. It is the simplest starting point because it supplies the compiler and linker dependencies together.

Extract the complete archive into a directory you can keep. For the commands below, replace VERSION with the version in the downloaded filename:

tar -xzf dq-VERSION-x86_64-linux-full.tar.gz
cd dq-VERSION-x86_64-linux-full

Keep the package directories together. The compiler locates the standard packages and bundled tools relative to its installation.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Set Up the Shell Environment
docs.text:
From the extracted full package directory, load its environment script:

source ./dq-env.sh
dq-comp --version

This configures the current Bash shell to find the DQ tools and their bundled toolchain. PATH is the list of directories the shell searches for commands. You need to source the script again in a new terminal unless you install DQ or add the setup to your shell startup file.

To try an included example from the extracted package directory:

dq-run examples/basic/test1.dq

docs.title: 3.3.2.1 Install DQ
docs.text:
Both full and smaller Linux compiler archives include an installer. From the extracted archive, install for the current user with:

./install.sh --prefix "$HOME/.local"
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
dq-comp --version

Add the export PATH=... line to ~/.bashrc to make it available in future Bash terminals. The installer places the tools and supporting files under ~/.local/lib/dq and creates command symlinks in ~/.local/bin.

For a system-wide installation, use this alternative:

sudo ./install.sh
dq-comp --version

The default installation directory is /usr/local/lib/dq, with command symlinks in /usr/local/bin. Installing a full archive also installs its bundled toolchain. Examples and the VS Code extension remain in the extracted archive, so keep it if you want to use those files.

docs.title: 3.3.2.2 Using a Package Without a Bundled Toolchain
docs.text:
If the release provides a smaller archive named dq-VERSION-x86_64-linux.tar.gz, it uses the system's compiler and linker dependencies. Follow that release's dependency instructions.

For a release built with LLVM 21, an Ubuntu 26.04 setup is:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install clang-21 lld-21 g++ libc6-dev libbacktrace-dev
export DQ_LINKER_DRIVER=clang++-21

The selected linker driver must match the LLVM major version used to build DQ, especially when using link-time optimization. Ubuntu 26.04 provides Clang 21. On distributions without the required version, the LLVM APT repository provides installation instructions and a script for selecting a specific version. The full DQ package avoids this additional setup.

docs.title: 3.3.3 Set Up Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Install Visual Studio Code, then install the DQ extension shipped in the compiler archive:

  1. Open the Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P.
  2. Run Extensions: Install from VSIX....
  3. Select the dq-syntax-*.vsix file in the archive's VSCode directory.
  4. Reload the VS Code window if prompted.

Open the extracted package's examples directory with File > Open Folder, then open langdemo.dq. It should appear with DQ syntax highlighting. Click the play button in the editor title bar or run DQ: Run Current File from the Command Palette.

The extension runs the current file through dq-run with debugging options -g -O0. It also starts dq-comp as a language server to provide compiler diagnostics and document symbols. Both commands must be available to VS Code.

If you sourced dq-env.sh in a terminal, start VS Code from that terminal with code . so it inherits the environment. After changing persistent environment settings, close and reopen VS Code.

For a portable installation that is not on PATH, you can set explicit tool paths in VS Code's settings.json:

{
    "dq.languageServerPath": "/home/yourname/dq/bin/dq-comp",
    "dq.runPath": "/home/yourname/dq/bin/dq-run"
}

Replace these example paths with your actual installation paths. See VSCode Setup and Debugging for the chapter dedicated to editor and debugger configuration.

docs.title: 3.3.4 Add External Libraries
docs.text:
Some DQ packages call external C libraries. Install the development package for each library you use so the linker can find it. For example, on Ubuntu:

sudo apt install libsqlite3-dev

For the MySQL client library:

sudo apt install libmysqlclient-dev

These are optional dependencies for applications that use the corresponding database packages. A database server is a separate installation.

docs.title: 3.3.5.1 The Shell Cannot Find dq-comp
docs.text:
Check which command the shell finds:

command -v dq-comp

Source the full package's dq-env.sh, or add the installation's command directory to PATH. If multiple versions are installed, check that the reported path is the version you intend to use.

docs.title: 3.3.5.2 Linking Fails
docs.text:
Keep the full package's toolchain and stdpkg directories with its tools. When using system tools, check clang++-21 --version and ld.lld-21 --version and select the matching driver with DQ_LINKER_DRIVER.

An error such as unable to find library -lsqlite3 means the linker cannot find the requested library. Install its development package. If the problem only occurs in VS Code, check that the editor inherited the same environment as the working terminal.

docs.title: 3.3.6 Next Steps
docs.text:
Return to Getting Started to write and run your first program.

Building the DQ compiler itself requires additional C++ and LLVM development packages. That workflow belongs in Building the Compiler from Source.

docs.title: 3.4. Windows Development Environment
docs.text:
This chapter sets up Windows for developing DQ applications with the Windows UCRT compiler package. The compiler produces native .exe files. Its archive includes the compiler, standard packages, and the toolchain used to link programs.

The commands marked bat below are for Command Prompt (cmd.exe). The sh commands in the external-library section run inside MSYS2 UCRT64.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Download and Extract DQ
docs.text:
Download the x86_64 Windows UCRT archive from the DQ releases page. Its filename is dq-VERSION-x86_64-windows-ucrt.zip, where VERSION is the release number.

Extract the complete archive to a directory such as C:\dq. In this guide, C:\dq\bin\dq-comp.exe is the resulting compiler path. If extraction creates an additional directory containing the version number, use that directory as your DQ root instead.

Use a simple directory name without spaces, and keep all the package directories together. In particular, retain bin, stdpkg, gcclibs, and toolchain. The compiler finds its bundled linker relative to its own installation, so the toolchain directory does not need a separate PATH entry.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Make the Tools Available
docs.text:
For the current Command Prompt window, run:

set "PATH=C:\dq\bin;%PATH%"
dq-comp --version

The command should print the compiler version. The package also includes dq-env.cmd, which prepares the current Command Prompt when run from the extracted package directory.

For permanent setup:

  1. Open Edit environment variables for your account from the Start menu.
  2. Under User variables, select Path and choose Edit.
  3. Add C:\dq\bin, using your actual installation path if different.
  4. Confirm the dialogs and open a new terminal.

Completely close and reopen VS Code if it was running, so it inherits the new environment. PATH is the list of directories Windows searches for commands and runtime DLLs.

Check which compiler Windows finds:

where dq-comp
dq-comp --version

If several versions are listed, Windows normally uses the first one.

docs.title: 3.4.3 Compile and Run a Program
docs.text:
Follow Getting Started to create hello.dq, then open a terminal in the directory containing that file:

dq-run hello.dq

To compile and run separately:

dq-comp -g -O0 hello.dq
.\hello.exe

The Windows compiler package provides the tools needed for this basic workflow. External libraries are required only when your application uses them.

docs.title: 3.4.4 Set Up Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Install Visual Studio Code, then install the DQ extension from the compiler archive:

  1. Open the Command Palette with Ctrl+Shift+P.
  2. Run Extensions: Install from VSIX....
  3. Select C:\dq\VSCode\dq-syntax-*.vsix, using the actual filename and path.
  4. Reload the VS Code window if prompted.

Open C:\dq\examples with File > Open Folder, then open langdemo.dq. Click the play button in the editor title bar or run DQ: Run Current File from the Command Palette. The extension saves the file and invokes dq-run with -g -O0.

The extension uses dq-comp as its language server. If you keep a portable installation outside PATH, set the paths explicitly in VS Code's settings.json:

{
    "dq.languageServerPath": "C:\\dq\\bin\\dq-comp.exe",
    "dq.runPath": "C:\\dq\\bin\\dq-run.exe"
}

Running a program with the play button does not start a debugger. For breakpoints and stepping, the Windows setup uses the LLDB DAP extension (llvm-vs-code-extensions.lldb-dap) with the bundled lldb-dap.exe. Its executable path can be configured in settings.json:

{
    "lldb-dap.executable-path": "C:\\dq\\toolchain\\llvm-mingw\\bin\\lldb-dap.exe"
}

Build debug executables with -g -O0. The VSCode Setup and Debugging chapter is the place for build-task and debugger launch configurations.

docs.title: 3.4.5 Add External Libraries with MSYS2
docs.text:
Packages such as the SQLite and MySQL bindings need external C libraries. A convenient source of Windows builds is MSYS2.

Install MSYS2, using C:\msys64 for the paths below. Open MSYS2 UCRT64 from the Start menu and update the installation:

pacman -Syu

If the update asks you to close the terminal, reopen MSYS2 UCRT64 and run the command again to finish. Follow the MSYS2 update instructions for further details.

Install whichever client libraries your application needs:

pacman -S --needed mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-sqlite3
pacman -S --needed mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-libmariadbclient

The SQLite package provides the SQLite runtime and development libraries. The MariaDB client package provides libraries for the MySQL-compatible client interface. Installing a client library does not install a database server.

Use the UCRT64 environment and packages beginning with mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64- for this setup. Its libraries live under ucrt64. MSYS2's other environments use different toolchain or runtime combinations; see the MSYS2 environment overview.

docs.title: 3.4.5.1 Configure Library and DLL Search Paths
docs.text:
DQ needs to find the libraries during linking and their DLLs when the program runs. Add these directories to your user environment:

Variable Directory Purpose PATH C:\dq\bin DQ tools and their runtime DLLs. PATH C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin External libraries' runtime DLLs. LIBRARY_PATH C:\msys64\ucrt64\lib External libraries used by the linker.

Use the same Windows environment-variable editor as for the DQ tools. Create the user variable LIBRARY_PATH if it does not exist. If it already exists, add the new directory to its semicolon-separated list while preserving the existing directories. Keep the DQ bin entry ahead of the MSYS2 entry in PATH.

To configure the current Command Prompt temporarily:

set "PATH=C:\dq\bin;C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;%PATH%"
set "LIBRARY_PATH=C:\msys64\ucrt64\lib;%LIBRARY_PATH%"

Open a new terminal and restart VS Code after changing persistent settings. You can then run the SQLite example from the extracted DQ package directory:

cd /d C:\dq
dq-run stdpkg\sqlite3\examples\sqlite_test.dq

docs.title: 3.4.6 Run Applications on Another Computer
docs.text:
When distributing a compiled program, include the runtime DLLs it needs. For the standard Windows runtime, these normally include libc++.dll and libunwind.dll from the DQ package's bin directory. Include any additional DLLs required by the particular build, such as libwinpthread-1.dll when used.

Applications that use external libraries also need those libraries' runtime DLLs and their dependencies. For example, SQLite's DLL is C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\libsqlite3-0.dll.

Place the required DLLs beside the application executable, preserving their filenames. You can inspect direct DLL imports with the bundled tool:

"C:\dq\toolchain\llvm-mingw\bin\llvm-readobj.exe" --coff-imports hello.exe

Static linking is available through dq-comp --static, when the required static libraries are available. It can reduce external DLL dependencies, but does not guarantee a completely standalone executable. Include the applicable license notices for libraries you distribute.

docs.title: 3.4.7.1 Windows Cannot Find dq-comp
docs.text: Run where dq-comp. Check that your DQ bin directory is in PATH and that you opened a new terminal after editing the environment. If running from VS Code, restart the entire editor rather than only its integrated terminal.

docs.title: 3.4.7.2 The Linker Cannot Find SQLite
docs.text:
For an error such as unable to find library -lsqlite3, check:

echo %LIBRARY_PATH%
dir C:\msys64\ucrt64\lib\libsqlite3.dll.a

Install the UCRT64 SQLite package if the import library is missing. Adding ucrt64\bin to PATH supplies DLLs for execution; LIBRARY_PATH supplies libraries for linking.

docs.title: 3.4.7.3 A Runtime DLL Is Missing
docs.text: Check where libsqlite3-0.dll for SQLite and your DQ bin directory for libc++.dll and libunwind.dll. Verify the PATH inherited by the program or place the required DLLs beside its executable.

docs.title: 3.4.7.4 A Library Has the Wrong Architecture or Format
docs.text: Use native x86_64 Windows UCRT libraries with this compiler package. Linux/WSL libraries and MSYS libraries do not replace those native Windows libraries. Check that both the selected package and the search paths use ucrt64.

docs.title: 3.5. Compiler Usage and Options
docs.text: Compile a source file or a project file with dq-comp. Use dq-comp --help to see the options accepted by your installed version.

docs.title: 3.5.1 dq-comp
docs.text:
Basic use:

dq-comp app.dq
./app

Useful options:

Option Meaning -o <file> set output filename -c compile only; do not link --ifgen generate a standalone .dqm_if interface file --ifdump dump a standalone .dqm_if interface --no-use-sys disable implicit merged sys import --target=<name> select a compiler target --sysroot=<path> select the target system root used for linking --cpu-features=<features> append LLVM CPU features to the target defaults --targets list canonical targets and their LLVM/default settings --exceptions, --no-exceptions enable or disable DQ exception handling --dynstrings, --no-dynstrings enable or disable heap-backed dynamic strings --pkg-path <path> add a package search root; repeatable --build <tag> select .dqbuild/<tag> --build-suffix <suffix> append to the selected build tag --build-root <path> select the local artifact build root --package-build-root <path> select a separate package artifact build root --lto[=full|off] control full LTO bitcode sidecars -Dname define a compile-time symbol as true -Dname=value define an integer or boolean symbol -O0..-O3, -Os, -Oz optimization level -g generate debug info --static link statically; equivalent to --linker-arg=-static -v, -vv, -vvv increasing compiler verbosity -ir print generated LLVM IR

The default optimization level is currently -O1.

The rtl/sys prelude is implicitly merged for hosted and bare targets. Use --no-use-sys only for low-level bootstrap or RTL work that must opt out. Exception handling defaults to enabled on hosted targets and disabled on bare targets; when enabled, #ifdef EXCEPTIONS selects exception-aware source code. Runtime checks remain active when exception handling is disabled. Dynamic strings follow the same target defaults; when enabled, #ifdef DYNSTRINGS selects str-dependent source. With dynamic strings disabled, strslice, rostr, string literals, and bounded embstr remain available, but owning str operations are rejected at compile time.

docs.title: 3.5.2 Package Search Path
docs.text:
Bare imports such as use print or use json are resolved through package search roots. The compiler adds standard roots automatically, including:

/usr/lib/dq/stdpkg
<compiler-dir>/../lib/dq/stdpkg
<compiler-dir>/../stdpkg
/usr/lib/dq/packages
<compiler-dir>/../lib/dq/packages
~/.dq/packages

Additional roots can be appended with --pkg-path. Search uses the last matching package root first, so later --pkg-path entries can override earlier roots.

docs.title: 3.5.3 Linking Native Code
docs.text:
--link requests linking explicitly; -c produces an object without linking. --linker-arg=<arg> passes an argument to the native linker. For repeatable linker inputs, library directories, or a linker script, use the corresponding project properties.

DQ_LINKER_DRIVER selects the Clang driver used for linking. Match its LLVM major version to the compiler's LLVM version, particularly for full LTO builds. The full release packages supply a matching toolchain.

See Targets and Cross-Compilation for application targets, sysroots, and Windows cross-linking. The tool overview covers dq-run.

docs.title: 3.6. Project Files (.dqproj)
docs.text:
Some projects may require a large amount of compiler options to compile. In order to make the complex project compilation easier the DQ compiler supports project files.

The DQ project files are basically a set of compiler options in a more manageable way.

The project files use the .dqproj extension:

Example usage:

dq-comp application.dqproj
dq-comp -O0 -g -o build/application application.dqproj

(the dq-comp options provided in the command line override the options in the .dqproj file)

Unless output or -o selects another path, the executable is named after the project file and written beside it. Build artifacts are kept below the project directory's .dqbuild directory, independently of the main source location.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Project File Example
docs.text:
// application.dqproj

packagepath = 'packages'
var BOARD_SUPPORT = PackagePath('board_support')

include '${BOARD_SUPPORT}/project/stm32f746.dqproj'

main      = 'src/application.dq'
output    = 'build/${PROJECT_NAME}.elf'
target    = 'arm_m7f-bare'
cpu_features = '+no-movt'
compiler_runtime = 'libgcc'
c_runtime = 'newlib-nano'
link      = true
optlevel  = 2
debuginfo = true
lto       = false

define BOARD_NUCLEO_F746
define CPU_CLOCK_HZ = 216000000

linkobject = '${BOARD_SUPPORT}/lib/startup.o'
linkoption = '--gc-sections'

arm_m7f-bare selects the Cortex-M7 single-precision FPU and makes float 32-bit. Use arm_m7fd-bare for Cortex-M7 devices with a double-precision FPU; on that target float is 64-bit. The explicit float32 and float64 types do not change with the target.

Use dq-comp --targets for the canonical target list and detailed defaults. The additional hosted Linux targets are armhf-linux, arm64-linux, and rv64g-linux; select the target distribution or SDK root with sysroot when linking for one of them. The additional cross targets are wasm32-wasi, wasm32-bare, and rv32imac-bare. WASI exceptions are unsupported, so a project selecting wasm32-wasi must not set exceptions = true.

An included fragment might contain the shared target and linker configuration:

// board_support/project/stm32f746.dqproj

linkerpath = '${THIS_DIR}/../lib'
linkscript = '${THIS_DIR}/../ld/stm32f746.ld'

docs.title: 3.6.2 Lexical Rules
docs.text:
The format uses DQ-like identifiers, strings, comments, and statement terminators. Property and keyword names are case-sensitive.

An identifier starts with an ASCII letter or _ and may continue with ASCII letters, decimal digits, or _:

FEATURE
CPU_CLOCK_HZ
board2

Strings may use single or double quotes. They must end on the same physical line on which they begin.

'src/main.dq'
"arm_m7f-bare"

The recognized string escapes are:

Escape Result \n newline character \r carriage return \t tab \\ backslash \" double quote \' single quote

An unrecognized escape is preserved as a backslash followed by the escaped character.

Both DQ comment forms are supported:

// line comment

/* block
   comment */

An unterminated string or block comment is an error.

Statements normally end at a newline. A semicolon is optional at the end of a statement and is required between multiple statements on the same line:

main = 'main.dq'
output = 'app'

main = 'main.dq'; output = 'app'

The parts of one statement, including =, its value, and the arguments of PackagePath(), may not continue onto another line.

docs.title: 3.6.3 Statements
docs.text:
A project consists of property assignments and three special statements: define, var, and include.

property = value
define NAME
define NAME = value
var NAME = value
include 'file.dqproj'

Unknown properties, invalid value types, trailing tokens, and duplicate single-value properties are errors.

docs.title: 3.6.3.1 Properties
docs.text:
Property Value Repetition Meaning main path string once, required DQ source file compiled as the project entry module. output path string once, optional Final executable or object filename. Normal compiler output defaults apply when omitted. target string once, optional Compiler target name, using the same names accepted by --target. sysroot path string once, optional Target system root passed to the Clang linker driver for hosted cross builds. cpu_features string once, optional Append LLVM CPU feature flags to the target defaults, separated by commas. packagepath path string repeatable Add a DQ package search root. link boolean once, optional Force linking when true; compile only when false. static boolean once, optional Pass -static to the linker when true, equivalent to --static or --linker-arg=-static. Defaults to false, which adds no linker argument. exceptions boolean once, optional Enable or disable DQ exception handling. Defaults to enabled on hosted targets and disabled on bare targets; wasm32-wasi always disables and rejects enabling exceptions. dynstrings boolean once, optional Enable or disable heap-backed dynamic strings. Defaults to enabled on hosted targets and disabled on bare targets. compiler_runtime string once, optional Bare-target compiler support runtime: libgcc (default) or none. c_runtime string once, optional Bare-target C runtime: newlib-nano (default) or none. linkobject path string repeatable Add an existing object or other positional linker input. linkerpath path string repeatable Pass --library-path=<path> to the linker. linkoption string repeatable Pass one argument directly to the linker. linkscript path string once, optional Pass --script=<path> to the linker. debuginfo boolean once, optional Enable or disable debug information. optlevel integer or string 0 through 3, or string 's' or 'z' once, optional Set the optimization level. Numeric levels may be quoted or unquoted; 's' and 'z' optimize for size. lto boolean once, optional Enable full LTO when true; disable LTO when false.

main is required only after the top-level file and all its includes have been assembled. An included fragment therefore does not need its own main. output is always optional.

The cpu, abi, and floatabi property names are reserved for future target tuning. They are currently rejected as unsupported. They are not silently ignored.

docs.title: 3.6.3.2 Link Mode
docs.text:
Without a link property, the compiler retains its automatic link mode:

  • A hosted target links a module that contains *Main.
  • A bare target produces an object by default.

link = true is equivalent to explicitly selecting --link. It can force a bare target to link an ELF image. link = false is equivalent to -c and always requests compile-only output.

docs.title: 3.6.3.3 Exception Handling
docs.text:
Exception handling is enabled by default for hosted targets and disabled by default for bare targets. Projects can override the target default explicitly:

exceptions = false

When enabled, the compiler defines EXCEPTIONS in the @def scope, so source and RTL code can select exception-dependent code with #ifdef EXCEPTIONS. Disabling exceptions removes native unwind generation and rejects try, except, finally, and raise; runtime checks remain enabled and report through the RuntimeError hook.

docs.title: 3.6.3.4 Dynamic Strings
docs.text:
Dynamic strings are enabled by default for hosted targets and disabled by default for bare targets. Projects can override the target default explicitly:

dynstrings = true

When enabled, the compiler defines DYNSTRINGS in the @def scope. When disabled, heap-owning str declarations, conversions, concatenation, and methods are rejected with DynStringsDisabled. Non-owning and bounded text facilities—text literals, rostr, strslice, and bounded embstr—remain available.

docs.title: 3.6.3.5 Bare-Metal Runtimes
docs.text:
For supported bare-metal targets, the compiler selects bundled libraries that match the target CPU and floating-point ABI. The defaults are equivalent to:

compiler_runtime = 'libgcc'
c_runtime = 'newlib-nano'

compiler_runtime supplies compiler-generated ABI helper routines and, when exceptions are enabled, the C++ exception ABI support and target unwinder. c_runtime supplies Newlib Nano and its no-system fallback stubs, and makes the matching bundled math library available to #linklib('m'). Static archive members are included only when referenced. Board or application implementations override the fallback stubs and must provide functional system calls where the application requires them.

Either property may be set to none when the application supplies that part of the runtime explicitly. These properties are rejected for hosted targets, whose runtime libraries continue to be selected by the system linker driver.

docs.title: 3.6.3.6 Defines
docs.text:
define creates a symbol in the compiler's @def scope:

define FEATURE
define LOGGING = true
define TRACE = false
define BUFFER_SIZE = 4096
define OFFSET = -16

A define without a value has boolean value true. Explicit values are limited to true, false, or a signed 64-bit decimal integer. Strings, hexadecimal integers, expressions, and variables are not accepted as define values.

Define names are identifiers and must be unique throughout the assembled project, including all included files. A command-line -DNAME or -DNAME=value replaces the project define with the same name.

Project defines are inherited by imported child modules.

docs.title: 3.6.4 Paths
docs.text:
The following properties contain paths:

  • main
  • output
  • packagepath
  • linkobject
  • linkerpath
  • linkscript
  • include

After variable expansion, a relative path is resolved against the directory of the file containing that statement. The result is converted to an absolute, lexically normalized path. This rule applies independently to every included file.

For example, in project/boards/board.dqproj:

linkscript = '../ld/board.ld'

the path is relative to project/boards, not to the process working directory or the top-level project directory.

The project parser requires included files and PackagePath() results to exist. It does not check the existence of main, output, packagepath, linkobject, linkerpath, or linkscript; the compiler, filesystem, or linker reports problems with those paths when they are used.

docs.title: 3.6.5 Variables
docs.text:
A variable stores a path for later substitution. Its value must be either a quoted path string or the result of PackagePath():

var SOURCE_DIR = 'src'
var SDK = PackagePath('sdk')

main = '${SOURCE_DIR}/main.dq'
include '${SDK}/project/common.dqproj'

A relative quoted value is resolved against the directory of the file that declares the variable. Consequently, it keeps the same meaning when it is used later from a different included file.

Variable references use only the explicit ${NAME} form. Expansion is performed inside all quoted project values, including path properties, target, linkoption, include paths, and PackagePath() arguments.

Variable names are case-sensitive, must be declared before use, and are shared through includes. A variable cannot be declared more than once. User variables also cannot redefine either built-in variable:

Variable Meaning ${PROJECT_NAME} Name of the top level .dqproj file, without extension ${PROJECT_DIR} Directory containing the top-level .dqproj file. ${THIS_DIR} Directory containing the file with the current statement.

The project language does not expand environment variables, ~, $NAME, or %NAME%. A dollar sign has no special meaning unless it starts ${NAME}.

docs.title: 3.6.6 Package Lookup
docs.text:
PackagePath() locates a package using the same package-root resolver as a DQ use statement:

var SDK = PackagePath('sdk')

The argument must expand to one identifier. If /opt/dq/packages/sdk is the selected package, the function returns the absolute normalized path /opt/dq/packages/sdk, not /opt/dq/packages.

Package roots are searched from highest to lowest precedence:

  1. Command-line --pkg-path roots, with the last command-line root winning.
  2. Project packagepath roots already encountered, with the last project root winning.
  3. Compiler default package roots, with the later default root winning.

Command-line package roots are collected before the project is evaluated, so they are available to every PackagePath() call regardless of command-line position. A project packagepath becomes available only after its statement is evaluated. Includes follow the same textual ordering rule.

A missing package is a project-evaluation error.

docs.title: 3.6.7 Includes
docs.text:
An include inserts another .dqproj file at the point of the statement:

include 'common.dqproj'
include '${SDK}/project/board.dqproj'

The path is expanded and resolved relative to the including file. Included files must also use the .dqproj extension.

Includes behave like textual insertion with file-local path anchoring:

  • Variables declared before an include are visible inside it.
  • Variables declared by an included file remain visible after it returns.
  • packagepath statements affect later PackagePath() calls.
  • Single-property, variable, and define duplicate checks span all files.
  • Repeatable property ordering follows statement order across includes.

The same file may be included again after its earlier inclusion has completed. Normal duplicate rules still apply to the repeated statements. Including a file that is already active is a cycle and is rejected with the canonical include chain.

docs.title: 3.6.8 Linker Argument Ordering
docs.text:
linkerpath, linkscript, linkoption, and static = true produce linker arguments in their assembled project statement order. Included statements retain their position in that order. Command-line --linker-arg=<arg> and --static entries follow all project linker arguments.

The compiler constructs linker inputs in this order:

  1. The object generated for main.
  2. Objects generated for imported DQ modules.
  3. Project linkobject inputs, in statement order.
  4. -o and the final output filename.
  5. Libraries requested by DQ modules.

Each project or command-line linker argument is passed through the compiler driver as one linker argument before those positional inputs. -static is passed directly to the driver so it also selects static startup files and runtime libraries.

Project parsing does not verify that linker objects, library paths, or linker scripts exist. Such errors are reported by the linker.

docs.title: 3.6.9 Command-Line Precedence
docs.text:
The project is parsed before normal command-line option evaluation and before target-dependent compiler initialization. Project values act as defaults; explicit command-line selections are then applied on top.

Setting Precedence Target --target overrides target; otherwise the project target overrides the host default. CPU features --cpu-features= overrides cpu_features; the effective value is appended to the selected target defaults. Output -o overrides output; otherwise normal output defaults apply when the property is absent. Optimization -O0 through -O3, -Os, and -Oz override optlevel. Debug information -g enables debug information even when debuginfo = false. There is currently no command-line option to force it off. LTO --lto or --lto=full|off overrides lto. Exceptions --exceptions or --no-exceptions overrides exceptions; the last command-line flag wins. Dynamic strings --dynstrings or --no-dynstrings overrides dynstrings; the last command-line flag wins. Link mode The first explicit -c or --link replaces the project mode. Conflicting subsequent command-line link modes are errors. Defines The first command-line definition of a name removes the project definition of that name. Package roots Command-line roots have higher lookup precedence than project and default roots. Linker arguments Project arguments precede command-line --linker-arg and --static entries.

The project target is selected early enough to initialize target-dependent built-in types correctly. Imported child modules inherit the effective target, optimization level, debug and LTO settings, defines, build settings, and package roots through compiler arguments. Child compilations receive the resolved .dq source file and do not parse the project again.

docs.title: 3.6.10 Errors and Diagnostics
docs.text:
Project evaluation stops at the first error. Diagnostics identify the file, line, column, diagnostic identifier, and message:

/work/app/application.dqproj(12,8) ERROR(ProjectValue): optlevel must be 0 through 3, 's', or 'z'

Project errors include, among others:

  • unreadable project or include files;
  • wrong project extensions;
  • malformed strings, comments, or statements;
  • unknown, duplicate, or unsupported properties;
  • invalid property types or values;
  • duplicate or unknown variables;
  • duplicate project defines;
  • missing packages;
  • include cycles;
  • an assembled project without main.

docs.title: 3.6.11 Compact Grammar
docs.text:
The following grammar is descriptive. newline or ; terminates a statement, and the final statement may end at end-of-file.

project       := { terminator | statement terminator } [ statement ] EOF

statement     := property '=' property-value
               | 'define' identifier [ '=' define-value ]
               | 'var' identifier '=' variable-value
               | 'include' string

property      := 'main' | 'output' | 'target' | 'packagepath'
               | 'link' | 'static' | 'linkobject' | 'linkerpath' | 'linkoption'
               | 'linkscript' | 'debuginfo' | 'optlevel' | 'lto'
               | 'exceptions' | 'dynstrings' | 'cpu_features'

property-value := string | boolean | signed-decimal-integer
variable-value := string | 'PackagePath' '(' string ')'
define-value   := boolean | signed-decimal-integer
boolean        := 'true' | 'false'
terminator     := newline | ';'

Whitespace and comments may occur between tokens as long as they do not move the remainder of the current statement onto another line.

docs.title: 3.7.1 Artifact Locations
docs.text:
DQ packages and the RTL are source-first. The compiler writes generated module artifacts under .dqbuild.

.dqbuild/<build-tag>/
  local/
    app.o
    app.dqm_if
  pkg/
    print/
      print.o
      print.dqm_if
    rtl/
      rtl_linux.o
      rtl_linux.dqm_if

Each module has a normal native .o object and a standalone .dqm_if interface. Both are generated artifacts, not source package contents.

By default the build root is the directory containing the main .dq file. The default build tag is <target-arch>-<target-rtl>, for example x86_64-linux.

The build tag is only a namespace. A tag named debug does not imply -g, and a tag named release does not imply -O3.

By default, local and package artifacts use the same build root. With --package-build-root <path>, package and RTL artifacts are instead written to <path>/.dqbuild/<build-tag>/pkg, while local artifacts remain under the normal build root. This allows several projects with the same build context to share compiled package modules.

DQ compilation uses paired .o and .dqm_if artifacts.

Artifact Meaning .o native compiled module object file .dqm_if serialized public module interface and freshness metadata

Both files normally live under .dqbuild. The object is a regular linker input and contains no DQ-specific interface section. The compiler always reads semantic module data from the standalone .dqm_if.

docs.title: 3.7.2 Why Interfaces Exist
docs.text: When a module imports another module, the compiler needs that imported module's public declarations: exported functions, objects, types, constants, properties, and imported or reexported interface symbols. Loading a compact interface is faster and simpler than reparsing implementation code for every import.

docs.title: 3.7.3 Interface Payload
docs.text:
The .dqm_if payload is a compiler-owned binary format designed for fast loading, strict validation, regeneration, and versioning. It records source dependencies with their paths, sizes, and modification times. Interfaces emitted by a full compile also identify the matching object by its size and modification time.

Reexports are flattened into the facade interface. The payload contains:

  • the facade module's own public declarations;
  • selected reexported declarations, grouped by their canonical origin module;
  • facade export references that map visible names to the canonical declarations;
  • non-exported declarations required to describe exported types and signatures.

The last category is the referenced-type closure. It includes aliases, bases, fields, methods, properties, function parameters and results, and nested pointer, array, function-reference, and object-reference types. Closure-only declarations remain inaccessible through the facade.

Named type references in embedded declarations identify both their origin module and original name. Consequently a type reached through a facade and the same type reached through a later direct import share canonical ownership, linkage identity, and one in-memory representation.

Freshness metadata is flattened as well. A facade records the source metadata and canonical module-to-source resolution for its complete public-use dependency graph. Loading the facade therefore reads only its own .dqm_if; child interface files are not opened merely to load reexported declarations. Child source files are still checked with filesystem metadata, and a facade is regenerated if a source changes or package-path resolution selects a different source.

The binary format is versioned as a compiler cache. Incompatible interfaces are rejected and regenerated rather than read through an older reexport layout.
