It is not a source format, is not intended for hand editing, and is not a stable ABI contract between unrelated compiler versions.

docs.title: 3.7.4 Inspecting Interfaces
docs.text:
Use --ifdump to inspect a standalone .dqm_if.

dq-comp --ifdump .dqbuild/x86_64-linux/local/app.dqm_if

For flattened facades, the dump lists facade export mappings and origin groups. Declarations used only for the referenced-type closure are marked closure.

Use --ifgen when only the public interface is needed.

dq-comp --ifgen module.dq

Normal builds do not require checking in .o or .dqm_if files.

docs.title: 3.7.5 Cleaning
docs.text:
Clean .dqbuild/<tag> when the compiler version, target, ABI-relevant options, package sources, or important build defines change.

rm -rf .dqbuild/x86_64-linux

Rebuild after changing compiler versions or target settings if an old cache is in doubt. Keep .dqbuild out of source control; packages are distributed as source, and generated interfaces are specific to a compiler/build context.

The compiler also tracks textual include and #srcdep inputs. For source-level visibility and reexport rules, see Modules and Packages. Contributor details are in Module and Interface Internals.

docs.title: 3.8. Targets and Cross-Compilation
docs.text: A target describes the machine and runtime on which your DQ application will run. Selecting a foreign application target does not require rebuilding dq-comp. To build a compiler executable that itself runs on another machine, see Compiler Cross-Builds.

docs.title: 3.8.1 Compiler Targets
docs.text:
Run dq-comp --targets to print the canonical target names together with their architecture, platform, LLVM triple, CPU/features, feature defaults, and default link mode. In addition to the current host and Cortex-M targets, the compiler supports:

Target Behavior x64-windows Windows x64 GNU/UCRT executable; also accepts x86_64-win, x64-win, and x86_64-windows armhf-linux ARMv7-A hard-float Linux executable arm64-linux AArch64 Linux executable rv64g-linux RV64G/LP64D Linux executable wasm32-wasi Hosted WASI command module; links automatically and defaults to a .wasm output wasm32-bare Bare WebAssembly object generation; compile-only by default rv32imac-bare Bare RV32IMAC ELF object generation; compile-only by default

wasm32-wasi requires Clang/LLD and a WASI sysroot containing libc at link time. DQ exceptions are not supported on this target: --exceptions and exceptions = true are rejected, while dynamic strings remain enabled by default. The resulting command module uses WASI libc startup and can be run by a WASI runtime such as Wasmtime.

The foreign Linux targets require a target sysroot at link time. Select it with --sysroot=/path/to/sysroot or the sysroot project property. DQ passes this to its Clang linker driver as --sysroot; the sysroot must come from the target distribution or SDK and match the deployed C library and development packages.

For example, an ARM64 Debian sysroot is selected per build:

dq-comp --target=arm64-linux --sysroot=/path/to/debian-arm64-sysroot app.dq

The two bare targets do not bundle startup code, linker scripts, libc, or compiler-runtime libraries. They emit objects without linking unless --link is requested. A forced bare link must supply the appropriate objects and linker arguments and normally sets compiler_runtime = 'none' and c_runtime = 'none'.

Target selection defines architecture and ABI markers as applicable: 32-bit x86 uses X86_FAMILY and X86, while 64-bit x86 uses X86_FAMILY and X64. Arm targets use ARM plus ARM_M or ARM_A; the hosted hard-float target also defines ARMHF. AArch64 defines ARM_A, ARM64, and AARCH64. RISC-V targets define RISCV plus RV32 or RV64. Bare targets also define BARE, and WASM/WASI, TARGET_32BIT/TARGET_64BIT, EXCEPTIONS, and DYNSTRINGS continue to reflect the selected target and feature settings.

docs.title: 3.8.1.1 Windows cross-compilation from Linux
docs.text:
When built with LLVM's X86 backend, the Linux compiler can produce Windows x64 executables using a Linux-hosted llvm-mingw UCRT toolchain. With the toolchain extracted under sysroots/llvm-mingw-x86_64, source the setup script in Bash before compiling and running:

source tools/dqcrosswinsetup.sh
build/dq-comp --target=x64-windows app.dq
wine app.exe

The script detects the repository root from its own location, sets DQ_MINGW_ROOT, and uses winepath to set WINEPATH to the toolchain's target runtime DLL directory. Wine loads the DLLs directly from that directory, so you do not need to copy them beside each executable. The script also sets MESA_VK_IGNORE_CONFORMANCE_WARNING=1 to suppress Mesa's RADV Vulkan conformance warning. Wine and winepath must be installed.

You can source the script by its absolute path from any working directory. For example, add this line to ~/.bashrc to configure new Bash terminals automatically (adjust the path to your checkout):

source /path/to/dq-lang/tools/dqcrosswinsetup.sh

Source the script in the current terminal as well to apply the settings immediately. Running it as a separate process does not configure the current shell.

Windows outputs default to .exe. An explicit -o filename is used exactly as given, including filenames without an extension. Object generation with -c does not require the Windows libraries or Wine.

Set DQ_MINGW_ROOT to the extracted llvm-mingw root when it is installed elsewhere:

DQ_MINGW_ROOT=/path/to/llvm-mingw build/dq-comp --target=x64-windows app.dq

The linker search order is DQ_LINKER_DRIVER, the cross driver under DQ_MINGW_ROOT/bin, compiler-relative toolchain/llvm-mingw, llvm-mingw, and sysroots/llvm-mingw-x86_64 installations, then x86_64-w64-mingw32-clang++ on PATH. An invalid explicit DQ_MINGW_ROOT fails when linking. Native Windows compiler installations retain their Windows-hosted driver discovery. --sysroot is still passed through when set.

The toolchain must provide Clang/LLD, startup objects, UCRT and Windows import libraries, libc++, and libunwind. Full LTO also requires a toolchain with the same LLVM major version as DQ. Windows full-LTO links use LLD's default optimization pipeline rather than the ELF-specific O1 inlining pipeline.

As an alternative to setting WINEPATH, copy the toolchain's target runtime DLLs beside the executable: libc++.dll, libunwind.dll, and libwinpthread-1.dll when provided. These are under x86_64-w64-mingw32/bin in llvm-mingw.

The opt-in compatibility suite copies the runtime DLLs automatically:

make test-windows
# Custom installation:
DQ_MINGW_ROOT=/path/to/llvm-mingw make test-windows
# Direct invocation with explicit tool paths:
python3 tools/test-windows.py --compiler build/dq-comp \
    --mingw-root /path/to/llvm-mingw --wine /path/to/wine

It requires Linux, Python 3, llvm-mingw, and usable 64-bit Wine. Missing prerequisites fail the requested run; they are not silently skipped. Windows fixtures live in autotest/cross-windows; the suite also reuses the portable thread/channel autotests and the threads examples. It checks native thread lifecycle and handle cleanup, atomics, event deadlines, channel capacity and waits, producer/consumer stress, and work distribution at O0 and O3 with full LTO. Normal make test, make autotest, and make check runs do not invoke the Windows suite or require these dependencies. Executables, caches, runtime DLLs, command logs, and a dedicated Wine prefix are stored under build/test-windows. The suite leaves the user's Wine prefix untouched.

docs.title: 3.8.2 Bare-Metal Projects
docs.text: Bare targets need board-specific startup objects, a linker script, and suitable runtime libraries when linking a complete image. Put those settings in a project file. The bundled support libraries cover the supported CPU/ABI combinations; they do not supply a board's reset handler or hardware initialization.

docs.title: 3.8.3 WebAssembly Examples
docs.text:
A WASI command module uses a hosted C library:

dq-comp --target=wasm32-wasi --sysroot=/path/to/wasi-sysroot app.dq
wasmtime app.wasm

For a browser or another custom embedding, wasm32-bare produces an object by default. Supply the embedding's link options and imports explicitly. See C Interoperability for import declarations, and examples/wasm, examples/wasm_webgl, and examples/wasm_gpu in the repository for integration examples.

docs.title: 3.9. VSCode Setup and Debugging
docs.text: Install the DQ tools using the Linux or Windows environment chapter first. Confirm that dq-comp --version and dq-run --help work in the terminal from which you start VS Code.

docs.title: 3.9.1 DQ Extension
docs.text:
Install the bundled VSCode/dq-syntax-*.vsix with Extensions: Install from VSIX... in the Command Palette, then reload VS Code. In a source checkout, the extension files are under tools/vscode-dq.

The extension supplies syntax highlighting, compiler diagnostics, document symbols, block completion, the $dq problem matcher, and DQ: Run Current File. The run command uses dq-run with -g -O0. It does not start an interactive debugger.

Both tools must be on the editor's PATH. Alternatively set dq.languageServerPath and dq.runPath to their full paths in settings.json. On Linux, starting VS Code with code . from a configured terminal lets it inherit that terminal's environment. Restart the editor after changing persistent environment variables.

docs.title: 3.9.2 Debugging on Linux
docs.text:
Install GDB and the Microsoft C/C++ extension (ms-vscode.cpptools). Open the program directory as a VS Code workspace. The following configuration builds and debugs the active .dq file; keep that file active when starting the task.

Create .vscode/tasks.json:

{
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "tasks": [
        {
            "label": "DQ: build current file",
            "type": "shell",
            "command": "dq-comp",
            "args": [
                "-g", "-O0", "${file}",
                "-o", "${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension}"
            ],
            "options": {"cwd": "${workspaceFolder}"},
            "group": "build",
            "problemMatcher": "$dq"
        }
    ]
}

Create .vscode/launch.json:

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "DQ: Debug current program",
            "type": "cppdbg",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension}",
            "args": [],
            "cwd": "${fileDirname}",
            "stopAtEntry": false,
            "externalConsole": false,
            "MIMode": "gdb",
            "preLaunchTask": "DQ: build current file"
        }
    ]
}

Set a breakpoint and press F5. Add program arguments to the launch configuration's args array. For a .dqproj application, replace the active-file build argument with the project path, and set program to the output executable. The working directory controls relative file access at runtime.

You can also debug outside the editor:

dq-comp -g -O0 app.dq
gdb ./app

The repository contains optional GDB helpers in tools/gdb/dq_gdbinit.py and tools/gdb/dq_printers.py for inspecting DQ values.

docs.title: 3.9.3 Debugging on Windows
docs.text: DQ programs can be source-debugged with the lldb-dap debugger included in the Windows DQ package. The compiler must generate debug information, so the debug build uses -g -O0.

docs.title: 3.9.3.1 Install the extensions
docs.text:
Install LLDB DAP (llvm-vs-code-extensions.lldb-dap) from the VS Code Marketplace and reload VS Code.

For DQ syntax support and the $dq build problem matcher, also install the bundled VSCode\dq-syntax-0.1.4.vsix using Extensions: Install from VSIX....

The Microsoft C/C++ extension may remain installed, but the configuration below does not use its cppdbg adapter. On Windows, configuring cppdbg with lldb-mi.exe can hang in WindowsDebugLauncher.exe.

Open the DQ project directory as the VS Code workspace. The project may be in a different directory from the DQ installation.

docs.title: 3.9.3.2 Configure the target
docs.text:
Add the DQ compiler's bin directory (e.g. c:\\prg\\dq\\bin) to the system path, so the dq-comp.exe or dq-run exe are accessible from command line without full path specification.

Add these values to .vscode/settings.json:

{
    "dq.debugTarget": "examples/langdemo",
    "dq.debugCwd": "examples",

    "lldb-dap.executable-path": "C:\\prg\\dq\\toolchain\\llvm-mingw\\bin\\lldb-dap.exe"
}

(dq.debugTarget has no .dq extension!)

For example, to debug the NanoNet echo client, use:

{
    "dq.debugTarget": "stdpkg/nanonet/examples/binecho_client",
    "dq.debugCwd": "stdpkg/nanonet/examples"
}

docs.title: 3.9.3.3 Add the build task
docs.text:
Create .vscode/tasks.json:

{
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "tasks": [
        {
            "label": "dq: build configured target",
            "type": "shell",
            "command": "dq-comp.exe",
            "args": [
                "-g",
                "-O0",
                "${config:dq.debugTarget}.dq",
                "-o",
                "${config:dq.debugTarget}.exe"
            ],
            "options": {
                "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}"
            },
            "group": "build",
            "problemMatcher": "$dq"
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: 3.9.3.4 Add the launch configuration
docs.text:
Create .vscode/launch.json:

{
    "version": "0.2.0",
    "configurations": [
        {
            "name": "DQ: Debug configured target (LLDB-DAP)",
            "type": "lldb-dap",
            "request": "launch",
            "program": "${workspaceFolder}\\${config:dq.debugTarget}.exe",
            "args": [],
            "cwd": "${workspaceFolder}\\${config:dq.debugCwd}",
            "stopOnEntry": false,
            "console": "internalConsole",
            "preLaunchTask": "dq: build configured target"
        }
    ]
}

docs.title: 3.9.3.5 Start debugging
docs.text:
1. Open the .dq source file and set a breakpoint.
  2. Open Run and Debug (Ctrl+Shift+D).
  3. Select DQ: Debug configured target (LLDB-DAP).
  4. Press F5.

VS Code builds the selected target first, then starts it under LLDB. Command-line arguments can be added to the args array in launch.json.

docs.title: 3.9.3.6 Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• If VS Code does not recognize the lldb-dap debug type, verify that the LLDB DAP extension is installed and reload the window.
  • If startup hangs while mentioning WindowsDebugLauncher.exe and lldb-mi.exe, VS Code is using a cppdbg configuration. Select the lldb-dap configuration above instead.
  • If a breakpoint is not resolved, confirm the build task still contains both -g and -O0, then rebuild the target.
  • If the executable or a runtime DLL cannot be found, check the target path and the DQ installation on PATH. Keep its toolchain directories together.
  • If the program reads relative files, set dq.debugCwd to the directory it normally runs from.

docs.title: 3.9.4 Diagnostics and Build Configuration
docs.text:
If diagnostics use the wrong compiler, check dq.languageServerPath. If the run command cannot find dq-run, check dq.runPath and the editor environment. The syntax extension and a debugger extension serve different purposes; install both when using interactive breakpoints.

A breakpoint requires the executable built from the source currently open. Use -g -O0, confirm the output and launch paths agree, and rebuild. Program arguments and working directories belong to the launch configuration; package roots and compiler flags belong to the build task or project file.

docs.title: 4. Standard Packages
docs.text:
The runtime and standard packages ship as DQ source. Begin with the Library Overview for imports and package discovery.

  • sys: implicit runtime services, memory, and process arguments.
  • print: console output.
  • file: files, directories, and paths.
  • json: JSON trees, parsing, and serialization.
  • threads: native threads, atomics, and channels.
  • time: timestamps, elapsed time, date formatting, and sleeps.
  • nanonet: sockets and HTTP servers.
  • shell: child processes, captured output, and environment variables.
  • Additional Standard Packages: math, parsing, database bindings, and lower-level platform interfaces.

docs.title: 4.1. Library Overview
docs.text: DQ provides runtime services and source packages. The compiler builds imported package modules for the selected target and stores the results in .dqbuild. Installing a package does not require prebuilding it for every application.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Runtime and Explicit Imports
docs.text:
The implicit sys interface supplies basic runtime helpers. Other packages are imported explicitly:

use print

func *Main():
    var message : str = Format("{} items", [3])
    PrintLn(message)
endfunc

print writes to standard output. Format and the string helpers are available through the implicit sys runtime interface, so they need no explicit import.

Need Documentation Process arguments, memory blocks, runtime helpers sys Console output print Formatting and text helpers String Functions, Text Formatting Files, directories, paths file JSON trees json Native threads and channels threads Timestamps, elapsed time, date formatting, sleeps time Event-driven sockets and HTTP nanonet Child processes, captured output, environment variables shell Math, parsing, databases, C bindings Additional Standard Packages

docs.title: 4.1.2 Package Discovery and Platform Dependencies
docs.text:
A bare import is resolved through the compiler's package search roots. Add project packages with --pkg-path or packagepath in a .dqproj file. Later roots take precedence. See Modules and Packages for identity and lookup rules.

Packages can depend on native libraries and platform APIs. For example, threads has hosted Linux and Windows implementations; database bindings need the corresponding client libraries. A package's presence in stdpkg does not imply that it is available on a bare-metal or WebAssembly target.

The package chapters include the maintained package-local API manuals, so the website, PDF book, and standalone package documentation use the same source.

docs.title: 4.2. sys
docs.text:
rtl/sys is implicitly merged into ordinary DQ modules. You can call its public helpers without writing use sys. --no-use-sys opts out for low-level modules.

Reexported module Services rtl/rtlint Runtime intrinsics, type helpers, runtime error hook. rtl/mem Allocation and byte-block operations. rtl/strfunc Runtime string operations. rtl/exception Exception and exception helpers, when exceptions are enabled. rtl/prgargs Arguments and exit_code, on hosted targets.

String methods, anyvalue, and formatting are documented with their language chapters: String Functions, anyvalue, and Text Formatting.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Arguments and Process Status
docs.text:
func ArgCount() -> int
func ArgStr(i : int) -> ^char
func Exit(status : int)
func Errno() -> int32

On hosted targets, ArgCount() includes the program name at index zero. ArgStr(i) returns a borrowed C string or nil for an invalid index. Read the string before the process ends; do not free the pointer.

Set exit_code and return normally from *Main to select a process status. Exit(status) terminates immediately; it does not unwind DQ scopes. Errno() reads the C runtime's error value. Interpret it only according to the native operation that just failed, since successful calls need not clear it.

See Runtime and Program Execution for a complete argument-handling example and target differences.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Raw Memory
docs.text:
func MemAlloc(allocbytes : int, zeromem : bool = false) -> pointer
func MemFree(memptr : pointer)
func MemFreeRef(memptrvar : ref pointer)
func MemRealloc(memptr : pointer, newsize : uint) -> pointer
func MemReallocRef(memptr : ref pointer, newsize : uint)
func MemCopy(dest : pointer, src : pointer, size : uint)
func MemSet(dest : pointer, value : int, size : uint)
func MemBlockSize(memptr : pointer) -> uint

MemAlloc returns raw storage, optionally zeroed. Check for nil before use. MemFreeRef frees an allocation and clears the pointer variable. MemFree does not clear other aliases. Neither function runs object destructors.

use print

func *Main():
    var buffer : ^byte = ^byte(MemAlloc(64, true))
    if buffer == nil:
        exit_code = 1
        return
    endif
    buffer^ = 42
    PrintLn("First byte: {}", [buffer^])
    MemFree(buffer)
    buffer = nil
endfunc

MemCopy copies bytes and handles overlapping source and destination ranges. MemSet fills a block with the low byte of value. Sizes are measured in bytes; these operations do not check the size or lifetime of the supplied storage. Do not use byte copying to duplicate managed strings, arrays, or owning fields.

MemRealloc can move an allocation. On allocation failure with a nonzero size, it returns nil while the old block remains allocated; keep the old pointer until the result has been checked. MemReallocRef directly replaces the pointer and therefore does not preserve that recovery handle on failure.

MemBlockSize reports the allocator's usable block size on Linux and Windows; the fallback on other targets returns zero. It is not a portable way to track application buffer lengths.

Prefer managed strings, arrays, and objects for ordinary storage. See Memory Management and Autofree for cleanup and owning pointers.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Exceptions and Backtraces
docs.text: With exceptions enabled, Exception supplies a formatted message and a captured backtrace. A handler can inspect error.message and call error.PrintBacktrace(). Compile with -g -O0 for useful source-line diagnostics. The complete rules and examples are in Exceptions and Error Handling.

docs.title: 4.3. print
docs.text:
Import print to write text to standard output:

use print

func *Main():
    Print("Items: ")
    PrintLn("{}", [3])
    PrintLn()
endfunc

This writes Items: 3, followed by an empty line.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Functions
docs.text:
func Print(fmt : strslice)
func Print(fmt : rostr, args : []anyvalue)
func PrintLn()
func PrintLn(fmt : strslice)
func PrintLn(fmt : rostr, args : []anyvalue)
func PrintFlush()
func PrintSetUnbuffered()

Print writes without a newline. PrintLn appends a newline; its no-argument form writes only that newline.

The one-argument forms write text literally. Braces have a formatting meaning only when you supply the []anyvalue argument list:

PrintLn("{name}")              // prints {name}
PrintLn("{} = {:04X}", ["id", 255]) // prints id = 00FF

Use a bracketed list even when there is only one formatted argument. See Text Formatting for widths, precision, number formats, escaping braces, and formatting error behavior.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Buffering
docs.text:
PrintFlush() asks the C runtime to flush standard output. This is useful for a prompt without a newline. PrintSetUnbuffered() disables stdout buffering via the runtime; configure buffering before normal output begins.

These functions use the shared stdout sink and formatter. For custom output sinks or building a string instead of printing, see Text Formatting and String Functions.

docs.title: 4.4. file
docs.text:
The file module provides simple file, directory, and path helpers.

use file

FileWriteText("hello.txt", "hello\n")
var text : str = FileReadText("hello.txt")

Errors raise EFileError.

docs.title: 4.4.1 OFile
docs.text:
OFile wraps a libc file handle and closes it from its destructor.

var f <- OFile()
f.Open("data.bin", "rb")
var bytes : [*]byte = f.ReadBytes()
f.Close()
Method / property Meaning Open(name, mode) open with a libc-style mode such as "r", "rb", "w" Close() close if open Opened() / .opened true when a handle is open Size() / .size file size, preserving current position Seek(pos) / .position = pos seek from file start CurPos() / .position current offset Read(ptr, size) read bytes into memory ReadText() read the whole file as str ReadBytes() read the whole file as [*]byte Write(ptr, size) write bytes from memory WriteText(text) write text WriteBytes(bytes) write a byte slice

docs.title: 4.4.2 Convenience Functions
docs.text:
FileRead(name, ptr, maxlen)
FileReadText(name)
FileReadBytes(name)

FileWrite(name, ptr, len)
FileWriteText(name, text)
FileWriteBytes(name, bytes)

FileExists(name)
FileRemove(name)

FileExists returns false for directories. FileRemove removes an existing file and raises EFileError for an empty, missing, or unremovable file.

docs.title: 4.4.3 Directories
docs.text:
DirExists("out")
DirCreate("out/nested", true)
DirRemove("out/nested")

DirCreate(path, true) creates missing parent directories. Without true, an existing directory is an error.

docs.title: 4.4.4 Path Helpers
docs.text:
PathSlashSeparators(path)
PathPlatformSeparators(path)
PathToAbsolute(path)
GetCurrentPath()
SetCurrentPath(path)
PathDirName(path)
PathFileName(path)
PathFileExt(path)

PathSlashSeparators() normalizes separators to /, while PathPlatformSeparators() uses \\ on Windows and / elsewhere. PathToAbsolute() resolves a relative path against the current directory and normalizes . and .. path segments. GetCurrentPath() returns the absolute current working directory. SetCurrentPath(path) changes the process working directory.

docs.title: 4.5. json
docs.text:
The json module provides a mutable JSON tree with parsing and serialization.

use json

var j <- OJson()
j.AddStr("name", "dq")
j.AddNum("version", 1)
PrintLn("{}", [j.pretty_json])

Errors raise EJson.

docs.title: 4.5.1 Node Kinds
docs.text:
enum NJsonNodeKind = (nkNull, nkBool, nkNumber, nkString, nkObject, nkArray)

An OJson node stores its kind, optional scalar value, parent pointer, name, and children.

docs.title: 4.5.2 Building Trees
docs.text:
var root <- OJson()
root.AddStr("title", "example")
root.AddBool("ok", true)

var items : OJson = root.AddArr("items")
items.AddStr("", "first")
items.AddNum("", 2)

var cfg : OJson = root.ForcePath("settings/theme")
cfg.as_str = "dark"
Method Meaning AddNull(name) append null child AddBool(name, value) append boolean child AddStr(name, value) append string child AddNum(name, value) append number child AddObj(name) append object child AddArr(name) append array child Clear() delete all children

For array items, the name is usually "".

docs.title: 4.5.3 Reading And Writing Values
docs.text:
Property / method Meaning .name node name, or "0" for root .parent parent node .as_str read/write scalar as string .as_num read/write scalar as float .as_bool read/write scalar as bool .is_null true for JSON null .json compact JSON string .pretty_json indented JSON string .length child count .child[index] child by index, or null 
var title : str = root.ChildByName("title").as_str

docs.title: 4.5.4 Finding Nodes
docs.text:
var jv : OJson

// most practical:
if root.Find("settings.theme", jv):
    PrintLn("theme={}", [jv.as_str])
endif

// traditional:
jv = root.FindNode("settings/theme")
if jv <> nil:
    PrintLn("theme={}", [jv.as_str])
endif

Paths can use . or / between object names. ForcePath creates missing object nodes.

docs.title: 4.5.5 Parsing And Files
docs.text:
var j <- OJson()
j.Parse('{"answer":42}')
j.LoadFromFile("config.json")
j.SaveToFile("out.json", true)

The root JSON text must be an object or array. Strings support JSON escapes, including Unicode escapes and surrogate pairs.

docs.title: 4.6. threads
docs.text:
threads provides native threads, atomic values, spinlocks, thread notifications, and a bounded message channel for hosted Linux and x86_64 Windows programs.

use threads

All the types below are available through this import. The .dqh and .dqi files are parts of the threads module, not separate modules to import. On Linux, the package links pthread and atomic; their libraries must be available to the linker. OThread.IsRunning() uses pthread_tryjoin_np, and OThreadEvent and channel waits use futexes. On 32-bit Linux, waits require futex_time64 (Linux 5.1 or later).

On Windows, the package uses _beginthreadex, interlocked atomic operations, and WaitOnAddress/WakeByAddressSingle. It links kernel32 and synchronization from the llvm-mingw toolchain, without requiring pthread or libatomic. Address-based waits require Windows 8 / Windows Server 2012 or later. The same thread, channel, spinlock, and event APIs work on both platforms.

Type / function Purpose OThread start and join a native thread OMsgChannel bounded FIFO shared by producers and consumers SChMsg fixed 16-byte channel message OAtomicUint32, OAtomicUint64, OAtomicPtr atomic value access OSpinLockVar, OSpinLockHolder shared lock and scope-based lock holder OThreadEvent notification used when waiting for a shared condition SchedYield() give other runnable threads an opportunity to run

docs.title: 4.6.1 Threads
docs.text:
OThread starts one thread at a time. Choose a free function, a bound object method, or the thread object's virtual Run method:

Method Meaning StartFunc(afunc : FThreadFunc, aarg : pointer) -> bool run a free function StartMethod(amethod : FThreadMethod, aarg : pointer) -> bool run a bound object method StartSelf(aarg : pointer) -> bool run this object's Run(aarg) Run(aarg : pointer) -> pointer virtual entry point for StartSelf; default returns nil Join() wait for the thread to finish and collect its return value IsRunning() -> bool try to join without waiting; collect the return value if finished

The callback types are:

type FThreadFunc   = func(arg : pointer) -> pointer
type FThreadMethod = func(arg : pointer) -> pointer of object

Each start method returns false if the wrapper still has an unjoined thread or native thread creation fails. A successful start sets thread_id (a pthread ID on Linux, a numeric thread ID on Windows); the callback's full pointer result is available in retval after joining. Join() on an idle wrapper does nothing. After a successful join, the same wrapper can start another thread.

use threads
use print

func ThreadMain(arg : pointer) -> pointer:
    return arg
endfunc

func *Main():
    var value : int = 42
    var thread <- OThread()
    if not thread.StartFunc(ThreadMain, %value):
        Exit(1)
    endif
    thread.Join()
    PrintLn('result = {}', [^int(thread.retval)^])
endfunc

For a bound method, use thread.StartMethod(worker.ThreadMain, arg). For a subclass of OThread, override Run and call worker.StartSelf(arg) as shown in the channel worker example.

IsRunning() has a side effect: it reaps a completed thread just as Join() does, including closing the native thread handle on Windows. On Linux it also returns false on try-join errors other than “busy”; on Windows a native wait error retains the running state. It is not an error-reporting API. Join() returns no status; if the native join fails, the wrapper retains its running state.

Threads share the process address space. The wrapper, bound-method receiver, and argument storage must remain alive until the thread finishes. OThread does not automatically stop or join from a destructor. Manage each wrapper from one controlling thread; its lifecycle fields are not synchronized. Join before destroying a worker or reading results that only that worker writes.

docs.title: 4.6.2 Message Channels
docs.text: OMsgChannel is a ring-buffer FIFO with a fixed size chosen at construction. It supports multiple producers and multiple consumers with its default locking = true setting. Each successful Get removes one message for one consumer; it does not broadcast a message to all workers.

docs.title: 4.6.2.1 Capacity and Nonblocking Operations
docs.text:
use threads
use print

func *Main():
    var channel <- OMsgChannel(64) // capacity: 64 messages
    var message : SChMsg = {msg: 1, par.u32: 7, data.u64: 12345}
    if not channel.Put(message):
        Exit(1)
    endif

    var received : SChMsg = {}
    if channel.Get(received):
        PrintLn('message {}, job {}, value {}',
                [received.msg, received.par.u32, received.data.u64])
    endif
endfunc

The constructor argument is the usable message capacity: OMsgChannel(n) holds at most n messages. The channel allocates one additional ring slot internally to distinguish a full queue from an empty queue. OMsgChannel(1) holds one message; OMsgChannel(0) always rejects puts and gets. The argument is uint32; 0xFFFFFFFF raises Exception because the additional slot would overflow the internal slot count. Allocation must also fit available memory.

Method Success Failure Put(amsg : SChMsg) -> bool copy the message into the queue; return true full queue; return false without changing queued messages Get(rmsg : refout SChMsg) -> bool remove the oldest message into rmsg; return true empty queue; return false and leave rmsg unchanged PutWaitMillis(amsg : SChMsg, atimeoutms : int) -> bool enqueue, waiting for space if needed return false if waiting ends without space GetWaitMillis(rmsg : refout SChMsg, atimeoutms : int) -> bool dequeue, waiting for a message if needed return false if waiting ends without a message; leave rmsg unchanged

Put and Get do not wait for queue space or data. They can still contend for the internal spinlock. FIFO describes the order of successful enqueues and dequeues; concurrent producers have no predetermined relative order, and workers can finish processing messages in a different order.

Set locking before sharing the channel. Keep it true for concurrent use. Disabling it removes synchronization of the buffer and indices: it requires single-threaded access or external synchronization of every buffer operation. The volatile indices alone do not establish a safe lock-free channel, even with one producer and one consumer.

docs.title: 4.6.2.2 Message Layout and Ownership
docs.text:
SChMsg has a message identifier, a 4-byte parameter union, and an 8-byte data union. Choose the union view that matches your own message protocol:

Field Available views msg uint32 identifier par bytes : [4]byte, i16 : [2]int16, u16 : [2]uint16, i32 : int32, u32 : uint32, f32 : float32 data bytes : [8]byte, i16 : [4]int16, u16 : [4]uint16, i32 : [2]int32, u32 : [2]uint32, f32 : [2]float32, i64 : int64, u64 : uint64, f64 : float64, ptr : pointer

The views of each union overlap; writing data.u64 replaces the same storage as data.f64 or data.ptr. There is no automatic payload type tag. Initialize the structure, for example with var message : SChMsg = {}, and agree on which fields each msg identifier uses.

Messages are copied by value. A successful Put lets the sender reuse its local SChMsg, but data.ptr copies only an address. The channel neither copies the pointed-to data nor frees it. Keep payload storage alive until the consumer is done, and define who releases it. If enqueueing fails, no message or payload has been handed to a consumer. Destroying a channel also does not free payloads referenced by messages still in the queue.

docs.title: 4.6.2.3 Waiting and Timeouts
docs.text:
The timeout argument has the same meaning for both waiting methods:

atimeoutms Behavior 0 one immediate Put or Get attempt negative wait indefinitely until the operation succeeds or the wait fails positive attempt immediately, then wait using one monotonic deadline

An available operation succeeds immediately even with a positive timeout. Failed attempts and signal interruptions reuse the original deadline; they do not restart the timeout. Very large timeouts saturate the deadline rather than overflowing it. Scheduling and internal lock contention can delay the return beyond the requested timeout, so it is not a strict bound on execution time.

Successful enqueues signal a waiting consumer; successful dequeues signal a waiting producer. Waiters sleep using process-private Linux futexes or Windows address-based waits. A sequence snapshot taken before checking the queue prevents a notification between that check and the kernel wait from being missed. A wake only causes another queue attempt; a different worker may already have taken the available message or space. Native wait errors other than an interruption or changed sequence also produce false, so the result does not distinguish a timeout from such an error.

docs.title: 4.6.2.4 Distributing Work
docs.text:
This complete example sends jobs to one worker and then sends an explicit stop message. The worker's result is read after joining:

use threads
use print

const MSG_WORK : uint32 = 1
const MSG_STOP : uint32 = 2

object OWorker(OThread):
    channel : OMsgChannel
    total : uint64 = 0

    func *Create(achannel : OMsgChannel):
        channel = achannel
    endfunc

    func Run(arg : pointer) -> pointer [[override]]:
        use *
        var job : SChMsg
        while channel.GetWaitMillis(job, -1):
            if job.msg == MSG_STOP:
                break
            endif
            if job.msg == MSG_WORK:
                total += job.data.u64
            endif
        endwhile
        return nil
    endfunc
endobject

func *Main():
    var channel <- OMsgChannel(4) // capacity: four messages
    var worker <- OWorker(channel)
    if not worker.StartSelf(nil):
        Exit(1)
    endif
    var job : SChMsg = {msg: MSG_WORK, par.u32: 0, data.u64: 0}
    for i : int = 1 to 10:
        job.data.u64 = i
        if not channel.PutWaitMillis(job, 1000):
            Exit(1)
        endif
    endfor
    job.msg = MSG_STOP
    if not channel.PutWaitMillis(job, 1000):
        Exit(1)
    endif
    worker.Join()
    PrintLn('total = {}', [worker.total]) // 55
endfunc

Waiting on a full queue gives the producer backpressure. To use several workers, give each the same channel and enqueue one stop message per worker after all producers have finished enqueueing jobs. FIFO places those stops after the jobs; join every worker before inspecting its results or releasing the channel. Processing completion order and distribution among workers are not guaranteed.

There is no channel close, cancellation, or broadcast API. An indefinite wait needs a cooperating producer or consumer to make progress. Use finite waits if workers need to check a separate shutdown condition. Do not destroy a channel while operations or waits are still running. Channels and events operate among threads in one process, not between processes.

docs.title: 4.6.3 Atomic Values
docs.text:
Construct an atomic wrapper with its initial value, for example var flag <- OAtomicUint32(0) or var current <- OAtomicPtr(nil). All three types expose Load(), Store(value), and Exchange(value). Exchange replaces the value and returns its previous value. The integer wrappers also expose Add(value), which returns the value before addition; unsigned overflow wraps.

Load(), Store(value), Exchange(value), and Add(value) are sequentially consistent and take no memory-order argument. Loads acquire published data, stores release earlier writes, and exchanges and additions do both. These operations also participate in a single ordering across atomic variables.

All three types provide LoadRelaxed(). The integer types also provide AddRelaxed(value), which returns the value before addition and wraps on unsigned overflow, just like Add(value). For example, use counter.AddRelaxed(1) and counter.LoadRelaxed() for independent statistics. Relaxed operations remain atomic but do not synchronize other shared storage; do not use a relaxed load of a ready flag to acquire data published by another thread.

On Windows, all these operations use interlocked functions with full memory barriers, providing stronger ordering for the relaxed methods. Linux uses the method's specified ordering. Do not rely on the stronger Windows behavior in portable code.

Each method call is atomic; a sequence of calls is not a single atomic operation. Use a lock when several accesses must happen together. Atomic pointer publication still requires separate management of the pointed-to allocation's lifetime.

OAtomicUint32.Address() exposes the value's address for native address-based waits. Keep the wrapper alive while using this address, and access its value through the atomic methods.

SchedYield() -> int32 wraps sched_yield on Linux and Sleep(0) on Windows; it returns zero on Windows. Yielding does not synchronize shared data.

docs.title: 4.6.4 Spinlocks
docs.text:
OSpinLockVar inherits the atomic integer constructor. Initialize an unlocked lock with OSpinLockVar(0). Lock() acquires it, yielding while contended; Unlock() releases it. The lock is not recursive and has no timeout or fairness guarantee. Keep protected sections short.

OSpinLockHolder(lock) acquires in its constructor and releases in its destructor. An embedded local holder provides scope-based release, including early return and exception unwinding:

use threads

var lock <- OSpinLockVar(0)
var counter : int = 0

func IncrementCounter():
    var holder <- OSpinLockHolder(lock)
    ++counter
endfunc

Every concurrent access to the protected data must use the same lock. The lock must outlive all holders and users. A holder does not own the lock; explicitly delete a heap-allocated holder to release it, or use an embedded local as above.

docs.title: 4.6.5 Thread Events
docs.text:
OThreadEvent is a notification primitive used by the channel. It does not store a job or represent a persistent boolean condition.

Method Meaning Snapshot() -> uint32 read the notification sequence Signal() advance the sequence and wake at most one registered waiter WaitUntilNanos(asequence : uint32, adeadline : int64) -> bool sleep only while the sequence still matches; negative deadline means indefinite wait

For a finite deadline, pass an absolute monotonic time such as NanoTime() + 100000000 for 100 ms, with use time. true means recheck the shared condition: the thread woke, the sequence changed, or a signal interrupted the wait. false means the deadline expired or another native wait error occurred. An already-expired deadline returns false before checking for a changed sequence.

Use the event with a separately synchronized condition:

  1. Take a sequence snapshot.
  2. Check the condition under its lock or with the appropriate atomic operations.
  3. If satisfied, continue with the work.
  4. Otherwise, wait using that snapshot and the original absolute deadline.
  5. After a true result, repeat from the snapshot step.

The thread changing the condition updates it first, then calls Signal(). Taking the snapshot before checking ensures a notification in between checking and sleeping is observed. A signal before the snapshot does not count as a pending notification; the shared condition is the source of truth. Keep the event alive until every waiter and signaler has finished.

docs.title: 4.6.6 Examples and Checks
docs.text:
The source examples are in stdpkg/threads/examples/. Run these commands from the repository root:

Example Shows thread_test.dq free-function threads, a Run override, completion polling; also includes a bound-method example wait_test.dq immediate, finite, indefinite, and very large waits; unchanged output on failure; notification races and signal interruptions stress_test.dq full/empty queues, FIFO and ring wraparound, one/many producers and consumers, corruption/duplicate/missing-message checks work_distribution.dq a bounded queue feeding a worker pool, stop messages, and deterministic Monte Carlo jobs compared against one worker 
build/dq-run stdpkg/threads/examples/thread_test.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/threads/examples/wait_test.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/threads/examples/stress_test.dq -- 4 50000 256 15
build/dq-run stdpkg/threads/examples/stress_test.dq -- 4 20000 1 15 100
build/dq-run -O3 --lto stdpkg/threads/examples/work_distribution.dq -- 4 256 1000000

The stress tester's arguments are worker count, messages per producer, queue capacity, scenario timeout in seconds, and operation wait timeout in milliseconds. Defaults are the detected online processor count, 50,000 messages, capacity 256, 15 seconds, and zero (nonblocking operations). Its consumer bookkeeping uses roughly producers * consumers * messages_per_producer bytes. Exit status is 0 for success, 1 for failed checks or timeout, and 2 for invalid arguments or thread creation failure.

The work-distribution arguments are maximum workers, job count, and samples per job; defaults are the detected processor count, 256, and 1,000,000. It compares one worker with progressively larger pools, using the same work each time. Timing includes creation, dispatch, computation, and joining, with validation afterward. Use -O3 --lto for speed comparisons.

On a Linux host with llvm-mingw and Wine installed, make test-windows cross-compiles and runs thread lifecycle, atomic, event, channel capacity, wait, stress, and work-distribution checks at -O0 and -O3 --lto=full. See Windows application cross-compilation.

docs.title: 4.7. time
docs.text:
time provides wall-clock timestamps, monotonic clocks, date/time formatting, and sleeps for hosted Linux and Windows programs.

use time

docs.title: 4.7.1 Choosing a Clock
docs.text:
Function Return type Unit Use Time() float64 seconds since the Unix epoch(1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC) dates, timestamps, and wall-clock deadlines MilliTime() int64 milliseconds elapsed time and monotonic deadlines MicroTime() int64 microseconds elapsed time and monotonic deadlines NanoTime() int64 nanoseconds elapsed time and monotonic deadlines

Time() includes a fractional second. It reads the system wall clock, so clock corrections can change its value forwards or backwards. Use it when a value must correspond to a calendar date, such as a log timestamp.

The monotonic clocks have a system-defined origin unrelated to the Unix epoch. Subtract two readings from the same clock to measure a duration, or add a duration to form a deadline. Their values are unaffected by wall-clock changes; do not pass them to the date/time formatters or store them as calendar timestamps. The unit names describe the returned scale, not a guarantee of clock resolution.

docs.title: 4.7.1.1 Measuring Elapsed Time
docs.text:
use print
use time

func *Main():
    var started : int64 = MicroTime()
    SleepMillis(20) // Replace with the operation to measure.
    var elapsed : int64 = MicroTime() - started
    PrintLn('Elapsed: {} us ({:.3f} ms)', [elapsed, elapsed / 1000])
endfunc

The elapsed value can exceed the requested sleep because the operating system decides when the thread runs again.

docs.title: 4.7.2 Formatting Dates and Times
docs.text:
All three formatters take the format first and a Time()-style timestamp second:

func FormatTime1(fmt : rostr, atime : float64) -> str ..
func FormatTime2(fmt : rostr, atime : float64) -> str ..
func FormatTimeUtc(fmt : rostr, atime : float64) -> str ..
Function Time zone Format language FormatTime1 system local time Delphi-style tokens FormatTime2 system local time native strftime directives, plus %f for microseconds FormatTimeUtc UTC native strftime directives; %f is not expanded

The timestamp itself has no local-time offset. FormatTime1 and FormatTime2 apply the system's local time-zone and daylight-saving rules during conversion. FormatTimeUtc formats the same instant in UTC. None of the formatters accepts an explicit time-zone argument.

use print
use time

func *Main():
    var now : float64 = Time()
    PrintLn('Local: {}', [FormatTime1('yyyy-mm-dd hh:nn:ss.zzz', now)])
    PrintLn('Local with microseconds: {}',
            [FormatTime2('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f', now)])
    PrintLn('UTC: {}', [FormatTimeUtc('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ', now)])

    // Fixed timestamp: 2024-01-01 00:00:00 UTC.
    PrintLn(FormatTimeUtc('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S', 1704067200))
endfunc

The last line prints 2024-01-01 00:00:00 regardless of the local time zone. Only append the literal Z when formatting UTC.

docs.title: 4.7.2.1 Delphi-Style Tokens (FormatTime1)
docs.text:
Tokens are case-insensitive. Prefer nn for minutes to distinguish them from the month token mm.

Token Meaning yy, yyyy two-digit year, full year m, mm month without padding, two-digit month mmm, mmmm abbreviated month name, full month name d, dd day of month without padding, two-digit day ddd, dddd abbreviated weekday name, full weekday name ddddd locale date representation h, hh hour without padding, two-digit hour; normally 24-hour time n, nn minute without padding, two-digit minute s, ss second without padding, two-digit second z, zz, zzz milliseconds padded to at least one, two, or three digits am/pm, ampm locale AM/PM marker; switches hours to 12-hour time a/p a or p (A or P for uppercase token); switches hours to 12-hour time c locale date and time representation t, tt locale time representation

m and mm mean minutes immediately after an hour token, optionally separated by a colon: hh:mm:ss works, but hh:nn:ss is clearer. Text inside matching single or double quotes is copied literally; other characters are copied unless they form a recognized token. For example:

PrintLn(FormatTime1('yyyy-mm-dd "at" hh:nn:ss', Time()))
PrintLn(FormatTime1('hh:nn am/pm', Time()))

This is the token set implemented by DQ, rather than the entire Delphi formatting API. Name and locale tokens use the native C library. Unpadded numeric tokens use native strftime %- directives, whose support varies by platform; prefer the padded forms for portable output.

docs.title: 4.7.2.2 strftime Directives (FormatTime2 and FormatTimeUtc)
docs.text:
Directive Meaning %Y, %y full year, two-digit year %m, %d two-digit month, two-digit day of month %H, %I two-digit 24-hour hour, two-digit 12-hour hour %M, %S two-digit minute, two-digit second %a, %A abbreviated weekday name, full weekday name %b, %B abbreviated month name, full month name %p locale AM/PM marker %j day of year, padded to three digits %w weekday number, Sunday = 0 %x, %X, %c locale date, time, date and time %% literal percent sign %f six-digit microseconds; FormatTime2 only

Other directives and flags are passed to the native C library, so their support and output can differ between platforms. In particular, FormatTime2 does not implement all of Python's date/time API; it adds %f to native strftime.

Calendar conversion rounds the fractional second to the nearest microsecond, carrying into the next second when necessary. FormatTime1 then takes the millisecond part for z tokens. FormatTimeUtc outputs no fractional seconds with the directives above.

An empty format returns an empty string. Conversion failures or a native formatting result that cannot be produced within the internal buffer limit also return an empty string; the functions do not return a separate error status.

docs.title: 4.7.3 Sleeping for a Duration
docs.text:
Function Argument type Unit SleepSecs(asecs) float64 seconds; fractions are accepted SleepMillis(ams) int64 milliseconds SleepMicros(aus) int64 microseconds SleepNanos(ansecs) int64 nanoseconds

These functions block the calling thread and return no value. Zero or negative durations return immediately. SleepSecs rounds its duration to nanoseconds. On Windows, positive durations are rounded up to whole milliseconds before calling the native sleep API. On Linux, the package uses nanosleep and retries after signal interruptions with the remaining duration.

SleepSecs(0.05)   // 50 milliseconds.
SleepMillis(50)
SleepMicros(500)
SleepNanos(500000)

Actual wake-up time depends on OS timer resolution and scheduling. A nanosecond argument does not imply nanosecond scheduling accuracy. Keep durations within the int64 range after conversion to nanoseconds; conversion does not saturate on overflow.

docs.title: 4.7.4 Sleeping Until a Deadline
docs.text:
Function Deadline type Matching clock SleepToTime(asecs) float64 Time() SleepToMilliTime(ams) int64 MilliTime() SleepToMicroTime(aus) int64 MicroTime() SleepToNanoTime(ansecs) int64 NanoTime()

These functions take an absolute deadline, not a duration, and return no value. Use a reading from the matching clock plus the desired delay:

SleepToTime(Time() + 0.05)
SleepToMilliTime(MilliTime() + 50)
SleepToMicroTime(MicroTime() + 50000)
SleepToNanoTime(NanoTime() + 50000000)

A deadline already reached, or a nonpositive deadline, returns immediately. Prefer a monotonic clock for timeouts and periodic work. SleepToTime follows wall-clock time, so clock adjustments can affect the wait. Sleep functions do not expose native errors to the caller; they are not a hard real-time guarantee.

docs.title: 4.7.4.1 Periodic Work Without Accumulating Work-Time Drift
docs.text:
Advance the previous deadline by a fixed interval. Sleeping for an interval after every iteration would add each iteration's work time to the period.

use print
use time

func *Main():
    const period_ms : int64 = 100
    var deadline : int64 = MilliTime()
    for tick : int = 0 count 5:
        deadline += period_ms
        SleepToMilliTime(deadline)
        PrintLn('Tick {} at {}',
                [tick + 1, FormatTime1('hh:nn:ss.zzz', Time())])
    endfor
endfunc

The first tick is scheduled one period after the initial clock reading. If work takes longer than the period, past deadlines return immediately and this loop catches up. Applications that should skip missed ticks need an explicit policy for advancing the deadline past the current time.

docs.title: 4.7.5 Running the Examples
docs.text:
The complete programs above are also provided in stdpkg/time/examples/. Run them from the repository root:

build/dq-run stdpkg/time/examples/elapsed.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/time/examples/formatting.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/time/examples/periodic.dq

With an installed release, use dq-run in place of build/dq-run.

docs.title: 4.8. nanonet
docs.text:
nanonet is a small event-driven networking package. It currently targets the hosted socket runtime used by the project examples.

use nanonet/nano_sockets
use nanonet/nano_http

docs.title: 4.8.1 Sockets
docs.text:
nano_sockets provides non-blocking TCP/UDP sockets, an event watcher, and a server/connection framework.

Type Purpose ONanoSocket low-level socket wrapper OSocketWatcher event loop around platform socket events OSConnection base server-side connection object ONanoServer listener and connection manager ENanoNet socket/server exception

Server connections are object types derived from OSConnection. Override HandleInput and optionally HandleOutput.

object OMyConnection(OSConnection):
    func HandleInput(aobj : Object) [[override]]
endobject

func OMyConnection.HandleInput(aobj : Object) [[override]]:
    var buf : [256]byte
    var n : int = sock.Recv(%buf[0], SizeOf(buf))
    if n <= 0:
        Close()
    endif
endfunc

Create a server with the connection type and listen port:

var svr <- ONanoServer(OMyConnection, 8080)
svr.InitListener()
while true:
    svr.WaitForEvents(1000)
endwhile

docs.title: 4.8.2 HTTP
docs.text:
nano_http builds an HTTP request/response layer on top of nano_sockets.

Type Purpose OStrMap simple string map used for headers, query values, cookies OSConnectionHttp HTTP connection base class ONanoHttpServer HTTP server with content-type map

Override ProcessRequest() to handle dynamic responses:

object OConn(OSConnectionHttp):
    func ProcessRequest() -> bool [[override]]
endobject

func OConn.ProcessRequest() -> bool [[override]]:
    response_headers["Content-Type"] = "text/plain"
    response = "hello"
    return true
endfunc

Important request fields on OSConnectionHttp include:

Field Meaning method request method, uppercase uri path without query string url original request URL getstr raw query string http_ver HTTP version text keep_alive connection reuse flag ucheaders request headers with uppercase keys qsvars parsed query string values cookies parsed cookie values

Response fields:

Field Meaning response_code status code, default 200 response_headers output headers response in-memory response body full_content_length length for streamed file responses

docs.title: 4.8.3 Static Files
docs.text:
HandleStaticFiles(root) serves files below a directory and rejects unsafe .. paths.

func OConn.ProcessRequest() -> bool [[override]]:
    if HandleStaticFiles("public"):
        return true
    endif
    response_code = 404
    response = "not found"
    return true
endfunc

The HTTP server maps common extensions such as .html, .css, .js, .png, .jpg, .svg, and .ico to content types. Unknown extensions use application/octet-stream.

See the examples in examples/nanonet/, especially http_static_files.dq.

docs.title: 4.9. shell
docs.text:
shell runs child processes, captures their output, supplies standard input, and reads or updates environment variables.

use shell

The package supports hosted Linux and x86_64 Windows. Linux uses fork, execvp, and poll; Windows uses Unicode CreateProcessW, redirected pipes, and job objects. Both use threads for background execution. Windows stdin is fed by a separate writer thread so large input cannot block output capture.

docs.title: 4.9.1 Running Commands
docs.text:
Create an OShellRunner and use Run for a foreground command:

use print
use shell

func *Main():
    var runner <- OShellRunner()
#ifdef WINDOWS
    var code : int = runner.Run('echo hello& echo warning >&2& exit /b 7', false)
#else
    var code : int = runner.Run('printf hello; printf warning >&2; exit 7', false)
#endif
    PrintLn('exit: {}', [code])
    PrintLn('stdout: {}', [runner.out])
    PrintLn('stderr: {}', [runner.err])

    // Argument arrays launch an executable directly.
#ifdef WINDOWS
    runner.RunWithInput(['sort'], 'pear\napple\n')
#else
    runner.Run(['printf', '%s', 'literal $HOME; *.dq'])
#endif
    PrintLn(runner.out)

    try:
#ifdef WINDOWS
        runner.Run('exit /b 3')
#else
        runner.Run('exit 3')
#endif
    except EShellResult as e:
        PrintLn('Caught exit {}: {}', [e.code, e.message])
    endtry
endfunc

The first command returns 7, with hello in out and warning in err (including the newlines written by Windows echo). The direct-execution example sorts input on Windows and prints a literal argument on Linux. The last command demonstrates the default exception behavior for a nonzero exit code.

docs.title: 4.9.1.1 Command Strings and Argument Arrays
docs.text:
Each command-starting method has two overloads:

Argument Execution acmd : rostr run through the platform's command interpreter; shell quoting, expansion, pipes, and redirection apply args : []rostr execute args[0] with the remaining elements as individual arguments

On Linux, command strings run through /bin/sh -c. On Windows, they use COMSPEC (falling back to cmd.exe) with /d /s /c: AutoRun commands are disabled, and the command's own quoting is preserved. Shell syntax differs: use ; and $NAME on Linux, versus & and %NAME% in Windows command strings. Windows built-ins such as dir, and .bat or .cmd scripts, need a command string. PowerShell is not selected automatically.

For argument arrays, Linux searches PATH for names without a slash. Windows uses the native CreateProcessW executable search and .exe suffix rules. An explicit executable path avoids the search. The child inherits the caller's working directory and environment; there is no per-command directory or environment option.

Use argument arrays for values that should be passed literally. A filename with spaces is one array element and needs no additional quoting. In an argument array, |, >, *, and $HOME are ordinary arguments unless the executable itself interprets them. Windows arguments are encoded using the usual C runtime quoting rules: empty values, spaces, embedded quotes, and trailing backslashes are preserved. Programs with their own command-line parsers can differ; use command strings for cmd.exe syntax. Executable names, arguments, and environment names/values are converted between DQ's UTF-8 strings and Windows UTF-16 APIs.

docs.title: 4.9.2 Foreground API
docs.text:
Method Behavior Run(acmd : rostr, exitcerr : bool = true) -> int execute a shell command and wait Run(args : []rostr, exitcerr : bool = true) -> int execute an argument array and wait RunWithInput(acmd : rostr, ainput : strslice, exitcerr : bool = true) -> int execute a shell command with supplied stdin and wait RunWithInput(args : []rostr, ainput : strslice, exitcerr : bool = true) -> int execute an argument array with supplied stdin and wait

These calls collect output while the child runs and return its exit code after monitoring finishes. By default, a nonzero result raises EShellResult instead of returning normally. Pass false as exitcerr when nonzero exit codes are expected and inspect the returned value yourself. This only suppresses exit-code exceptions; process-start errors can still raise EShellStart. Calling a runner while it is busy returns -1 without replacing the running command's state.

docs.title: 4.9.2.1 Captured Results
docs.text:
Field Type Meaning after completion out str captured standard output err str captured standard error output str both streams merged in the monitor's pipe-read order exitcode int process exit status; -1 for Linux signal termination, Windows Kill(), or an unavailable result finished bool initially true; set to false for a new run and true when monitoring finishes

A new run clears all three output strings and sets exitcode to -1. Output is captured as bytes without encoding or newline conversion. A Windows child can produce CRLF or a different text encoding from a Linux child; the runner does not normalize or decode it. Nothing is printed automatically: use Print or PrintLn to display the captured strings. The fields remain available when a foreground call raises EShellResult.

output does not guarantee the original write order across stdout and stderr. The streams use separate pipes, and reads can combine multiple writes or split them into chunks. The package does not provide a streaming callback or an output-size limit; it keeps the complete captures in memory. Since the child writes to pipes, its buffering can differ from an interactive terminal.

docs.title: 4.9.3 Supplying Standard Input
docs.text:
Run and StartBg leave stdin inherited from the caller. A command waiting for input can therefore block. Their WithInput variants supply a pipe instead: the input is copied into runner-owned storage, sent while output is drained, and the pipe is closed after all input has been written. An empty input string provides EOF without supplying any bytes.

use print
use shell

func *Main():
    var runner <- OShellRunner()
    runner.RunWithInput(['sort'], 'pear\napple\n')
    PrintLn('Sorted input:\n{}', [runner.out])

    runner.RunWithInput(['sort'], '')
    PrintLn('Empty input produced {} bytes', [runner.out.length])
endfunc

The same input mechanism is available through StartBgWithInput for background commands. The package offers one input string per run, rather than an interactive stdin-writing API. Supply input to commands that consume it; the API does not report how many input bytes the child actually accepted.

docs.title: 4.9.4 Background Commands
docs.text:
Method Behavior StartBg(acmd : rostr) -> int start a shell command and a monitor thread StartBg(args : []rostr) -> int start an executable and a monitor thread StartBgWithInput(acmd : rostr, ainput : strslice) -> int start a shell command with supplied stdin StartBgWithInput(args : []rostr, ainput : strslice) -> int start an executable with supplied stdin Finished() -> bool poll completion and try to reap the monitor thread WaitFinishMs(ams : int) -> bool poll for completion for up to the requested milliseconds Kill() terminate the process group (Linux) or job (Windows), then wait up to 2000 ms for completion Join() inherited from OThread; wait for and reap the monitor thread without a timeout

The start methods return 0 when the process and monitor thread were started, or -1 if the runner is busy or the monitor thread cannot be started. They can also raise EShellStart. A successful start returns neither a PID nor the child's exit code. Background completion does not raise EShellResult; inspect exitcode after waiting.

use print
use shell

func *Main():
    var runner <- OShellRunner()
#ifdef WINDOWS
    var command : rostr = 'echo finished'
#else
    var command : rostr = 'sleep 0.05; printf finished'
#endif
    if runner.StartBg(command) <> 0:
        PrintLn('Could not start background command')
        Exit(1)
    endif

    // Other work can run here while the command executes.
    if not runner.WaitFinishMs(1000):
        PrintLn('Timed out; stopping the command')
        runner.Kill()
    endif
    runner.Join()
    PrintLn('exit: {}, stdout: {}', [runner.exitcode, runner.out])

    if runner.StartBgWithInput(['sort'], 'pear\napple\n') <> 0:
        Exit(1)
    endif
    runner.Join()
    PrintLn(runner.out)
endfunc

WaitFinishMs uses a monotonic deadline and sleeps in 10 ms intervals. It returns true when completion is observed and false when the deadline is reached. Zero or negative values make an immediate completion check; a negative value does not mean wait indefinitely. Scheduling and polling can delay the return beyond the requested duration. A timeout leaves the command running.

docs.title: 4.9.4.1 Lifetime and Cleanup
docs.text:
Use one runner for one command at a time. Wait for and join a background run before reading its output, reusing the runner for a foreground call, or destroying the runner. Treat the public result fields as read-only, and do not inspect or change the strings while the monitor thread is writing them. Manage the runner from one controlling thread.

OShellRunner has no destructor that automatically kills or joins a running command. Join() is the simplest way to wait indefinitely; for a bounded wait, use WaitFinishMs, handle a timeout explicitly, and join before releasing the object.

Kill() is forceful termination, with no graceful shutdown phase. On Linux it sends SIGKILL to the process group created for the child; a descendant that leaves that group can escape the kill. On Windows, the child is created suspended and assigned to a job before it runs, so Kill() terminates the job's process tree, including descendants. Windows termination uses status 0xFFFFFFFF, which the runner maps to -1; other Windows exit statuses are returned as their unsigned 32-bit values.

Kill() returns no success status, and its internal wait is bounded; use Join() to finish cleanup. Descendants keeping captured pipe ends open can postpone completion after the original child exits, because monitoring drains the pipes before collecting the exit result. Windows process and job handles are retained until reuse or destruction to avoid racing termination against handle cleanup.

docs.title: 4.9.5 Errors
docs.text:
Exception When it is used EShellStart empty command or executable, or failure to set up pipes or create the process; Windows job/handle setup failures also use this exception EShellResult foreground command finishes with a nonzero result and exitcerr is true

Both derive from Exception and expose its message field. EShellResult also has code : int, matching the runner's exit result. Its constructors accept either (acode : int, amsg : rostr) or (acode : int, afmt : strslice, avalues : []anyvalue).

On Linux, failure to execute a program after the fork is reported by the child: it writes a diagnostic to captured stderr and exits with 127, producing EShellResult by default in foreground execution. Windows CreateProcessW failure instead raises EShellStart, including the native error number. If the interpreter starts but cannot find a command, its own exit code and diagnostic are captured on either platform. A failed process launch leaves the runner available for reuse. The API does not separately report all native read, write, or wait failures.

docs.title: 4.9.6 Environment Variables
docs.text:
func GetEnv(name : rostr, default_value : rostr) -> str ..
func SetEnv(name : rostr, value : rostr) ..

GetEnv returns a copy of the variable's value, or default_value if the variable is absent. An existing empty value remains empty. SetEnv creates or overwrites a variable in the current process and raises Exception if the native update fails. There is no unset function in this package. Windows environment names are case-insensitive; Linux names are case-sensitive.

use print
use shell

func *Main():
    PrintLn('HOME: {}', [GetEnv('HOME', '(not set)')])
    SetEnv('DQ_SHELL_EXAMPLE', 'hello from DQ')
    PrintLn('Current process: {}', [GetEnv('DQ_SHELL_EXAMPLE', '')])

    var runner <- OShellRunner()
#ifdef WINDOWS
    runner.Run('echo %DQ_SHELL_EXAMPLE%')
#else
    runner.Run('printf "%s" "$DQ_SHELL_EXAMPLE"')
#endif
    PrintLn('Child process: {}', [runner.out])
endfunc

Environment changes apply to the current process and children started afterward; they do not change the parent shell or an already-running child. Since the environment is process-wide, perform setup before launching worker threads or coordinate concurrent access yourself.

docs.title: 4.9.7 Running the Examples
docs.text:
The complete programs above are available in stdpkg/shell/examples/. From the repository root:

build/dq-run stdpkg/shell/examples/capture.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/shell/examples/input.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/shell/examples/background.dq
build/dq-run stdpkg/shell/examples/environment.dq

With an installed release, use dq-run in place of build/dq-run. On Windows, the built tool path is build\dq-run.exe. The examples select platform-specific shell commands with #ifdef WINDOWS and use the system's sort executable for stdin demonstrations. Linux command strings also use printf and sleep.

docs.title: 4.10. Additional Standard Packages
docs.text:
The following modules are also shipped in stdpkg. They have focused source interfaces and examples rather than separate API manuals. Check each module's public declarations for exact signatures and supported platforms.

For timestamps, date/time formatting, and sleeps, see the dedicated time package manual. For child processes and environment variables, see the shell package manual.

Import Purpose Source or example math Mathematical functions backed by the native math library. math.dq strparse Cursor-based text parsing. test_strparse.dq collections/strstrmap String-to-string map. strstrmap.dq db Shared database abstractions. db.dq sqlite3 SQLite binding using the SQLite library. sqlite_test.dq mysql MySQL client binding. mysql_test.dq socket Low-level socket declarations. socket.dq libc/stdio C standard I/O declarations and stream helpers. stdio.dq

docs.title: 4.10.1 Native Dependencies
docs.text:
A DQ import supplies declarations and code; it does not install a native library. Database applications need the matching client development libraries at link time and the corresponding shared libraries at runtime. For cross targets, the libraries must match the target ABI and be available in the selected sysroot or linker search paths.

Use C Interoperability when adding bindings, and Project Files for explicit linker inputs. For networking applications, start with the higher-level nanonet package.

docs.title: 5.1. Example Programs
docs.text: The repository contains small focused examples and larger demonstrations.

See the time package documentation for clock selection, formatting tokens, and sleep behavior.

Example Shows stdpkg/time/examples/elapsed.dq measuring a duration with a monotonic clock stdpkg/time/examples/formatting.dq local and UTC timestamps, milliseconds and microseconds stdpkg/time/examples/periodic.dq periodic work using absolute deadlines

Example Shows stdpkg/shell/examples/capture.dq stdout/stderr capture, argument arrays, and exit-code handling stdpkg/shell/examples/input.dq supplying stdin and closing it with EOF stdpkg/shell/examples/background.dq background execution, timeouts, and cleanup stdpkg/shell/examples/environment.dq reading, setting, and inheriting environment variables
